v db — User Guide

Note

Hand-written, not generated — the words are v-db’s, from docs/guides/v-db-user-guide.md. What this site guarantees about them is coverage, not correctness.

The complete command surface of the v db domain: what each verb does, what it guarantees, and a worked example of every one of them proven on a live VistA instance.

Version covered: v-db v0.1.0 (contract 1.0), engine half VSL*1.0*39 (the M9 build — the RPC face and its post-install shipped 2026-08-09; the CLI verb surface is unchanged from VSL*1.0*37). Every transcript below was produced on vehu (YottaDB VistA) or foia (IRIS VistA) on 2026-08-09 and is reproducible with the commands as printed.

1. What v db is

Section titled “1. What v db is”

v db is a command-line client for VistA’s database.

That sentence is doing a lot of work, so unpack it. VistA is the US Department of Veterans Affairs’ electronic health record — a MUMPS system that has been running continuously since the early 1980s and still carries the care of millions of patients. Its database is not Postgres, not Oracle, not anything with a SELECT statement. It is a hierarchical tree managed by a 1978-vintage DBMS called VA FileMan, and until now the ways to reach it were: a terminal-menu UI, a MUMPS programmer API, raw access to the storage tree, or a set of remote procedure calls built for Delphi client applications.

v db adds one more: a modern CLI. Verbs you can guess, flags you can discover with --help, JSON on stdout, real exit codes, and — the part that matters most — an answer that tells you how complete it is.

If you have never touched VistA, you are not missing prerequisites. Read section 2; it maps every piece of VistA vocabulary onto something you already know, and after it the rest of this guide is just a database CLI.

What it covers

Section titled “What it covers”

v db is the FileMan domain of the v CLI — VistA’s dictionary and its data, reachable from a shell or from a script. (The same engine-side data plane is also reachable by VistA client applications over the RPC Broker — see 7.8; this guide’s verbs are the CLI face of it.)

It has two sides:

  • the dictionary side — walk files, fields, cross-references and structure (schema, indexes, refs, census), and get it off the engine as an artifact (export, estimate);
  • the data side — a read spine (rows, get, count, find, distribution, fields-profile) and a gated write plane (put, edit, delete, reindex, text).

One property runs through all of it and is the reason the domain exists: every read answer carries a completeness block that says how the answer was computed and what stopped it. There is no flag to turn that off.

v db is the Go host. It holds no VistA knowledge of its own: it consumes the VSLDD (dictionary walk), VSLROW (read/write spine) and VSLPOL (authorization) modules shipped in v-stdlib, and reaches the engine only over the m-driver-sdk seam — the org’s single transport artifact.

How to read this guide

Section titled “How to read this guide”
if you are… start at
new to VistA 2 — the database in familiar terms
a VistA hand who wants the rationale 3 — how it was managed before
looking for the equivalent of a query you already know 4 — commands in familiar terms
after one picture that puts it all together the master map — every verb drawn on the tree it touches
ready to run something 5 — getting started
debugging a surprising answer 6.1 — the completeness block and 9 — troubleshooting
looking up a flag 7 — command reference and 10 — reference

One sentence on why this exists, for readers who want it before the detail: the legacy generic read path answers from whichever index it happened to traverse, which is not the same thing as the file — measured across 15 ground-truthed files it under-reports to as little as 62.5% of the file, over-reports by emitting records twice, and on one 855,565-record file returns zero rows with zero errors. None of it is signalled, so a caller cannot tell a complete answer from a broken one. v db walks the file itself and publishes what it did. That is the whole idea; everything else is consequence.

2. VistA’s database, in terms you already know

Section titled “2. VistA’s database, in terms you already know”

If you have used any database before, you already know most of what follows — it is just wearing unfamiliar clothes. This section hands you the translation, because every noun in the command reference comes from here, and the commands make very little sense until the shape does.

2.1 The shape: one enormous tree

Section titled “2.1 The shape: one enormous tree”

Most databases you have met are made of flat tables and are queried with a language that plans its own execution. VistA is neither.

Underneath everything, VistA is one gigantic persistent tree — a sparse, sorted, on-disk nested dictionary. In MUMPS (the language VistA is written in) these trees are called globals, and a global reference looks like this:

Those three values are real — patient 1 on vehu, whose stored .01, .02 and .03 you can read back through the API at 2.6 (2350407 is a FileMan internal date: year offset from 1700, so 1935-04-07). The exact piece positions are a per-field property recorded in the data dictionary as node;piece, which v db schema and v db export now carry per field as storageLocation (VSL*1.0*65) — so the layout above is the shape, and the byte map is a read away.

The shape is the point, though, and it has a consequence you will meet again in 8.14: several fields share one string, delimited by ^, with no escaping. A ^ inside a value does not get quoted — it becomes a new piece boundary, and the record silently means something different.

The closest thing in a modern stack is a persistent, ordered key–value store whose keys are tuples — think a giant SortedDict keyed by ("DPT", 1, 0) that survives restarts, or a filesystem where every directory can also hold a value. Three properties matter and are worth internalising before anything else:

  • Sorted. You can always ask “what is the next key after this one”, which is the operation VistA is built out of. ($ORDER, in MUMPS.)
  • Sparse. A node exists only if something was stored there. There is no fixed row width and no NULL-padding; absence is the default.
  • Schema-less at the storage layer. The tree itself does not know that ^DPT(1,0) holds a name, a sex code and a birth date crammed into one string separated by ^ characters. Something else has to know that.

That “something else” is FileMan.

FileMan is VistA’s database management system — the layer that gives the tree a schema, a type system, validation, indexes, and an API. It is the counterpart to a relational engine’s catalog + query layer, except that it sits on top of storage that other code can also reach directly. Every VistA application is written against FileMan; the tree underneath is FileMan’s business.

So: the tree is the disk; FileMan is the database.

2.2 The tree, drawn

Section titled “2.2 The tree, drawn”

Two pictures. The first is the whole database; the second is one record.

Every file lives in the same namespace. There are no separate databases, schemas or tablespaces — each file simply owns a subtree, and the subtree it owns is recorded in its data dictionary entry as the global root:

Note the two on the left. ^DD holds the schema — every field name, type, pointer target and index definition in the system — and ^DIC holds #1 FILE, the catalog of files, which is itself an ordinary file. VistA describes itself, in its own data model, in the same tree as the data. That is what lets a generic tool walk an instance it has never seen.

The diagram draws the five as siblings for clarity, but roots can nest: #1 FILE is at ^DIC( and #19 OPTION is at ^DIC(19, — so the OPTION file physically lives inside the catalog’s own subtree. A global root is just an address, and nothing requires two files’ addresses to be disjoint.

Now one record, exploded. This is #2 PATIENT on vehu:

Four things that picture is trying to tell you, in rising order of importance:

  1. A record is a subtree, not a row. It has no fixed width. Fields are packed several-to-a-node and read by position, which is why a ^ inside a value is not an escaping problem but a structural one — it creates a boundary that was not there (8.14).
  2. A sub-file is physically inside its parent. #2.01 ALIAS is a real file with its own fields and its own B index, but no global root — its rows hang off the record they belong to. There is no join because there was never a separation. On vehu, 671 patients have exactly one alias, 12 have two, and one has three.
  3. The two orders are different, and the picture shows it. Records sit in IEN order; the B index sits in name order. Its first two entries on vehu are ALPHATEST,NEW ONE → 100841 and ANOTHER,CLONE → 101042 — alphabetically first, numerically nowhere near the front. Walking the index and walking the file visit the same records in completely different sequences, which is why a cursor for one is not a cursor for the other. Gaps are normal too: #3.1’s records run 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 9 — never iterate 1..n.
  4. ⚠️ The index is a sibling of the data, not a view of it. "B" sits under the same root as records 1, 2 and 3 — but it is a separate structure, written by code that fires when a field changes. If that code did not run, ran twice, or was added after the data landed, the index and the records disagree. Nothing about reading the index reveals this.

That last point is the whole reason this domain exists, and the diagram makes it physical. The two things you can walk are not the same thing:

The legacy generic read path walks the second and reports it as though it were the first. v db walks whichever you asked for and stamps which one answered on every page — that is the population line you will see in every transcript from here on.

What is measured here, and what is drawn. Measured live on vehu today: the global roots and record counts of all five files above; that #2.01 ALIAS is a sub-file of #2 with an empty global root, three fields and a B cross-reference; the ALIAS depth distribution (671/12/1); IEN 1’s stored .01, .02 and .03 values; and the first two B-index entries with the IENs they resolve to. Drawn as FileMan’s standard layout, not measured: the exact node subscripts for the multiple and the index, and the piece positions within the 0 node. A field’s real storage location is recorded in the data dictionary as node;piece, varies per field, and is surfaced per field as storageLocation (VSL*1.0*65) — so this drawing can be checked against v db schema 2.

2.3 An analogy: the records room

Section titled “2.3 An analogy: the records room”

FileMan was designed in the late 1970s for people who had spent their careers running a hospital medical-records room, and it shows — in a good way. The analogy is not a teaching aid bolted on afterwards; it is the actual design. Hold it in your head and almost every quirk becomes predictable.

in the records room in VistA in a modern database
a filing cabinet, with a number stencilled on it a file (#2) a table
a numbered folder in that cabinet a record, identified by its IEN a row, identified by its primary key
a pre-printed form inside the folder, with numbered lines the file’s fields columns
line 1 of every form: the patient’s name field .01 the natural-key / name column
a continuation sheet stapled inside the folder a multiple / sub-file a child table — but physically nested inside the parent
writing “see cabinet 11, folder 2” instead of copying the text a pointer a foreign key
the card catalogue by patient name at the front of the room a cross-reference (index) an index
the master list of what every cabinet contains the data dictionary (^DD) information_schema / the system catalog
the clerk who knows the forms, checks your handwriting, and refuses a bad date FileMan the DBMS

The room has one more property that turns out to be the crux of this whole guide: the card catalogue is not the cabinet. If a card was never filed, or was filed twice, the catalogue disagrees with the drawer — and looking things up through the catalogue will never tell you so. Hold on to that; it is 3.4.

2.4 Files — the cabinets

Section titled “2.4 Files — the cabinets”

A file is VistA’s table. The first thing to know is the thing that surprises everyone:

Files are identified by number, not by name. #2 is the patient file. The number is the identity; the name is a label that could in principle change.

Those numbers are assigned nationally, so #2 is PATIENT at every VA site in the country. They are also hierarchical by convention — related files cluster in a numeric neighbourhood, and a sub-file’s number extends its parent’s (#2.025 lives under #2).

Read that line as: the table called PATIENT is table number 2, its rows live in the tree ^DPT(, it has 594 columns, and 379 other tables have a foreign key into it. A production VistA carries thousands of them: vehu’s dictionary walk covers 8,262 files and sub-files, of which 2,919 are top-level entries listed in #1.

Four you will meet constantly:

file name tree records on vehu what it is
#1 FILE ^DIC( 2,919 the file of files — the catalog, itself a file
#2 PATIENT ^DPT( 1,755 the master patient record
#200 NEW PERSON ^VA(200, 1,496 every user, provider and staff member
#19 OPTION ^DIC(19, 13,198 the menu/option tree — VistA’s application registry

#1 is worth a pause. VistA’s catalog is not a special system view outside the data model; it is an ordinary FileMan file that you can read with the same verbs as any other. That self-description is why a generic tool like v db can exist at all.

2.5 Records and IENs — the folders and their numbers

Section titled “2.5 Records and IENs — the folders and their numbers”

A record’s identity is its IEN — Internal Entry Number. It is the primary key, and it is what the tree is subscripted by: ^DPT(1,…) is patient 1.

Four things about IENs that will bite you if you assume otherwise:

  • They are per-file. IEN 2 in #11 and IEN 2 in #2 are unrelated. An IEN is only meaningful paired with its file number.
  • They are allocated ascending, but not densely. Deletions leave holes. Never assume 1..n:
  • They are not always integers. .5 is a real IEN in #200 (it is POSTMASTER). This is why v db get treats the IEN as a byte-exact string and not a number — .5 and 0.5 are different keys.
  • ⚠️ They are site-local and not portable. Patient 1 here is a different human from patient 1 at the next VA hospital. An IEN is a physical address within one instance, never an identifier you may carry across systems or store in an export. (The portable identity is the .01 value, or a genuine national identifier where one exists.)

2.6 Fields — the lines on the form

Section titled “2.6 Fields — the lines on the form”

Fields are numbered too, and like file numbers the number is the identity. Field numbers are decimals, they are not contiguous, and their order is historical rather than meaningful — #2 has fields .01, .02, .03, .05, .09 and 991.01.

Field .01 is special and always exists: it is the record’s name — the natural key, the thing the default index is built on, and the value FileMan will show you when something points at this record. In the records-room analogy it is line 1 of the form.

Real fields from #2 PATIENT, live:

That typeSpec column is FileMan’s compact type language, and it is worth being able to read at a glance:

letter means modern equivalent
R required NOT NULL
F free text VARCHAR
N numeric NUMERIC
D date/time DATE / TIMESTAMP
S set of codes ENUM — the codes follow, M:MALE;F:FEMALE;
P<n> pointer to file n REFERENCES <table>
V variable pointer a polymorphic foreign key
W word processing TEXT / CLOB, stored as a line array
C computed a generated / virtual column
X has an input transform a CHECK constraint + parser on the column
O outputs through a transform a display formatter
a audited change-data-capture on that column
' (on a pointer) no LAYGO the FK will not create its target

So RP11'a reads: required · pointer to file #11 · may not create a new target · audited. And RDXOa reads: required · date · validated on input · formatted on output · audited.

Values have two forms, and the difference is not cosmetic. FileMan stores an internal value and renders an external one:

A command pair, and the whole model is visible: .02 is stored as the enum code M and rendered MALE; .05 is stored as the bare number 2, which is an IEN in file #11 — and file #11’s record 2 has .01 = "MARRIED":

That is a foreign-key join, resolved for you, and it is what --tier external (the default) buys. Keep the distinction in mind, because v db’s filters run against the internal value — --where '.05 = 2' matches, --where '.05 = MARRIED' does not (7.4).

2.7 Hierarchy — multiples and sub-files

Section titled “2.7 Hierarchy — multiples and sub-files”

Here is where VistA departs from the relational model for real.

When a patient can have several addresses, a relational schema gives you a second table with a foreign key back. FileMan instead lets a field contain a whole table. Such a field is a multiple, and the table it contains is a sub-file with its own file number:

A sub-file is a real file with real fields — and it knows its parent, and it has no global root of its own, because it does not live anywhere independently:

That empty globalRoot is the entire point: the child rows are physically inside the parent’s subtree. There is no join to perform because there was never a separation. Sub-files nest arbitrarily deep — a multiple inside a multiple inside a multiple is ordinary VistA.

Because a sub-record’s identity is the path to it, addressing one takes more than an IEN. That address is the IENS, written innermost-first and always comma-terminated:

IENS means
42, top-level record 42
1,42, sub-record 1, inside record 42
3,1,42, sub-sub-record 3, inside sub-record 1, inside record 42
+1, “a new record” — used when creating
+1,42, a new sub-record under record 42

You will pass IENS strings to v db edit, delete and text. The trailing comma is not decoration — an IENS without it is refused.

2.8 Pointers — a folder number instead of a copy

Section titled “2.8 Pointers — a folder number instead of a copy”

A pointer field is a foreign key: it stores the target record’s IEN, and FileMan resolves it on the way out. #2’s .05 MARITAL STATUS is P11' — points at file #11.

Two variants worth knowing:

  • Variable pointer (V) — a polymorphic foreign key: the field may point into any one of several files, and the stored value carries which. The modern analogue is a (type, id) pair collapsed into one column.
  • DINUM — a file whose records take the same IEN as the record they point at. It is the FileMan idiom for a strict 1:1 extension table: “row N of this file is by definition about patient N.” v db schema reports it as dinum: true, and v db put refuses such files outright, because every way FileMan offers to create one was measured defective.

Pointers are also how you find a file’s blast radius. pointerIn counts the files pointing at this one, and it is the number to look at before you touch anything:

1,244 files point at #200 NEW PERSON. That is what “load-bearing” means in VistA, and it is not something FileMan surfaces conveniently — which is why schema computes it.

2.9 Cross-references — the card catalogue

Section titled “2.9 Cross-references — the card catalogue”

A cross-reference is an index: a secondary tree, maintained as data changes, that maps a value to the IENs holding it. By near-universal convention the index on .01 is called B — so “the B index” means “the by-name index,” on every file in VistA.

Indexes are what make lookup fast, and v db find walks one directly. But an index is a separate structure from the data, maintained by code that runs when a field changes — and code can fail to run, run twice, or have been added after the data. So an index can be incomplete, or can hold an entry twice, and nothing about reading it tells you which.

This is the records-room point again: the card catalogue is not the cabinet. It is the single most important thing to understand about VistA data access, it is the reason v db distinguishes find from rows, and it is the reason every read answer states which population it came from:

  • population index:B — this answer is the catalogue’s.
  • population file — this answer is the drawer’s, walked directly.

2.10 Where it physically lives — globals and the data dictionary

Section titled “2.10 Where it physically lives — globals and the data dictionary”

Two trees, side by side:

  • The data lives at the file’s global root — ^DPT( for #2, ^VA(200, for #200. Within a record, values are packed into nodes as ^-separated pieces: ^DPT(1,0) holds name, sex, date of birth and more in one string. This is where the ^ character earns its reputation — a ^ inside a value would split the node and silently corrupt the record, which is why v db refuses one at the door (8.14).
  • The schema lives in ^DD — the data dictionary. Field names, types, pointer targets, input transforms, index definitions: all of it is data in a tree, readable at runtime. v db schema is a structured read of ^DD.

That the schema is itself queryable data is the property everything in this domain rests on. A generic tool can walk any VistA file on any instance without being told anything in advance, because the instance can be asked.

2.11 The translation table

Section titled “2.11 The translation table”

The whole vocabulary in one place:

VistA / FileMan what it means closest modern term
file (#2) a collection of like records table
file number the file’s identity table identity (numeric, national)
record / entry one item row
IEN internal entry number primary key — site-local, never portable
IENS (1,42,) the path to a record or sub-record composite / hierarchical key
field (.01) one datum on a record column
.01 field the name field, always present natural key / display name
multiple a field containing many values one-to-many child relation
sub-file (#2.025) the table inside a multiple child table, physically nested
pointer (P11) stores another record’s IEN foreign key
variable pointer (V) points into one of several files polymorphic foreign key
DINUM shares its parent’s IEN 1:1 extension keyed by the parent
set of codes (S) a closed value list ENUM
word-processing field (W) multi-line text, stored per line TEXT / CLOB
computed field (C) evaluated on read generated / virtual column
input transform (X) code validating a value on write CHECK constraint
cross-reference / B index value → IEN index index / the default name index
screen a filter, expressed as executable M a WHERE clause — but arbitrary code
LAYGO “Learn As You GO” — create if absent upsert / find-or-create
global (^DPT() the persistent tree data lives in the physical storage / tablespace
^DD the data dictionary information_schema / system catalog
file #1 the file of files the catalog table
FileMan schema + validation + CRUD + indexes the DBMS
DBS (^DIC, ^DIE, ^DIQ) FileMan’s programmer API the driver / client library
DDR RPCs the generic remote data API a generic REST/ORM data endpoint
Kernel sign-on, users, keys, scheduling the OS + auth layer
KIDS ships code and data between systems the package manager / migration tool
^ the piece separator inside a node a field delimiter — with no escaping

2.12 Where the analogy breaks

Section titled “2.12 Where the analogy breaks”

Every analogy has an edge, and running into these at speed is how people form wrong expectations about VistA. Four to hold on to:

  1. There is no query language and no planner. Nothing takes a declarative request and decides how to execute it. You choose the access path — walk the file, or walk a named index — and that choice is the plan. This is why v db makes you say rows or find, and why it reports which one answered.
  2. There are no joins. A pointer is resolved one record at a time, on demand. Nothing assembles a result set across files. If you need data from two files, you read two files.
  3. COUNT(*) is not free. There is no maintained row count. Every file header carries a number, but it is a claim that maintenance code updates — and it drifts. v db count walks the file to answer honestly, which is why it prints walked and claimed side by side, and why on #757.02 those differ by 167.
  4. The storage layer is reachable without the schema. Nothing physically stops code from reading and writing ^DPT( directly, bypassing every type, transform and index FileMan would have applied. Plenty of VistA code does. This is the deep reason a database “constraint” in VistA is a convention enforced by a layer, not an invariant enforced by storage.

None of this is criticism. It is a design from 1978 that has run a national health system for four decades, and its priorities — self-describing schema, data that outlives the code, no dependency on a commercial engine — were the right ones. But if you arrive expecting Postgres, you will misread what you see.

3. How VistA’s database was managed — and why v db exists

Section titled “3. How VistA’s database was managed — and why v db exists”

Section 2 described the database. This section describes what it was like to use — first the four established paths and what they have in common, then a close reading of the one v db most directly replaces.

It is a condensed reading of the accepted proposal, The v db data plane (accepted 2026-08-07, decisions VD-D1…VD-D48). Almost every flag in the command reference exists as a direct answer to something measured here, which is the reason to read it before the reference rather than after. §N references below are sections of that effort’s measurement basis.

3.1 Four ways in, all of them insider work

Section titled “3.1 Four ways in, all of them insider work”

Before v db, reaching VistA data meant picking one of four paths. Each is still there, and each is still legitimate — this is context, not indictment.

1. FileMan’s own menus (roll-and-scroll). VistA ships an interactive, terminal-menu front end to its own database: Enter or Edit File Entries, Print File Entries, Search File Entries, Inquire to File Entries. It is complete, it validates everything, and it is genuinely well designed for the job it was built for — a clerk at a terminal. It is also modal, keyboard-driven, unscriptable, and it answers one question per session.

2. FileMan’s programmer API (the DBS). The supported way for VistA code to touch data: DIC for lookup, DIE for edits, DIQ for retrieval, DIK for indexes. GETS^DIQ fetches fields; FILE^DIE and UPDATE^DIE write; LIST^DIC lists. It is powerful and it is the correct layer — but it is a MUMPS API. Calling it means writing M, setting up its variables by name, and reading results back out of an array it leaves behind. There is no command-line surface.

3. Direct global access. Read ^DPT(1,0) and $PIECE out what you want. It is the fastest path by a wide margin, needs no API at all, and is what a great deal of real VistA code actually does. It also bypasses every type, input transform, index update and access check FileMan would have applied — so it is fast in the way that removing the brakes is fast.

4. The DDR RPCs. For client applications — CPRS and its contemporaries — a generic remote data API: name a file, some fields, maybe an index, get rows back. This is the one that most resembles what v db does, and it is the one the rest of this section is about.

What all four share is the thing worth naming, because it is what v db sets out to change:

  • You must already know the answer to ask the question. File #2, field .05, index B, global root ^DPT(. None of it is discoverable from the tool; it comes from documentation, tribal knowledge, or reading the DD by hand.
  • Nothing is self-describing at the command line. There is no --help that tells you a patient’s marital status is field .05 and points at file #11.
  • Output is for humans or for M, not for a pipeline. Formatted pages, or ^-delimited strings, or an array left in a local variable.
  • And — the finding this whole domain rests on — none of them tell you whether the answer was complete.

3.2 DDR, and who depends on it

Section titled “3.2 DDR, and who depends on it”

The FileMan Delphi Components RPCs — ten entry points in the DDR routine namespace, shipped with FileMan 22.2 — are how a VistA client application reads and writes FileMan data without knowing FileMan. DDR LISTER returns rows; DDR GETS ENTRY DATA returns one record; DDR FILER writes. They are the generic data access layer of the VistA client era, and they are still load-bearing: DDR RPCs sit on 29 of vehu’s 130 broker context options, with the write verbs travelling nearly as widely as the read verbs.

So DDR is not a legacy corner nobody calls. That fact shaped the whole design — see 3.8.

3.3 Four jobs fused into one routine

Section titled “3.3 Four jobs fused into one routine”

A three-pass measurement programme across both live engines produced the finding that reframed the effort. It is not a performance characteristic but a reporting one:

DDR’s failure mode is a success response.

A file with 855,565 records returns zero rows with zero error rows. A 25,226-record file returns 28,757 rows. The filer accepts a value that violates its own field’s input transform and reports success. None of it is signalled.

Structurally, DDR does four separable things at once and fuses all four inside LIST^DIC plus a ^TMP staging area returned as one global array. Every measured defect class maps onto one of those fusions:

fused job what it decides DDR’s answer measured cost
population which records are in the answer whatever index it traverses under-report to 62.5%, over-report to 114%, one total blackout — none signalled
predicate which of those survive filtering XECUTE of client-supplied M remote code execution on both engines; a 34× unbounded scan that MAX does not bound
projection what each row carries a ^-delimited packed string one accepted write leaves a record’s data node and its index permanently disagreeing
transport how the result reaches the client materialise everything in ^TMP, return the subtree 50.5 s and 191 MB in one call; 99.2% of vehu’s scratch region; orphaned subtrees never reclaimed on YottaDB

3.4 The population defect — the one that reframes everything

Section titled “3.4 The population defect — the one that reframes everything”

LIST^DIC returns the population of the index it traverses, and that is not the file. Measured across 15 ground-truthed files: five under-report (62.5–88.1%), three over-report by emitting the same record more than once (up to 114%), and one — #757.02 CODES, 855,565 records — returns zero rows with zero error rows on the default index and on IEN order.

A client cannot detect any of it. Nothing in a DDR response says which index defined the answer, how many candidates were examined, or how many distinct records were emitted.

That blackout file is worth running yourself, because it is the single clearest demonstration of what changed. On the same instance, v db:

Three things in that transcript are the whole design in miniature:

  • population file — the answer came from an IEN walk of the file’s own data root, not from an index. Complete by construction.
  • claimed 855398 versus walked 855565 — the file header’s own record count is reported beside the walked total and never trusted. Here it is wrong by 167.
  • hollow 25 — 25 subscripts exist with no 0 node. A record that renders identically to an empty one is flagged rather than quietly counted.

3.5 A ceiling on rows is not a ceiling on work

Section titled “3.5 A ceiling on rows is not a ceiling on work”

The number every guard has to be written around: a DDR screen that matches nothing turns a 20,000-row request into a full 2.14M-entry scan — 34× the cost, an empty result, and nothing in the response saying so. The same selectivity expressed as a lookup value costs 0 ms, because the index seeks instead of scanning. A genuinely executable computed field costs only +23%, because it runs once per emitted row and the row ceiling bounds it.

So the cost model has two rates:

Per-candidate work is unbounded by any row ceiling. Per-emitted-row work is bounded by it.

That is why v db has four bounds instead of one, why examined is charged for every candidate the verb touches — including a projection performed only to evaluate a filter — and why the completeness block reports examined and filtered separately from emitted. See 7.2.

3.6 The write path never validated anything

Section titled “3.6 The write path never validated anything”

Two one-line root causes, both reproduced on both engines:

  • FDASET^DDR3 NEWs the error array it is supposed to return, so every error FileMan reports while loading the FDA is destroyed — an unknown field is silently discarded under a success response.
  • It loads values with empty flags, so the value is treated as already-internal and no input transform ever runs. A value that violates its own field’s transform is filed, and the response is +1,^75 with zero error rows.

What that permits: one accepted write of a value containing ^ splits the record’s own storage node, after which the retriever reads the field truncated while the index keeps the full value — permanently disagreeing, no error at any stage.

v db’s write verbs answer each of those directly: values are external by default (so the transform always runs, --internal is an explicit opt-in), an unknown or unwritable field refuses the whole request while projecting FileMan’s own error text, and ^ plus control characters are refused at the door in non-word-processing values.

3.7 The design response — unfuse the four jobs

Section titled “3.7 The design response — unfuse the four jobs”

Each fused job gets its own answer, its own cost law, and its own place in the response:

concern DDR, measured v db
population the index it traverses; 62.5%–114%, one blackout the file’s own IEN walk; complete by construction, declared in the response
predicate XECUTE of client M — RCE, unbounded scan a closed operator table; seek constraints pushed to the index, row filters budgeted
projection ^-delimited packed string FileMan’s own retriever → JSON; word-processing as line arrays
transport all staged in ^TMP, returned as one global array one bounded page per engine visit; nothing staged
cursor MORE^value^ien^ with the IEN dropped; ~0.22 records lost per boundary opaque, total-ordered, binding-fingerprinted; a non-advancing token is a typed PAGE_STALL
truncation silent stopped names the bound that ended the page
validation advisory at best; transforms bypassed mandatory server-side; the whole write refuses on any failure
word processing no write path exists at all v db text, over WP^DIE, replace and append — plus a read face DDR never had
authorization “does your context option list this RPC” declared per-file policy, evaluated engine-side, default-deny for writes

Two consequences are worth stating because they are counter-intuitive:

The complete path is the cheap path. Walking the file rather than an index and projecting through FileMan’s retriever measures 22.0 µs/record against DDR LISTER’s 27.6 on the identical file, field, engine and row count. The IEN walk itself is 2.65 µs/record. Correctness here is not bought with throughput.

Four measured engine asymmetries vanish rather than being guarded. YottaDB rolls scratch storage back and IRIS does not; one un-capped DDR list consumes 99.2% of vehu’s fixed TEMP region while IRIS’s grows into 220 GB; 28 orphaned subtrees totalling 35.8 MB are never reclaimed on YottaDB; the two engines’ maximum string lengths differ by 3.5×. The first three are irrelevant to a design that stages nothing, and the fourth stops mattering once the page budget is derived from the smaller of the two. There are no engine branches in v db.

3.8 What v db deliberately does not do

Section titled “3.8 What v db deliberately does not do”
  • It does not replace, wrap, or fix DDR. DDR keeps running, untouched, on its own broker path. The blast radius is real and untestable here (29 of 130 context options, CPRS-era Delphi binaries among the clients); DDR’s defects are its observable behaviour, and some consumer may be shaped around them; and a guard layer could add ceilings but not completeness, because the population defects live inside LIST^DIC, below anything a wrapper could reach. v db is built beside DDR, adoptable per application.
  • It does not patch Kernel. The broker’s substring stream-bounding defect is real and affects every RPC returning a global array (return type 4) — but it lives in a VA-owned namespace. The data plane’s own broker face (M9, 7.8) registers return type 2 (a local array), so that defect class is designed out structurally, never patched and never guarded against.
  • It does not carry the legacy wire format. XWBAPVER 0/1/2 compatibility is explicitly out of scope; carrying the packed ^-delimited format forward would re-import the corruption class the effort exists to remove.
  • It does not claim snapshot isolation. Stated plainly rather than implied — see 7.3 for the guarantee it does make.
  • It does not invent a permission model. On the CLI/driver seam the platform runs every request as DUZ=1 with host-asserted attribution, and the declared per-file policy is an honest accident bound, not a security boundary — that bound is the driver seam’s forever (the ruled Shape B). On the broker face a real principal exists (Kernel signon), and authorization delegates to Kernel’s own machinery: the broker context option gates RPC access (XQCS), and the signed-on DUZ reaches the audit and the gate directly. See 7.8.

3.9 How it was built

Section titled “3.9 How it was built”

The effort was renamed v-ddr → v-db-data-plane on acceptance: the subject is the v db domain’s data side; DDR is the measured baseline and the oracle target, not the product.

Build order was measure first. Milestone M0 was a measurement milestone with no product code: the completeness oracle (the 15 ground-truthed files, red against DDR), transport-inclusive throughput, a single-record TSTART probe, and taggable-job reap verification. v1 is M0–M6 — the read spine (M1), index lookup (M2), filters (M3), writes (M4), word processing (M5) and authorization (M6). M7–M9 were sequenced fast-follows: pacing (M7, landed as --pace), the walked census and catalog (M8, landed as census and distribution in VSL*1.0*37), and the RPC face (M9, landed in VSL*1.0*39 on 2026-08-09) — so the data plane is now reachable from the CLI, the driver seam, and a VistA broker client (7.8). Every milestone of the accepted design is complete; the acceptance ran the full matrix live on both engines with real principals (record).

Two things about that history are useful to a user:

  • The oracle is the acceptance criterion. Every milestone’s acceptance is a live run on both engines, not a unit-test suite. The M0 oracle is green 15/15 on vehu.
  • The live lane repeatedly caught what suites missed. M4’s live acceptance found that a post-filer refusal returned ok:true with an empty IEN, because the verbs shadowed the run-level capture flags. That is why the build VSL*1.0*33 exists. If you ever see v db claim success with an empty result, that class of bug is the first thing to suspect and report.

4. What each command is, in familiar terms

Section titled “4. What each command is, in familiar terms”

With the vocabulary from section 2 in hand, the command surface stops looking like VistA and starts looking like a database CLI. Here is the whole thing against what you would reach for elsewhere.

v db roughly what it actually does
schema DESCRIBE / information_schema one file’s columns, types, pointer targets, indexes, and who points at it
census table sizes across the database walked record counts for every file, with the header’s claim beside each
export pg_dump --schema-only, to a file the whole dictionary as JSONL + a manifest — the extraction seam
refs information_schema.referential_constraints one file’s foreign keys, both directions, with --verify auditing FileMan’s own catalog
estimate capacity planning record count × sampled size over a file set, fitted to a cap
count SELECT COUNT(*) an honest count — walked, not read off a header
rows SELECT … LIMIT + a cursor (never OFFSET) one bounded page, walking the file itself
get SELECT … WHERE pk = ? one record by IEN
find an index seek / WHERE indexed_col LIKE 'x%' walks a named index, seeking rather than scanning
distribution GROUP BY col ORDER BY count(*) DESC value variety, or sub-file depth
fields-profile count(col) FROM t for every column at once which columns actually hold data here — one walk, not one per column
policy GRANT / REVOKE the declared per-file authorization surface
put INSERT create a record, validated whole-request
edit UPDATE file values into an existing record
delete DELETE remove a record — dry-run by default
reindex REINDEX rebuild one record’s cross-references
text reading/writing a CLOB column the word-processing accessor

Five of those have no clean equivalent anywhere else, and they are the ones worth understanding before you start:

count exists because COUNT(*) does not. No engine maintains a row count here. The number in a file’s header is a claim kept up to date by maintenance code, and it drifts — on vehu’s #757.02 it is wrong by 167. So count walks the file and prints both numbers, and leaves you to notice.

find and rows are separate verbs because the access path is your decision. There is no planner to make it for you. rows walks the drawer; find walks the card catalogue. They can legitimately return different answers, and which one you used is stamped on every response as population.

distribution exists because FileMan has no API for variety at all. “How many distinct values does this field have, and how many records are empty” is a question you cannot ask the DBS, and it is usually the first question worth asking before building anything on a field.

text exists because word-processing fields have no write path. FileMan’s validator refuses them, the FDA loader accepts them anyway, and DDR never calls WP^DIE. This verb is new construction, not a port — and its read face is something DDR never had.

estimate is the only verb here that is not a database read. It sizes a prospective extract — record count × sampled record size over a file set, fitted to a cap — because “will this slice fit” is a question somebody has to answer before any extract, and answering it by hand does not scale. It once had company: profile, list and diff classified every file into PIKS categories, and all three left this domain in 2026-08 along with the evaluator behind them (§7.7). v db surfaces the operational database as it is and adds no judgement of its own.

Why every read carries a completeness block. In a relational database you take for granted that SELECT returned everything matching, or told you it could not. Neither guarantee holds in the legacy VistA path — a lookup returns whatever its index contains, and a truncated result and a complete one look identical. So v db publishes, on every page, which population answered, how many candidates it visited, how many it rejected, how many it emitted, and which bound stopped it. That block is the guide’s real subject, and it is section 7.1.

The whole surface, on the shape of the database

Section titled “The whole surface, on the shape of the database”

One picture, and the rest of this guide is detail. Every verb is drawn at the point in the tree it actually touches — which is the fastest way to see why there are eighteen of them and not one.

Read it in four passes:

  1. Top to bottom is the tree, in the order you would meet it: the schema (^DD), the catalog of what exists (^DIC), then the data itself.
  2. Left is structure, right is the verb that reads it. Every verb is at the depth it operates on — schema never descends past ^DD, get lands on one record, count never projects a field at all.
  3. The two arrows into the same file are the whole design. rows/count walk the numeric subscripts; find walks "B". Same file, different populations, and every response says which one it was. If you take one thing from this diagram, take that.
  4. Writes touch two places at once. A record’s data and its index entries. That coupling is why put and delete are validated and transactional, and why reindex exists at all — when data and index disagree, something has to rebuild the second from the first.

Two things the picture deliberately leaves out, because they are the same for every verb: the transport (one bounded page per engine visit, over the m-driver-sdk seam — 1), and the completeness block that rides on every read answer (7.1). Node subscripts and piece positions are drawn as FileMan’s standard layout, not measured — the caption at 2.2 says exactly which parts of this shape were measured on vehu and which are convention.

5. Cheat sheet — every command, and what it replaces

Section titled “5. Cheat sheet — every command, and what it replaces”

This section is the one to print. It has three parts:

  • 5.1 — one card per command: where in the database it acts, what it is in modern terms, what FileMan surface it replaces, and a working example.
  • 5.2 — the plain-English as-is → to-be table: “I used to do X in FileMan; what do I type now?”
  • 5.3 — the honest coverage answer, including what v db deliberately does not cover and where that capability lives instead.

Every card carries the same locator bar, so you can place any command inside the master map at a glance:

A filled cell ▓▓▓ means the command reads or writes there; ··· means it does not go near it.

5.1 The cards

Section titled “5.1 The cards”

v db schema — describe one file

Section titled “v db schema — describe one file”

What it is: DESCRIBE <table> — columns, types, foreign keys, indexes. Plus one thing no relational DESCRIBE gives you: who points at this file. Replaces: $$GET1^DID · FIELD^DID · FILE^DID — and the hand-reading of ^DD that most people actually did instead. Example: v db schema 2 --engine vehu

v db refs — the reference map (foreign keys)

Section titled “v db refs — the reference map (foreign keys)”

What it is: what this file points at, and what points at it — at every dictionary depth, with each edge carrying the stored semantics that say what KIND of reference it is (identity/DINUM, required, LAYGO, a variable pointer’s target set) — and with --verify auditing FileMan’s own pointed-to-by catalog against the fields themselves, because that catalog can be stale. Replaces: hand-reading ^DD(f,0,"PT"). Example: v db refs 63 --resolve --engine vehu

v db indexes — what each cross-reference actually stores

Section titled “v db indexes — what each cross-reference actually stores”

What it is: the inventory schema cannot give. schema reads one of the two registers a cross-reference can be declared in and reports a seek contract; this reads both, and reports what is stored: walkability, whether the subtree exists here at all, where the record id sits inside an entry, and whether the key IS the indexed column’s value — the measurement that decides what may be looked up by key and what may not. Replaces: hand-reading ^DD(f,fld,1,…) and the #.11 INDEX file, then guessing which of them the engine actually resolves through. Example: v db indexes 44 --key-sample 20 --engine vehu · --all --out ./dir inventories every file on the instance in one pass (vehu: 9,739 cross-references across 2,879 files, about four seconds).

v db integrity — is the database self-consistent?

Section titled “v db integrity — is the database self-consistent?”

What it is: the instance-integrity census — the whole-instance engine sweeps (header claims vs walked truth, every stored pointer resolved, every set/date/number value against its own declared grammar, the declaration-driven index audit, hollow sub-records, the DD census, the KEY register, and the full-depth sub-file descent), as counts with denominators per file, never a pass/fail verdict: a stock release build is measurably nonzero in every class, so red only ever means a delta against a named expectation, which is the baseline comparison’s job, not this verb’s. Replaces: nothing shipped — FileMan has no instance-wide integrity census; the as-is practice was ad-hoc M one-liners over ^DD/^DIC and per-file spot checks. Example: v db integrity --engine vehu --out ./audit (whole instance, minutes; the artifact contract is integrity-jsonl-contract.md).

v db integrity-compare — did the instance move against a named expectation?

Section titled “v db integrity-compare — did the instance move against a named expectation?”

What it is: the audit’s RED, offline: an integrity artifact compared against a prior committed run of the SAME instance (any row difference is the delta outcome — the only red the audit has, per row, with the expectation’s identity beside the verdict) and/or against the shipped-state ledger (the cross-build floor: one-sided excess is the attention outcome, never red). Four pinned outcome words a script can branch on: clean · delta · attention · stopped. Replaces: nothing shipped — FileMan has no baseline comparison at all. Example: v db integrity-compare ./fresh --base baselines/integrity/vehu --ledger baselines/integrity/ledger.jsonl — see §8.21.

v db integrity-report — WHY do these pointers dangle?

Section titled “v db integrity-report — WHY do these pointers dangle?”

What it is: the attribution view of one integrity artifact (VD-D109): dangling mass grouped per TARGET and joined to the target file’s own header ledger — a scrubbed or empty target presents as ONE finding with its mechanism shown, and residual dangling into healthy targets is the class worth eyes, source lists attached either way. Root→file naming is asked of the live engine (one fileOf dispatch per distinct root), and it must be the SAME instance the artifact measured. Replaces: hand-tracing ^DD(f,0,"PT") against ad-hoc $DATA probes. Example: v db integrity-report baselines/integrity/vehu --engine vehu — see §8.22.

v db export — the whole dictionary, to disk

Section titled “v db export — the whole dictionary, to disk”

What it is: the data dictionary as JSONL plus a manifest that says which instance it came from, what was requested, and whether the artifact is complete. Every file rides with its whole sub-file tree (a sub-file is a table — VD-D80), so the artifact resolves its own subfileLink references. This is the extraction seam — everything downstream reads this file. Replaces: nothing; there was no export path. Example: v db export --files 2,19,63 --out ./dd --engine vehu

v db estimate — size an extract before you run it

Section titled “v db estimate — size an extract before you run it”

What it is: record count x sampled mean record size over a file set, fitted against a cap (exit 3 over cap). The sample basis rides the output in words. Replaces: guessing. Example: v db estimate --files 2,19,63 --cap 1 --engine vehu

v db census — the walked catalog

Section titled “v db census — the walked catalog”

What it is: table sizes across the whole database — honest counts, with each file header’s own claim printed beside as an integrity check. Replaces: the file header node (^DIC(n,0) piece 4), which is a claim maintained by other code and drifts. There has never been an API for this. Example: v db census --file 200 --engine foia

v db count — how many records, honestly

Section titled “v db count — how many records, honestly”

What it is: SELECT COUNT(*), with or without a predicate. It walks, because nothing maintains a count. --index counts the entries of one index instead of the records. Replaces: reading the file header’s own count and hoping. There has never been a maintained count or an API for one — only that claim. Example: v db count 757.02 --engine vehu · v db count 200 --where '9.3 bound'

v db rows — a page of records

Section titled “v db rows — a page of records”

What it is: SELECT <cols> FROM <table> LIMIT <n> with a cursor, walking the file itself so the population is the file. Replaces: LIST^DIC — deliberately not by wrapping it. LIST^DIC returns whatever index it traversed; the IEN walk returns the file. Example: v db rows 3.1 --fields .01 --max 3 --engine vehu

v db get — one record by key

Section titled “v db get — one record by key”

What it is: SELECT … WHERE pk = ?. Replaces: GETS^DIQ and $$GET1^DIQ — the single most-called read pair in VistA (106 and 85 packages). Example: v db get 200 .5 --engine vehu Follow a pointer: v db get --ref 3.2-9 --engine vehu — the same address in the form an --ids map hands you.

v db find — lookup through an index

Section titled “v db find — lookup through an index”

What it is: an index seek — WHERE indexed_col LIKE 'x%' with a range or a prefix, walking the index and projecting each hit. Replaces: $$FIND1^DIC · FIND^DIC · the classic ^DIC / IX^DIC lookup family (135 and 105 packages between them). Example: v db find 200 B --prefix USER --engine vehu · --out ./dir lands the whole index population as JSONL plus a manifest.

v db distribution — value variety and sub-file depth

Section titled “v db distribution — value variety and sub-file depth”

What it is: GROUP BY col ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT n, plus a depth mode that counts child rows per parent, --where to tally a subset, and --index to tally an index’s own keys without reading a record. Replaces: nothing — FileMan has no aggregation API at all. Statistics exist only as a print-time feature of the report writer. This is the largest genuinely new capability in the domain. Example: v db distribution 200 9.3 --top 5 --engine vehu · v db distribution 200 --index B --prefix SMITH

v db fields-profile — which columns actually hold data

Section titled “v db fields-profile — which columns actually hold data”

What it is: one walk, a per-field tally of how many records hold a stored value — count(col) for every column at once. Sites extend files by ADDING FIELDS (#63.04 carries 965), so “which of these are real here” is the first question an extract asks, and asking it a column at a time costs a walk per column. Replaces: nothing — there was no way to ask this. The nearest approach was one distribution per field. Example: v db fields-profile 63.04 --examined 3000 --engine vehu · --empty lists the columns holding nothing instead.

v db text — read and write a long-text field

Section titled “v db text — read and write a long-text field”

What it is: the TEXT/CLOB accessor. Word-processing fields are stored as a sub-file of numbered lines, which is why this cell and not RECORD. Replaces: WP^DIE for the write face. The read face replaces nothing — DDR never had one, and BROWSE^DDBR is a terminal display, not an API. Example: v db text 19 '999991,' 3.5 --show --engine foia

v db policy — the authorization surface

Section titled “v db policy — the authorization surface”

What it is: GRANT / REVOKE, declared per file, evaluated at every verb’s door before anything is touched. Replaces: in practice, nothing — effective authorization for the legacy generic path was “does your menu option list this RPC.” FileMan 22.2 does ship a policy engine (DAC, $$CANDO^DIAC1, POLICY file #1.6), but it was measured near-dormant, with FileMan itself as its only caller. Example: v db policy --engine vehu

v db put — create a record

Section titled “v db put — create a record”

What it is: INSERT — validated whole-request, transactional, audited. Replaces: UPDATE^DIE and FILE^DICN (the LAYGO add). Example: v db put 3.1 --value '.01=NEW TITLE' --yes --engine foia

v db edit — change a record

Section titled “v db edit — change a record”

What it is: UPDATE. One invalid value refuses the whole request. Replaces: FILE^DIE (96 packages) and the classic ^DIE DR-string edit (126 packages). Example: v db edit 3.1 '3,' --value '.01=RENAMED' --yes --engine foia

v db delete — remove a record

Section titled “v db delete — remove a record”

What it is: DELETE, dry-run by default — it shows you what would go before anything goes. Replaces: ^DIK (119 packages) and FILE^DIE with @. Example: v db delete 3.1 '3,' --engine foia (add --commit --yes)

v db reindex — rebuild one record’s index entries

Section titled “v db reindex — rebuild one record’s index entries”

What it is: REINDEX for one row — reads the record’s data, rewrites its index entries. The repair for when the two halves of the tree disagree. Replaces: IX1^DIK. (Whole-file IXALL^DIK / ENALL^DIK is deliberately not exposed — an unbounded index rebuild behind one confirmation is exactly the kind of engine occupation the design refuses.) Example: v db reindex 3.1 3 --yes --engine foia

5.2 As-is → to-be: the FileMan translation table

Section titled “5.2 As-is → to-be: the FileMan translation table”

“I used to do this in FileMan. What do I type now?” — every load-bearing FileMan data-access surface, in plain English. Package-reach figures are measured counts of distinct calling packages on VEHU.

I want to… FileMan, as-is reach v db, to-be in modern terms
see a file’s structure $$GET1^DID, FIELD^DID, FILE^DID 55 / 50 v db schema <file> DESCRIBE table
read one record’s fields GETS^DIQ, $$GET1^DIQ 106 / 85 v db get <file> <ien> SELECT … WHERE pk = ?
list many records LIST^DIC 59 v db rows <file> SELECT … LIMIT + cursor
look something up by name $$FIND1^DIC, FIND^DIC, ^DIC, IX^DIC 89 / 73 / 135 v db find <file> <index> an index seek
count the records (read the header node) — v db count <file> SELECT COUNT(*)
count every file (no API) — v db census table sizes
see a field’s value spread (no API — print-time stats only) — v db distribution <file> <field> GROUP BY … ORDER BY count DESC
see WHICH columns of a file hold data (no API — one report per field, or read the globals) — v db fields-profile <file> count(col) for every column at once
read a file’s nested table (read ^DPT(n,m,…) by hand) — v db rows <sub-file>, or --with-multiples for the whole record as a tree a child table, or a nested document
read a named set of records (one GETS^DIQ per record) — v db rows <file> --iens 1,5,.5 WHERE pk IN (…)
see what the indexes actually store (hand-read ^DD(f,fld,1) and the #.11 INDEX file) — v db indexes <file> · --all SHOW INDEXES
know what a read will cost first (none — ^DIC picks an index and never says which) — v db rows/find … --explain EXPLAIN
map the foreign keys of the whole instance ^DD(f,0,"PT"), one file at a time, and it can be stale — v db refs --all --out DIR the whole FK graph as an artifact
add a record UPDATE^DIE, FILE^DICN 94 / 105 v db put <file> --value … INSERT
change a record FILE^DIE, classic ^DIE 96 / 126 v db edit <file> <iens> --value … UPDATE
delete a record ^DIK, FILE^DIE with @ 119 v db delete <file> <iens> DELETE (dry-run first)
check a value before filing VAL^DIE, VALS^DIE, CHK^DIE 23 / 5 (automatic — every write validates) mandatory CHECK constraints
enforce uniqueness $$KEYVAL^DIE, KEY file #.31 3 (automatic, inside the write) a unique constraint
write a long-text field WP^DIE, EN^DIWE 55 / 31 v db text … --line/--from-file writing a CLOB
read a long-text field (none — BROWSE^DDBR displays it) 14 v db text … --show reading a CLOB
rebuild an index IX1^DIK 48 v db reindex <file> <ien> REINDEX one row
control who may read/write $$CANDO^DIAC1, POLICY #1.6 1 v db policy --declare … GRANT / REVOKE
reach it from a remote client the ten DDR * RPCs 29 of 130 menus the VSL DATA PLANE RPC + its broker context option (7.8) a remote data API

Two rows are worth reading twice, because they are where the shape of the answer changes rather than its spelling:

  • “list many records” is not a rename. LIST^DIC answers from whichever index it traversed; v db rows answers from the file. On the 15 measured files those are different answers — and on #757.02 the legacy call returns zero rows for 855,565 records.
  • “check a value before filing” moved from a call you could forget to make into something you cannot skip. DDR VALIDATOR existed as an optional pre-check, which is precisely why writes went in unvalidated.

5.3 Coverage: where this is a superset, and where it is not

Section titled “5.3 Coverage: where this is a superset, and where it is not”

The honest answer, because a cheat sheet that implies coverage it does not have is worse than no cheat sheet.

v db is a superset of FileMan’s record-grade data-access core, and is not a superset of FileMan. Those are different claims and the distinction is deliberate — it was ruled, surface by surface, in the effort’s coverage map, which enumerated 26 FileMan access surfaces and dispositioned every one.

Superset — covered, plus capability FileMan never had:

the core status
DBS read (DIQ), DD read (DID), lookup (DIC), DBS + classic write (DIE), WP filing, validation, keys, delete, reindex ✅ covered by the verbs above
honest record counts ➕ new — FileMan has only a header claim
distinct-value / depth distribution ➕ new — FileMan has no aggregation API at all
per-field population profile (which columns hold data) ➕ new — there was no way to ask this at all; the nearest approach was one distribution per field
a completeness assertion on every read ➕ new — nothing in FileMan reports what its answer was drawn from
export sizing against a cap ➕ new — FileMan cannot tell you how big an extract would be
an instance-wide cross-reference inventory (indexes --all) ➕ new — FileMan has no listing of what its indexes store, in either register
an instance-wide pointer graph (refs --all) ➕ new — the pointed-to-by catalog is per file, and stale; nothing assembled or audited it
a plan before the read (--explain) ➕ new — FileMan chooses an index inside ^DIC and never says which, or what it will cost
a named record set as a population (--iens) ➕ new — a cohort was one GETS^DIQ per record
the stored entries of an index a seek refuses (find --raw) ➕ new — these are most of them, and they were reachable only by hand-walking the global

Not covered, on purpose — and where the capability lives instead:

FileMan surface why not here where it lives
print / report / templates (EN1^DIP, EN^DIS, PRINT #.4, SORT #.401) presentation, not data access your own tooling over rows/find output — but note v db has no sort-order control, which is a real limitation of rows
SQL projection (SQLI, Octo) a different query model the fm-explorer effort’s SQL lane
bulk export/import (Extract, DDXP, Filegram, DIFROM, Import) measured near-dead (≤2 external callers each); bulk movement is a provisioning concern engine-native dump/load
merge / renumber (DIT, EN^XDRMERG) cross-record identity resolution, a genuinely harder problem never a v db verb
archiving (DIAR) operations; 0 external callers not addressed
ScreenMan / browser (^DDS, BROWSE^DDBR) UI the data underneath is reached by get / text
Entity / DDE (GET^DDE) FileMan’s own JSON projection — but needs a pre-defined mapping per shape, so it is not general declined as prior art
audit-trail reading (^DIA, ^DDA) keeps one owner for the audit plane the vista-observability effort
direct global access this is the thing v db is the alternative to —

Genuine gaps inside the intended scope — open, not ruled out:

gap status
sub-file enumeration and projection CLOSED 2026-08-13 (VD-D31/VD-D54 discharged). It was the largest in-scope gap: rows 2.01 refused, and projecting a non-word-processing multiple refused with “insufficient information to identify an entry in a subfile”. Both now work. rows <sub-file> walks a direct sub-file file-wide (population: sub:2.01, no parent needed), and --with-multiples projects every non-WP multiple inline and recursively into the record — the decoded tree in one invocation. Depth is no longer a limit either — #63.041, three levels down, walks file-wide on both engines. What remains is narrow and typed: a parent chain that does not resolve (over 20 levels or a dictionary cycle) refuses U-VSL-ROW-SUBFILE, and a record whose subtree outgrows the bytes budget comes back as a typed stub naming the paged alternative (U-VSL-ROW-TREESIZE) rather than a truncated tree.
whole-file reindex deliberately not a verb — but that means a full index rebuild still needs IXALL^DIK by other means.
creating or altering files and fields no verb. v db schema reads the dictionary; nothing in v db writes it. Schema changes remain a KIDS/FileMan job.
sort order on reads There is no ORDER BY, and a host-side --sort is refused on purpose: it could only sort the page it holds, producing a page-local ordering that looks global. What you get instead is order as a property of the population you chose, derivable from the population field every read already carries and stated in §11.5 — find <file> B is ordering by B’s key, and --explain says which index gives which order.
batch atomicity single-record atomicity is proven and claimed; multi-record transactions are not offered.

If you are migrating a workflow off FileMan and it depends on a row in the second or third table, v db is not yet a drop-in for it — and this guide would rather say so than let you discover it halfway through.

Which of these will actually stop you

Section titled “Which of these will actually stop you”

Enumerating gaps is not the same as saying which ones bite. Ranked against the three things people actually come to a database tool to do:

# gap stops you at why
1 audit-trail content auditing — hard stop There is no v db path to “who changed this field, when, from what.” Ruled to vista-observability (VD-D39), which is still a draft — so the capability FileMan has today has no tool at all. See below; the picture is more nuanced than “unimplemented”.
2 no multi-field grouping, no joins, no ORDER BY reporting — moderately distribution groups one field only. Nothing assembles across files in one invocation: what you get instead is the guided client loop — --explain says what a read will cost, --ids says where to go next, --iens fetches the set in one conversation, and refs --all plus an offline closure (§9.1) says which files you need at all. Ordering is a property of the population, not a clause (§11.5).
3 what points AT one record reporting — narrowly refs --all answers it completely at file level. Per record it needs an index on the pointing field, which VistA usually does not have — measured, 8.7 % (§14.1).
4 no DD editing; no whole-file reindex management Schema changes stay a KIDS/FileMan job; a full index rebuild has no verb (only per-record reindex).
5 no batch atomicity management Single-record atomicity is proven; bulk corrections have no transaction.

Two entries left this ranking rather than being fixed in place, and both are worth knowing about. The RPC face was gap #6 until 2026-08-09, when VSL*1.0*39 installed the context option through a real KIDS post-install and the full acceptance matrix passed on both engines (7.8). Sub-files were gap #2 — “cannot page or project; multiples are where the interesting data lives” — until 2026-08-13, when the file-wide sub-file walk and --with-multiples landed (§8.8). Both are struck from the list on evidence, not optimism.

On metadata specifically — you are ahead, not behind. schema, refs, census, export and distribution give you more than FileMan ever offered: inbound pointer maps with an audit of FileMan’s own catalog, honest record counts, a dictionary you can take off the engine, and value distributions FileMan has no API for at all. The gaps above are about data and audit content, not about the dictionary.

The audit picture, measured. It is worth being precise, because “no audit read” understates one part and overstates another:

  • ✅ You can see that auditing is configured. v db schema 2 reports audit: true per field — 101 of #2’s 594 fields are audited.
  • ✅ You can see how much audit data exists. v db census --file 1.1 on foia: 43 records, ~358 MiB estimated — and the file header claims 0, so the walked count is the only honest one. #.6 DD AUDIT walks 36 (vehu: 0 — its audit machinery ships off).
  • ⚠️ The top level of #1.1 reads, but does not mean what it says. Its records are keyed by audited file number (3.5 → DEVICE AUDIT), while the DD’s field set describes an audit entry — so .02 DATE/TIME RECORDED renders as 1701.1@1I:00. Plausible-looking output, wrong level.
  • ⛔ Two computed fields fault untyped. --fields 1 or 2.9 on #1.1 returns bare M6 / verb rows^VSLROW faulted, which also breaks --fields '*'. Computed projection works fine elsewhere (#200’s 9001 and 2.2 both return values), so this is specific to this file — and an untyped fault is a contract violation regardless.
  • ⛔ The change records themselves are out of reach, because they hang below the top level — which makes this gap #2 wearing a different hat.

That last point is the interesting one: fix sub-file enumeration and most of the audit gap closes through the ordinary verbs, with no bespoke audit surface required. That reframing is under review in the effort’s audit-read re-examination, and the whole gap-and-defect register — measured across both engines with a committed harness — is the gap remediation proposal. Two findings there change what is written above: only 37.5% of cross-references are walkable by find, and v db schema currently reports every cross-reference as regular, which contradicts it.

6. Getting started

Section titled “6. Getting started”

6.1 Two ways to run it

Section titled “6.1 Two ways to run it”

The same verbs run either standalone from the v-db binary or mounted under the v umbrella:

Everything in this guide is written as v db …; drop the space for the standalone form. The umbrella v is on $PATH (~/.local/bin/v); the standalone v-db is built into the repo’s dist/ by make check and is not installed globally.

One difference between the two: version and menu belong to the umbrella and to the standalone binary, not to the db domain. Under v, use v version and v menu — v db version is a usage error. See 8.18.

6.2 Choosing an engine

Section titled “6.2 Choosing an engine”

Every engine-touching verb takes --engine <profile>. Two profiles ship:

profile engine VistA
vehu YottaDB VEHU demo VistA
foia InterSystems IRIS FOIA VistA

The engine is resolved by the platform’s selection ladder — the --engine flag wins, then $M_ENGINE, then the instance’s committed config; if none resolves, the verb refuses with exit 4 rather than guessing. Transport is never fabricated: if you do not express one, the driver resolves it.

There are no engine branches in v db, so a verb behaves identically on both. The same command against the other engine:

(vehu’s #3.1 TITLE has 70 records; foia’s has 2. Different instances, same contract.)

6.3 Output formats

Section titled “6.3 Output formats”

-o auto (the default) renders the text face on a TTY and the JSON face when stdout is redirected — so an interactive run is readable and a piped run is machine-parseable with no flag change. Force either with -o text / -o json, and use --no-color to drop ANSI styling.

Every transcript in this guide that shows a box-drawn completeness rule was produced with -o text --no-color.

6.4 Your first commands

Section titled “6.4 Your first commands”

7. Core concepts

Section titled “7. Core concepts”

7.1 The completeness block

Section titled “7.1 The completeness block”

Every read response carries it. There is no flag to turn it off, because a caller who does not ask for it is exactly the caller who gets silently wrong answers.

field meaning
population file (IEN walk) or index:<name> — the answer set’s definition, stated rather than assumed
examined candidates visited
filtered candidates rejected by a predicate
emitted rows in this page
distinct distinct IENs in this page
stopped end | rows | bytes | examined | elapsed

stopped paired with more is what makes silent truncation structurally impossible. A page that ended because it hit a budget is distinguishable from a page that ended because the data did:

  • more: true, stopped: rows — your page size ended it; ask for the next page.
  • more: true, stopped: examined — a work budget ended it. If filtered is large and emitted small, you are paying for a scan.
  • more: false, stopped: end — the walk is complete. This is the only combination that means “that was all of it”.

Duplicates. An IEN-ordered enumeration is distinct by construction. An index walk is not, and cannot be made so by a stateless cursor — so index walks report emitted and distinct separately and never silently de-duplicate. If find shows emitted 400, distinct 397, three records were emitted twice. Silently de-duplicating would replace a visible over-report with an invisible one.

7.2 Four bounds, and stopped

Section titled “7.2 Four bounds, and stopped”

Every paged read carries four bounds, each with a default, each overridable, each reported in stopped when it is the one that ended the page:

flag bounds why it exists
--max emitted rows the conventional one — insufficient alone
--bytes page payload bytes cost tracks field count, not row count; and the engine’s own string ceiling
--examined candidates visited the one DDR lacks — the 34× scan is bounded by nothing else
--elapsed engine time in this page (ms) the backstop for what cannot be counted, since the DD permits arbitrary M in a computed field

--examined is charged for every candidate the verb touches, including a projection performed solely to evaluate a filter. That is deliberate: a filter on a non-indexed field must project that field per candidate, and a budget that charged only emitted rows would let a selective filter run an unbounded scan while reporting a small, tidy page — DDR’s central defect, rebuilt.

--elapsed 0 is legal and means stop after the first candidate — useful for probing cost, and a compact demonstration that stopped really does name the bound that fired:

7.3 Cursors and resumption

Section titled “7.3 Cursors and resumption”

Paged verbs return an opaque page.next token. Pass it back verbatim as --token:

(Note IEN 9 following 5 — the walk is over the file’s actual subscripts, gaps and all, not over 1..n.)

The token is opaque to you and carries a total order — (ien) for an enumeration, (key, ien) for an index walk — plus a binding fingerprint over file, population, field list and predicate. Replay it against a different request shape and you get a typed refusal rather than wrong rows:

The fingerprint covers the DD as well as the request, so a token also stops being valid if the file’s dictionary changed underneath it. A non-advancing token raises PAGE_STALL instead of looping forever.

What is not offered, stated plainly: no snapshot isolation. Nothing on either engine provides it cheaply, and claiming it would be the same class of lie this domain exists to remove. The IEN walk’s actual guarantee is precise:

  • a record present throughout the walk, at an IEN above the cursor’s start, is emitted exactly once;
  • a record deleted before the walk reaches it is not emitted;
  • a record created during the walk is emitted if its IEN sorts above the current cursor — which, since FileMan allocates IENs ascending, is the normal case.

That is a bias toward including late arrivals, not a loss.

7.4 Projection: fields and tiers

Section titled “7.4 Projection: fields and tiers”

--fields takes ;-separated field numbers, or * for all:

Omit --fields and you get all top-level fields — which on #200 is well over a hundred. Name what you need.

“All top-level fields” has one measured carve-out: FileMan’s retriever omits non-word-processing multiples from a '*' projection (on #200, 29 of 203 fields). The envelope now declares that instead of leaving it silent: every star page (and star get) carries a projection block naming each excluded field and why —

— so star ≡ the data dictionary minus the declared exclusions, checkably. An explicit field list never carries the block (you named the fields; nothing is omitted), and a WP multiple projects as a line array, so it is never in the list. Every read also carries completeness — including get (a minimal single-record block) and text --show (its total mapped into the same shape), so the “every read” contract holds verb-by-verb, not just where paging happens to run.

--tier selects the value form, and takes external, internal or raw. Which tier you pick decides whether your parser travels to another site — every result says so in its portability block (7.9). The engine default is external — FileMan’s own retriever, so pointers resolve, sets decode, computed fields evaluate and formatting is FileMan’s business rather than yours.

The difference is not cosmetic. #200’s field 9.3 is a pointer:

Note the asymmetry with filters: projection is external by default, predicates run on the internal value (11.7). So on that field --where '9.3 = 9' matches and --where '9.3 = C-VT100' does not, while the row you get back says C-VT100. On a free-text field the two forms coincide; on a pointer, a date or a set-of-codes they do not.

Word-processing fields are emitted as line arrays, never ^-pieced: 196 of 45,295 OPTION description lines carry a literal ^, and any consumer that re-splits them corrupts them. Read them with v db text --show.

The raw tier’s shape is nodes, not fields. --tier raw returns the record’s data nodes by subtree walk — clone-grade, below field semantics. On get the row is data.row.nodes (plus data.row.value when the record root itself holds a value); on rows each row is data.rows[n].nodes. Keys are the subscript path below the record, comma-joined; each value follows the standard value contract (a JSON string, or {"b64":…} when the bytes are frame-unsafe). Because nodes are not fields, --fields cannot combine with --tier raw — the combination refuses typed U-VSL-ROW-RAWFIELDS. (It used to be accepted and silently ignored: the same 338 nodes came back on #200 with or without the flag. An accepted flag that does nothing is a lie; now it is a refusal.)

Two more field-door refusals worth knowing. Explicitly projecting a non-word-processing multiple (say #19’s field 3.91) refuses typed U-VSL-ROW-MULTIPLE — sub-records are rows, not a scalar, and the sub-file read plane that will serve them is a later milestone. Whether a multiple projects is now predictable from schema: its wordProcessing flag carries the sub-file’s own .01 word-processing fact, which is the measured discriminator (214 observations, zero breaks). And two files — #1.1 and #.6 — refuse every top-level read typed U-VSL-ROW-NESTEDROOT: their top-level IENs are file numbers (audit content nests one level down), so a top-level render would return wrong-level values under ok:true.

7.5 The run-lock

Section titled “7.5 The run-lock”

The driver stack holds one run-lock per engine, so two v db invocations against the same engine serialize. That is deliberate — it is what keeps a long fold from interleaving with a write. --lock-wait sets how long to wait before refusing:

It is a typed refusal, not a crash — exit 4, with a code you can switch on:

--lock-wait 0 means try once and give up. A stale lock (the holder is gone) is reported on stderr as a notice and the verb proceeds.

Which verbs hold it for a long time is worth knowing before you start one. The whole-instance sweeps hold it for their full run — measured on vehu (v0.7.1-4-gec3abcf, 2026-08-17), each verb over the entire dictionary:

verb wall clock records
export 15m36s 8,171 tables
refs 15m19s 19,187 edges
census 3m20s 2,920 files
indexes --all 4s 9,740 indexes
