export and refs are the two that cost a fold; census is minutes; nothing else in the domain holds the lock for more than a moment. A single-file invocation of any of them is a moment too — it is the --all/whole-instance scope that sweeps.

7.6 Authorization and the @mutates gate

Section titled “7.6 Authorization and the @mutates gate”

Two layers, and the gate is engine-side at every verb’s door — never a host flag you could bypass by editing the client:

  1. A declared per-file policy, evaluated engine-side, default-deny for writes. Show it with v db policy.
  2. The instance class. class=demo versus class=real, beside a live reading of Kernel’s own PROD tripwire. The write verbs refuse to run against an instance holding real patient data until a real principal exists — refusing loudly rather than degrading quietly.

On top of that, every mutation needs --yes, which is refused both client-side and engine-side without it, and every engine-reaching mutation writes exactly one audit line.

Be honest about what this is, per transport: the CLI/driver seam runs every request as DUZ=1 with host-asserted attribution — it defends against operator accident, not against a malicious host, and that bound is the driver seam’s permanently (Shape B, ruled 2026-08-09). The broker face (7.8) carries a real Kernel principal: the declared per-file policy is bypassed for a real, active, signed-on user (their RPC access was already gated by the context option, and mutations audit under their real DUZ), while the driver seam keeps its declared bound and its real-data write refusal forever.

7.7 Classification — not here, on purpose

Section titled “7.7 Classification — not here, on purpose”

v db used to classify every file and field into PIKS categories (patient / institution / knowledge / system) from a registry of hand-written heuristics, with list, profile and diff as its faces. That history is stated plainly rather than erased — the tool really did carry it.

All of it was REMOVED in 2026-08 — a ~3,860-line evaluator, its registry corpus, and its verbs — and the whole PIKS line was RETIRED 2026-08-17.

The reason is worth understanding, because it is the line this whole tool is drawn along. A PIKS label is a purely analytical derivative of v db’s own extraction output: an inference computed on top of the export, never a measurement the tool makes. Nothing in the database says whether a file is “patient data” — that is a judgement, and no stored value can check it. v db surfaces the operational database as it is; anything derived by inference from that surface is downstream work by construction. A national-dictionary label join survived here until 2026-08-13 and went for the same reason plus one more: that dictionary is incomplete and untrusted, and an untrusted source must not be joined into an artifact whose charter is that every cell is a fact or a named non-fact.

Classification now happens downstream, in the bundle analysis, derived from the dictionary export this tool produces — one repeatable artifact, re-derivable by rerunning the export. Nothing is inferred inside v db.

What this means for you: the catalog and the dictionary export carry measurements, never judgements. If you want files labelled, derive the labels downstream from the export, at whatever trust level you can defend. See §15.

7.8 The RPC face — broker clients

Section titled “7.8 The RPC face — broker clients”

Since VSL*1.0*39 (M9, 2026-08-09) the data plane is reachable from a VistA RPC Broker client — the transport CPRS-class applications already speak — with the same engine-side contract as every CLI verb. This section is for application builders; nothing here changes the CLI.

What ships. The KIDS build registers one RPC, VSL DATA PLANE (RPC^VSLRPC, return type 2 = local array), and one type-B broker context option, also named VSL DATA PLANE, whose #19.05 multiple authorizes the RPC. The context’s RPC list is filed by a real KIDS post-install (EN^VSLRPCI) — measured fact: it cannot ship as KRN component data (the filer installs a lying header) — so a fresh install works with no manual wiring.

The call shape. One request parameter, one chunked response:

  1. Sign on (XUS SIGNON SETUP → XUS AV CODE) — the session now carries a real DUZ.
  2. XWB CREATE CONTEXT with VSL DATA PLANE. Kernel’s own option-access check ($$CHK^XQCS) gates this: the signed-on user must hold the option (menu tree or secondary menu) or the XUPROGMODE key, else the broker refuses with “does not have access to option VSL DATA PLANE” — that refusal is the authorization model, exercised live in the acceptance.
  3. Fire VSL DATA PLANE with one literal parameter: the base64-encoded JSON request — the same json^VSLAPI contract the dispatcher speaks ({"verb":"rows^VSLROW","params":{…},"page":{…},"envelope":2}; mutating verbs add "confirm":1, "attrib":{"osUser":…,"host":…} and optionally an "idem" token).
  4. The response arrives as CRLF-delimited type-2 array chunks; concatenate them and you hold the framed VSL envelope (##VSL2:<n>##…##VSLEND##), byte-identical to what $$run^VSLAPI returns on the driver seam — measured raw-equal on both engines (803 B vehu / 783 B foia) at acceptance. Completeness block, typed errors, cursors: all identical.

What the real principal changes. Mutations audit under the signed-on DUZ (not the driver seam’s asserted attribution); the declared per-file policy is delegated past for a real, active principal; and production-class writes are broker-only by design (VD-D48). Idempotency tokens and the typed U-VSL-ROW-LOCKTIMEOUT contention refusal work over this transport exactly as engine-side — a replayed token returns {"replayed":true,…} without re-filing or re-auditing, and a concurrent duplicate either serializes to a replay or refuses typed U-VSL-API-IDEMBUSY.

Concurrency is different here — plan for it. There is no run-lock on the broker path: sessions run in genuine parallel (measured ~6.2× effective parallelism at 8 sessions on vehu, graceful under composed load). Two rules from the acceptance:

  • Your read timeout must exceed the fired verb’s worst case. A client that gives up mid-RPC abandons its broker job, which can spin at 100% CPU engine-side until reaped — measured live. Budget the timeout from the verb’s bounds (elapsed defaults to 10 s/page), not from optimism.
  • On IRIS Community instances, respect the licence pool (foia: 8 connections, ~4 free after boot) — each broker session holds a slot for its lifetime.

Instance provisioning notes (operator, not client, concerns): broker signon needs per-instance credentials and — a measured gotcha — the XWB cipher table (XUSRB1) differs between instances (vehu’s and foia’s do not match); the org keeps foia’s extracted table beside auth.env. Details: the acceptance record and docs/memory/engine-auth-env-wiring.md.

The full evidence for everything above: m9-acceptance.md.

7.9 Which instance answered, and whether the rendering travels

Section titled “7.9 Which instance answered, and whether the rendering travels”

Every result v db produces — every read, every write, and every refusal — carries two blocks that answer questions you would otherwise have to discover the hard way.

instance — which VistA answered. --engine vehu is a name on your machine, not an identity; the station number is what everything downstream partitions on. Hold two result sets from two sites and this is the only field that tells them apart. It is an opaque string: foia’s is "050", and a numeric coercion anywhere downstream silently merges it with "50".

Three states, and they are three different facts:

state means
ok the engine read its own identity
unreadable the engine looked and could not — error says why (a bare engine with no Kernel says exactly this)
undeclared the engine predates VSL*1.0*52 and was never asked

undeclared is not unreadable. An engine that was never asked has not reported an absence, and rendering the two the same way would tell you this site has no station when in truth nobody looked.

portability — whether this tier’s rendering survives a change of site. This is the property the rest of this section exists to warn you about, stated in the envelope instead of left to be met as a bug.

contract means
portable the rendering was measured to be the same across instances
instance-specific it was measured to differ — a parser written against this site may not span another
unmeasured no claim either way (this is what raw gets — it was not in the comparison)

portableTier names the tier that is portable, so a caller reading an instance-specific rendering is told where to go rather than only that it has a problem.

Why external is instance-specific. Two live instances, every populated file, every field, both tiers: on the subset where the comparison carries weight and the rendering is FileMan’s rather than the data’s, the external tier had 180 subjects whose value shapes did not intersect and the internal tier had 1. Dates are the axis. The two instances hold different records, so the comparison is of the grammar, not of a value: #200’s field 2.2 renders JUN 10,2010 on vehu and APR 20, 2026 on foia — same field, and the difference that survives every change of data is the space after the comma. Every external date rendered in FileMan’s MMM DD, YYYY grammar differed between the two instances that way. It is a substrate property, not a v db defect: both renderings are legitimate FileMan externals, so no single consumer parser spans both instances.

And it is not reachable by filtering on type — #200 field 2.2 is computed, #776 field 9 is a pointer, and both carry the same divergence. Hardening “your date fields” does not cover it. Ask for --tier internal.

scope travels with the claim, deliberately. It reads “2 instances at FileMan 22.2” because that is what was measured — both class=demo. A bare “internal is portable” would read as a fleet-wide guarantee, and this is not one. Measurement: P3 closure.

What is NOT claimed. That two instances hold the same values — they do not. That free text agrees — it does not, and it diverges identically on both tiers, because there is no rendering for a tier to change. That a third FileMan flavor behaves like these two.

The same property bites find’s key bounds. --from, --to and --prefix operate on the stored, collated key space (8.10), and what is stored is site data: the same command can return different boundaries on two sites, and a prefix that selects a page here may select nothing there. That is not an inconsistency to file — it is the same “the rendering is the site’s” fact, one layer down, and the instance block on the result is what lets you say which site the boundary came from.

On the text face both blocks print as one line each, after the command’s own output:

Refusals declare too, which is when it matters most: two instances answering the same command differently is exactly when one of them says no.

7.10 How you know what you read is true

Section titled “7.10 How you know what you read is true”

Every other section of this chapter is about what a read says. This one is about why you should believe it — and it exists because on 2026-08-18 the tool was, briefly, wrong in the worst possible way: 32 export passes exited 0, every one reported complete: true, every stream matched its own sha256, and the payload was 8.6 MB lighter than the day before, with field descriptions gone from 7,166 of 8,170 tables. Nothing caught it. It was found by eye, three screens deep in a viewer, because one header count looked low.

The lesson that produced everything below is one sentence: a digest computed by the writer attests what the writer saw, not what the database holds. Four distinct guarantees now sit between the stored global and the bytes you parse, and they are worth knowing apart, because a consumer usually needs all four and they fail in different ways.

1. The engine is running the code this host was built against. Before its first dispatch, v db folds the installed source of every engine routine it will call — 62 of them — and compares against a table generated from the pinned manifest. A mismatch refuses, SOURCE_DRIFT or SOURCE_PIN, naming the routine and both folds. This is exact source identity, not a version string, so a hand-patched routine or an unregistered load is caught even when the version it reports is right.

This refusal is common and it is not a bug. Every engine ship trips it on every deployed consumer until that consumer’s pin is regenerated. It names four suspects — the engine, the committed pin table, the composed module pin, and the built binary — and the last is gitignored, so a repo that is completely current in git can still refuse every read. Check the binary’s age before you go looking for a broken engine.

2. The envelope arrived intact. The engine stamps every successful envelope as it is framed; the host recomputes on arrival and raises INTEGRITY_FAIL / INTEGRITY_MISSING if they disagree. That covers the truncation, escaping and transport band, on every page of every verb, for about a quarter-second per megabyte of payload.

3. What the read returns matches what the global holds. This one cannot be checked by the read itself — two readings that share a code path are one oracle presented as two, which is precisely why the dictionary fingerprint was byte-identical across the regression above. It is checked instead by instruments that do not share the path: a three-way join of the interpreted value against the storage location the dictionary declares against the bytes actually at that position; the same for the dictionary plane through two independent channels; and an out-of-band engine-native dump that uses no driver, no envelope and no JSON encoder at all. They are not part of make check — they need live engines — and they run per release. Detail: technical reference §2.11.

4. The database itself is self-consistent. That is a different question again, and it has its own verb: integrity is a census of the instance’s own damage — dangling pointers, hollow records, nonconforming values, key violations, index divergence — every class reported against its own denominator. It is worth internalising that a healthy VistA is not clean in any of those classes: a stock release build ships with nonzero counts, so an absolute number means nothing until it is compared against a baseline (integrity-compare).

What to take from this if you are consuming an artifact. Its sha256 says the file matches what the writer wrote. Guarantees 1 and 2 say the writer was talking to the engine it names, through verified code, over a transport that did not corrupt anything. Guarantee 3 says the read matched storage when the instruments last ran. Guarantee 4 says what was already wrong inside the data before anybody exported it. They are four different claims and an artifact’s digest is only the first one — which is the whole reason the manifest carries the instance identity, the request, the completeness block and the engine build alongside the hash.

8. Command reference

Section titled “8. Command reference”

Every verb below was run on a live instance; the transcripts are verbatim. Verbs that reach the engine share the flags in 11.2 — --engine and --lock-wait are not repeated in each section.

8.1 Inspect — schema

Section titled “8.1 Inspect — schema”

Dump one file’s data-dictionary structure: fields with their types, pointer targets, sub-file links, cross-references, the global root, inbound pointers, and the file’s access codes. Read-only.

Notes worth knowing:

  • pointerIn / pointerInFiles are inbound pointers — which files point at this one. That is not something FileMan surfaces conveniently, and it is how you find a file’s real blast radius before touching it.
  • dinum and variableTargets are the two edge facts the type spec cannot carry, so the engine reads them where FileMan stores them and they ride every field. dinum says the field’s value IS the target’s record number (an identity extension, not a reference): #9000001’s .01 reads RP2'X — the same shape as any other transformed pointer — and only this key separates it. variableTargets is a variable pointer’s declared target-file set, in the DD’s own order; it is empty for every other data type, and empty-but-real for a variable pointer that declares none.
  • storageLocation is the physical decode map (VSL*1.0*65): the node;piece this field is stored at — 0;1 above means “the record’s 0 node, first ^-piece”. It is what lets a data artifact be aligned to the dictionary that describes it. inputTransform beside it is FileMan’s own write-path validation code for the field, verbatim — in FileMan the type is the transform, so a field’s real constraint is readable here (.01 above rejects a leading -, a quote, and anything outside 3–30 characters). Both are empty on a computed field, which is a fact rather than an absence: a computed field has no storage location, and its dictionary tail holds the algorithm instead.
  • description is the field’s own documentation (VSL*1.0*66) — the word-processing lines FileMan stores against the field, joined with newlines, which is where a data dictionary explains itself. It is empty above because #3.1’s .01 carries none; most fields do (86 % on vehu):
  • screen and screenCode are a pointer’s filter, kept as two keys because they are two facts: screen is the message a user sees when a value is rejected (#.31’s field 3: “Root File of Index must equal File of Key.”), and screenCode is the executable DIC("S") that does the rejecting. A schema that draws a pointer edge without its filter overstates the relationship. Empty on a field with no screen — a real emptiness, not a missing key.
  • recordCount is 0 here because schema does not count records. Counting is a separate, heavier pass — count or census. This is deliberate: a dictionary read never silently becomes an O(records) operation.
  • Sub-files take a sub-file number directly, and report their parent:
    Note the empty globalRoot — a sub-file lives under its parent, which is also why rows refuses to enumerate one.
  • A word-processing field appears on the parent as a sub-file link (3.5 on file #19 has typeSpec 19.06); read its content with text --show, not rows.

Listing a file’s fields with their type specs — this is how you spot a word-processing field, which shows up as a sub-file number rather than a type letter (3.5 DESCRIPTION 19.06 below):

8.2 Inspect — census

Section titled “8.2 Inspect — census”

The walked catalog: an honest record count for every ^DIC entry on the instance, with the file header’s own claim printed beside it as an integrity signal, plus sampled record sizes.

One file:

The blackout file, censused — the same 855,565 count reports, with the header divergence made explicit and a size estimate attached:

The whole instance, one bounded page at a time:

Read the two n/a cells above literally: every cell in this table is a fact or a named non-fact (VD-D67). .6 and 1.1 are nested-root files — a walked count there would tally files, not records — so there is no count to report and the table says so rather than leaving a blank you would have to interpret. The states line carries the whole vocabulary with its zeros, because “0 denied” is a measurement and an absent word is not. And every optional pass (estimated size, labels, per patient) reports what it measured or why it did not run, so a column that is missing from the table is never merely missing.

The seven states are walked, nodata (a ^DIC entry with no data global), subfile-anomaly (the ^DD carries an UP parent), nested-root, denied (a per-file read declaration refused — the row carries the rung’s own words), row-error (the row exceeded the page’s byte budget), and unclassified. The last one should never appear: it means the engine emitted a row shape this version of the host cannot render, and it is printed with the offending key named rather than quietly absorbed into walked.

Read that output as follows:

  • Claimed with != (-36) — file #.6 DD AUDIT walks 36 records while its header claims 0. That is the header divergence count in the summary: a data-quality finding about the instance, not noise from the tool. The header is reported, never trusted.
  • stopped examined, more yes — this is one page. Feed --token back verbatim to continue, or drop --one-page to let the fold run to completion.
  • --no-sizes skips the sampled record-size pass. Sizes are estimates (sampled average × walked count) and the sample is small on small files — treat them as order-of-magnitude. A size pass that fails does not discard the completed walk: the counts publish, measured.sizes names the failure, and a --out artifact records it as a named incompleteness (exit 3).
  • --pace 500ms inserts a politeness gap between the fold’s engine visits. It is a gap between visits, never a session limiter — use it when you are censusing a busy instance and do not want to monopolise it.
  • --per-patient divides each file’s walked count by the patient file’s walked count (--patient-file, default #2 PATIENT), which is how you spot files that grow per encounter rather than per patient.
  • The census carries NO labels, and that is a ruling rather than a gap. A --canon flag joined the national-dictionary review sheet here until 2026-08-13, when it was removed: the national dictionary is incomplete and untrusted today, and an untrusted source must not be joined into an artifact whose charter is that every cell is a fact or a named non-fact. A consumer that wants labels joins them downstream, against its own copy, at whatever trust level it can defend (§15).

A full-instance census is genuinely expensive — vehu’s corpus was first measured at 15,084,845 records across 121 header-diverged files. Budget for it, pace it, and prefer --file when you have a specific question.

8.3 Inspect — export

Section titled “8.3 Inspect — export”

Write the whole data dictionary to disk as JSONL plus a manifest, for use away from the engine. This is the extraction path the downstream consumers use; schema is its interactive, one-file sibling.

  • The unit of the export is the table, and a sub-file is a table (VD-D80, 2026-08-16): every exported file is written together with its whole sub-file tree — descent is recursive, applies under --files too, and de-duplicates by file number (some multiple fields share one sub-file). Naming a sub-file directly (--files 4.03) exports it and its own tree. Every subfileLink in an artifact resolves to a record in that artifact (before descent: 0 of vehu’s 3,990 resolved), and the manifest counts the sub-file records in details.subfiles.
  • A sub-file’s record count is unmeasured (VD-D81) — never a 0 that types as a count, and never a walk performed inside a dictionary read; a sub-file record self-declares via its non-empty parent. To count one honestly, v db count <subfile> walks the parent. There is no opt-out flag: a consumer wanting the prior top-level-only shape filters .dd.parent == "".
  • --files takes a list and ranges (2,19,50-59); a malformed one refuses BAD_FILES. A named set costs one single-file census per named file — never the instance sweep — so a small export is seconds. Omit it for the whole dictionary, which does sweep the instance census (minutes, run-lock held).
  • The manifest records WHICH instance it came from, at what FileMan version, what was requested, and — separately — what was requested and not written (absent), what errored (failed), and any other reason the artifact is partial (incomplete). Branch on complete. absent means exactly “this instance has no dictionary for it” (the engine’s typed U-VSL-DD-NOTFOUND); a file that has a dictionary but no census row is exported with an unmeasured count, not reported missing.
  • sha256 covers the data file exactly, so a consumer can verify the stream it holds is the stream the manifest describes.
  • Accuracy-gated: A7 gave export a three-armed oracle — the manifest against the stream it describes, a round trip against schema, and a decoder-free field-set read straight off ^DD (the arm that can see the export losing a field, which a round trip is blind to because both sides would lose it).
  • The complete schema is a bundle, not a bigger export: scripts/dd-bundle.sh <dir> runs this verb plus census, indexes --all, refs --all and the metadata-file reads (#9.4/#9.44 package ownership, #1, #.11, #.31) into one directory, records each pass’s cost, tier and manifest digest in bundle.json, and names what it did not run (fields-profile, unless asked per file). The executed run — every pass, its cost and the bundle.json it produced — is A.18; the design is the technical reference §2.7.

8.4 Inspect — refs

Section titled “8.4 Inspect — refs”

The reference map (foreign keys) around one file: what it points at, and what points at it.

  • Outbound is read from this file’s own fields. Inbound is FileMan’s own pointed-to-by catalog (^DD(f,0,"PT")) — and it is a catalog, which is why --verify exists.

  • The enumeration descends the sub-file tree. A pointer inside a multiple is a pointer, and 10/.01 → 19 above is the menu system’s defining recursion: options contain options. The Field (column) value is the field-number PATH from the top-level file down to the pointing field, so it is something you can navigate; the machine face carries fromSubfile and fieldPath beside the leaf field. Until 2026-08-14 this walk stopped at the top level, and the difference is not small — #19 reported 6 edges instead of 9, #63 reported 10 instead of 225, and #2 reported exactly its 123 top-level pointers while all 105 that live in its multiples (the insurance pointers in #2.312 among them) were invisible.

  • That completeness is the cost. One round-trip for the file plus one per sub-file walked, both reported on every answer: #2 costs 49, #63 costs 59. Nothing is capped and nothing is sampled — if the number looks large, that is the shape of the file.

  • Semantics are stored DD facts, never inferences: identity (dinum) means the pointing field’s value IS the target’s record number (a 1:1 extension, not a reference — this is the discriminator that separates “points at the patient file” from “is an extension of a patient record”); required means an absent value is broken rather than optional; may add entries / no new entries is LAYGO. An attribute that does not apply is silent — a variable pointer declares LAYGO per target, so a single answer there would be an invention.

  • A variable pointer carries its declared target SET, rendered (one of: 4, 61.2, 62.06) and emitted as one edge with a targets array — never as N indistinguishable edges, which would misstate the cardinality.

  • --direction builds one half only — outbound, inbound, or the default both. It is a cost flag, and the two halves cost very differently: the outbound half descends the sub-file tree, the inbound half is one read of the catalog node. On #19 the whole map costs 9 round-trips and --direction inbound costs 1:

    The half you did not ask for is null in the machine face — absent, not empty, so a consumer cannot read “not requested” as “none”.

  • --resolve names the inbound files and their pointing fields (an extra pass — it is off by default because it costs a read per pointer).

  • --verify audits FileMan’s catalog against a field-level enumeration: the catalog can be stale, and this is the instrument that says so.

  • --depth follows the outbound graph more than one hop — and it is the expensive one: every file reached is dumped, and now so is every sub-file below it. Measured before this change, a six-edge file cost 1,294 dumps and 2m50s at --depth 3 and #2 could not complete at all; the affordable route to a closure is the whole-dictionary sweep artifact, not live recursion.

--all — the whole graph, once, so closures are free

Section titled “--all — the whole graph, once, so closures are free”

One pass over the dictionary emits every pointer of every file at every depth, plus FileMan’s own pointed-to-by claims, and reconciles the two against each other. It is the artifact the extraction pattern needs: live --depth recursion costs 1,294 dumps and 2m50s from a six-edge file and cannot complete #2 at all, while a closure computed from the artifact takes well under a second.

Three things to know:

  • It audits the catalog in BOTH directions, which one file cannot. refs <file> --verify can refute a claim, but finding a pointer the catalog never listed needs --scope — a guess about where to look. A sweep holds every file’s fields at once, so verified (on a catalog edge) and catalogClaimed (on a field edge) are both answerable for the whole instance.
  • A partial pass makes NO catalog claim. --max-files, --token, or an unreadable dictionary entry each leave the reconciliation absent with the reason named: a claim about a file the pass never read is neither confirmed nor refuted.
  • It holds the engine’s run-lock for the whole pass (measured on vehu: 8,270 dumps, ~17 minutes, 19,187 edges). Run it when the instance is free, or take it in bounded bites with --max-files + --token.

The consumer contract — every field, the cyclic statement, and the closure recipe — is the pointer-graph contract.

8.5 Inspect — indexes

Section titled “8.5 Inspect — indexes”

Which of this file’s indexes can I actually look things up with? schema lists a file’s cross-references. This measures them.

The gap between the two is not a detail. On vehu:

Five of #44’s cross-references are registered only in FileMan’s new-style INDEX file (#.11), which schema does not read. On #2 PATIENT the same gap is 384 → 485.

The columns

Section titled “The columns”
column what it measures
source which register declared the name — dd-ix (a traditional ^DD definition), index-file (a #.11 registration), or both
kind the shared classifier’s word, the same one find dispatches on. The vocabulary is open: a kind this catalog has no rules for rides through by name, is counted, and nothing is derived from it (kwic on #8925.1 is the measured example)
Seek whether a seek is admitted. unmeasured is a real state — see below
Cond whether the registration carries a SET CONDITION. A conditional index holds a subset of the file
Stored whether a subtree named after it exists under this file’s data root, on this instance
Shape the sampled subscript depth, then which positions hold a record number
Key whether the stored key is the indexed column’s value, and the measured key length ceiling

walkable and stored are different properties

Section titled “walkable and stored are different properties”

A seek needs a mechanically-maintained cross-reference. Storing entries needs nothing but a site routine that writes them. On #2 PATIENT, 446 of 485 cross-references store nothing on vehu, and most of the ones that do refuse a seek — those subtrees are how this database is actually navigated. Stored: present with Seek: no is the signal to reach for find … --raw; Stored: absent is a measurement about this instance, not an error.

The record id is not reliably the last subscript

Section titled “The record id is not reliably the last subscript”

Shape reads 4 · id@3 (not the last) on #100 AR — the patient-orders path. Four subscripts, the order number at position 3, and a trailing sequence number that a walk assuming “last subscript = record id” would have read as a record number. id@ lists every position that addressed a live record in every sampled entry; id@none means none did, which is also an answer.

Key — and why the byte figure is not decoration

Section titled “Key — and why the byte figure is not decoration”

FileMan’s stock B cross-reference stores $E(X,1,30) — the first 30 characters. Nothing in a mismatch sample can see that if every sampled value is shorter than 30:

300 entries agreed with the field’s value, and every key stopped at exactly 30 bytes. The agreement proves nothing; the ceiling is the tell. So:

  • identity (n=K) is unfalsified, never proven — a sample can only fail to refute one.
  • transformed is proof, and names the record it was proven at — or says (declared) when the #.11 registration declares a TRANSFORM FOR STORAGE, which is proof from the dictionary with no sampling at all.
  • unmeasured says why: not seekable, keyed on more than one field, the column is computed or word-processing, or the index stores nothing here.

The seek license table below the listing turns that into the sentence you can act on. Only prefix seeks are ever proposed over a sampled identity, and only up to the longest key the sample measured — an unfalsified identity means no sampled value was cut, so whatever length the index truncates at, it is at least that long, and a prefix inside it survives the cut. (Until Q4.1 this said minimum, which measures something else entirely — how short the shortest indexed value happens to be. On #44 B that is 2 bytes, against a real ceiling of 30.) Equality and range seeks are listed as sample-supported, residual under-return risk, because a seek over a truncating index positions past the stored bucket, visits zero candidates, and a kept predicate never runs on what the seek never reached.

A second risk rides beside that one and is reported separately: whether the index holds every record. A #.11 registration declaring no SET CONDITION provably does; a traditional ^DD definition declares no condition field at all, so whether its logic files every record is site M v db never evaluates — and that is 5,394 of vehu’s 5,665 seekable regular cross-references, including every stock B. The licence says POPULATION UNPROVEN there. The positioning is exact either way; what needs checking is the population, which is what --explain states, and what its equivalence check settles (§8.8).

Two more things it reports

Section titled “Two more things it reports”

Defined here, stored elsewhere. #.11 indexes registrations two ways — by the file an index is defined on and by the file at whose root its entries live. Membership here is the second, because that is what the engine resolves a name through. On vehu #2 the two differ by ten: AX/AY → #2.98, G202501–G202504 → #2.025, and so on. They are reported by name with their root file rather than listed as #2’s indexes, because find 2 AX has never heard of AX.

What it cost. One dictionary read, two #.11 seeks, one registration read, then one stored-entry probe per listed cross-reference and one key sample per seekable single-field one. indexes 2 is 489 round trips; indexes 2 --walkable --key-sample 10 is 61 and takes seven seconds. --kind and --walkable filter before any probe runs, and the listing always carries the full denominator so a filtered answer never reads as the whole file.

--all — the whole instance, in one engine-side pass

Section titled “--all — the whole instance, in one engine-side pass”

The per-file form probes once per cross-reference. --all does not repeat that loop 8,300 times: the sweep is computed engine-side (ixcensus^VSLDD, VSL*1.0*61) and paged back.

9,739 cross-references across 2,879 files in about four seconds (foia: 9,699 across 2,826). The cost is not a trick — roughly 90% of declared cross-references store nothing, so their enumerability is a single $DATA, and the rest cost a bounded 20-node walk.

Without --out it prints the same table the per-file listing does, with a File column in front — filter it, or it is 9,739 rows:

Three things to know before consuming it:

  • key is unmeasured on every row, and says so. Deciding whether a stored key IS the indexed column’s value costs a record read per sampled entry per cross-reference. That question belongs to one file at a time — the header block points at --key-sample, and the row never leaves the cell blank.
  • files represented is not the number of files swept. It counts the files the rows came from; a file declaring no cross-reference emits no row. Sub-files are outside the sweep entirely (the enumerability half needs a data root) — ask one by number instead.
  • The two scopes are one column set. A sweep row renders through the same cells as a per-file row, and the counts agree: #2 answers 485 and #44 answers 19 either way.

The dials are --sample N (stored entries read per cross-reference, default 20), --page-size N (rows per engine page, default 2000), --pace D (a politeness gap between pages for a background run — the artifact is pacing-invariant, same sha256), and --one-page/--token to walk it by hand. --all refuses beside a file number, and each single-file flag refuses beside --all, rather than being silently ignored.

--out DIR writes indexes.jsonl + manifest.json under the index-sweep input contract. A --kind/ --walkable run is a deliberate subset: it stays complete: true, records the filter in request, and carries the denominator it was cut from in details.declared. --one-page is a named incompleteness and exits non-zero.

8.6 Analyze — estimate

Section titled “8.6 Analyze — estimate”

How big would this extract be? Record count × sampled mean record size, summed over a file set, and fitted against a cap.

  • --cap fits the estimate against a size budget and exits 3 over cap, so a script can branch on it.
  • The sample basis rides the output, in words — ≤20 records per file. A file with skewed record sizes is coarsely sized and the line says so rather than implying precision.
  • A verdict exists only when everything asked for was sized. A named file this instance does not have lands in skipped; a named file whose census carries no size — a sub-file (its records store inside the parent’s global) or a file with no data root, the engine’s no-data-global provenance — lands in unsized. Either way fits is absent and the command exits 3 INCOMPLETE, naming every unsized file — even under --cap, where the refusal outranks the cap comparison it could not make. (Before 2026-08-16 an all-sub-file selection sized to zero and passed any cap green at exit 0.) The measured files are still reported; to count a sub-file honestly, v db count <subfile> walks the parent. A malformed --files refuses BAD_FILES.
  • A named --files set costs one single-file census per named file — never the whole-instance sweep — so sizing a handful of files is seconds. Omitting --files sizes everything and does sweep the instance census (minutes, run-lock held). --top 0 lists every file (0 = all, uniform across verbs).
  • ⚠️ This is the only shipped verb with no accuracy oracle, and that is a ruling rather than an omission: there is no stored true size to compare an estimate against, so the strongest constructible check is an error band — it can report plausible, never correct, and a probe that can only ever pass is not an oracle. It is printed on every green gate run so the gap stays visible (§12).

8.7 Data — count

Section titled “8.7 Data — count”

The honest record count of one file: a resumable IEN-walk fold with a completeness block. This is the verb that most directly answers the population defect.

  • walked is the answer. claimed is the header’s p4 field, printed so you can see when it is wrong — here by 167.
  • hollow counts subscripts with no 0 node. Such a record renders identically to one with an empty field, so it is flagged explicitly rather than silently counted.
  • pages is how many bounded engine visits the fold took. examined is the count charged on the final page, not the whole fold.
  • emitted/distinct are 0 because a fold emits no rows — it emits a number.

--one-page stops after one bounded page and prints a resume token; --token resumes verbatim. --pace spaces the visits.

--where — how many records match

Section titled “--where — how many records match”

The same closed filter table rows takes (§11.7), folded instead of emitted. walked becomes what passed, and the completeness block keeps it attached to its denominator:

8 is never printed on its own: examined 70 and filtered 62 ride beside it, so “8 matched” cannot detach from “…of 70 looked at, walk finished”. The predicate is folded into the cursor, so a mid-fold change to the filter or the DD refuses U-VSL-ROW-STALE rather than resuming a different question.

Filters apply to the top-level file population only. A --parent-scoped or depth fold refuses U-VSL-ROW-FILTER rather than accept a predicate it would have to ignore — filter that walk with rows instead, or count the instance unfiltered.

--index — how many entries

Section titled “--index — how many entries”

This is a different question from count 3.1, and three things say so:

  • population index:B — the answer set is the index’s.
  • The number is of entries, never de-duplicated. A record with several in-range keys counts once per key; a dangling entry (no record behind it) counts too, and is tallied in hollow.
  • claimed is omitted, and the omission is stated. The header’s p4 is a claim about records; printing it beside an entry count would invite exactly the comparison it cannot support. It reads as a sentence, not as 0.

--from/--to bound the walk inclusively in stored key space and --prefix is a byte-prefix (they do not combine). Passing any of them without --index is refused BAD_SEEK before an engine visit: a record walk has no keys to bound, so the constraint would be accepted and silently ignored.

Both --where and --index need VSL*1.0*55 on the engine. Below that floor the host refuses AGG_SINCE before dispatching — because an older engine does not refuse them either: it never binds the parameter and returns the unfiltered whole-file count under ok:true.

8.8 Data — rows

Section titled “8.8 Data — rows”

One bounded page of a file’s records over the declared IEN walk. The workhorse read.

--explain reports what the read would do — its population, which index can position which predicate, the cost class and the command to run — without reading a data page. It is documented once, below (The plan — --explain), and works the same on find.

Filtering. --where '<field> <op> <value>', repeatable (repeats AND together). The operator set is a closed table — no client M is ever XECUTEd:

examined 6, filtered 1, emitted 5 — six candidates were visited, one was rejected by the predicate.

Three refusals define the filter surface, and each names its reason:

The first is the closed table refusing to grow. The second is the whole reason the table is closed: DDR XECUTEd client-supplied M as a screen, and a computed field would smuggle site DD M back into the per-candidate loop by another door. The third has one exception, and only one: bound is admissible on a multiple — it reads storage rather than a value, so “this record has sub-records at all” is answerable where “a sub-record equals X” is not (§11.7).

The byte budget. Ask for every field of #200 and one record fills the page:

stopped bytes with examined 2: the second candidate was visited, would not fit, and the page closed cleanly at a record boundary. Cost tracks field count, not row count — which is why a row ceiling alone would not have caught this.

--iens — read the records you name, not the file. Every other population here is a walk. This one is a list you supply, and it exists because the alternative is a loop of single reads: measured, a get per record costs 253 ms (process, lock and envelope, per row) against ~25 ms/record paged — 10× at ten records, and linear in the count.

Three things in that output are the contract:

  • rows come back in SUPPLIED order, not collation order — 2, 1, 2, with each row carrying pos, its place in the list you sent;
  • a repeated IEN is served per request — the list is data, so asking twice answers twice, and emitted 3 · distinct 2 says so out loud;
  • misses is on every page, empty when there are none. A requested IEN with no record is named with the position that asked for it, never dropped:

A hollow record — a subscript with no 0 node — is not a miss. It is a record, and it comes back flagged ("hollow": true). Present-but-empty and absent are different facts, and only one of them is a hole.

--iens-file PATH takes the list from a file — one IEN per line, blank lines skipped — and - reads standard input, which is how a list of pointer values from one read feeds the next:

The list is chunked for you. The dispatch command has a hard engine ceiling (YottaDB’s indirection limit), so a cohort of any size cannot ride one request: the host cuts the list into chunks that fit and the cursor is a position in the whole list. A page that runs out of chunk says stopped chunk — the transport ended the page, not the population — and the continuation token picks up inside the same list. A 4,000-IEN cohort walks in three engine visits:

Exit 3, not 0: 1,441 of the records asked for are not there, and an artifact that did not say so would be the whole problem. absent names them; the per-page misses keep their positions.

Resuming needs the same list. The token an --iens read prints carries where in your list it stopped, so pass the same cohort back with it. An edited list refuses rather than serving a plausible subset — the cursor is bound to the list’s own identity:

--iens needs engine build VSL*1.0*54 or later, and the host checks before it asks. This one is worth stating plainly: an older engine does not refuse the flag — it never binds the list and reads the whole file instead.

--ids — the reference map

Section titled “--ids — the reference map”

A page of records tells you what each pointer field says. --ids tells you where each one goes, as a parallel map beside the fields — never a changed value, because the value contract is load-bearing everywhere here:

Every ref is a get --ref away (8.8), and a set of them feeds straight into --iens — which is what closes the loop without a join: --ids says where to go, --iens fetches the set in one conversation.

A variable pointer resolves per record. Its type is a bare V and the file it names is data: the stored value is <ien>;<global root>, and the root elects the target from the field’s declared set. On the page above, field 2 (DIALOG) is 101.41 on one record and 101 on the next — one field, two files, decided row by row. This is the case FMQL’s filter silently matched nothing on.

A root the dictionary does not declare still resolves — and says so:

#100’s ITEM ORDERED declares targets 19/60/101.41 and its records store ^ORD(101,, ^RAMIS(71, and ^PS(50.3, — 74 of 799 references over 200 rows on vehu (9.3 %). That is a real, measured disagreement between the dictionary and the data, and FileMan renders those values happily because it dereferences by the stored root and never consults the declared set.

So --ids asks the same question FileMan does: which file owns this root? ^DIC(f,0,"GL") is FileMan’s own statement of that, so the answer is read from the dictionary of files rather than guessed — and resolvedBy: "root" marks it, because “the DD declared this target” and “the data pointed here and the DD did not say so” are different provenances and a consumer reconciling against the dictionary needs to know which one it holds. A declared target carries no marker.

When no file claims the root, the entry keeps its old shape — the record number, the root it saw, and why it stopped:

⚠️ This needs VSL*1.0*63 on the engine. Against an older build the flag does not fail — it answers the smaller, older way, naming such a reference instead of addressing it. The refusal sentence tells you which you have: the and no file on this instance claims it either clause is present only when the engine was actually asked.

What it costs. The map needs each pointer’s internal value. On --tier internal the page already carries it, so --ids is free. On the default external tier it is one companion read per page — the same request re-issued at the internal tier projecting only the reference fields — which is density-dependent and bounded by roughly doubling the read on pointer-dense rows (measured at demo sparsity, the two tiers time the same: 470 ms vs 444 ms over 20 star rows of #2, because most pointer fields are empty and never resolve). A projection with no reference field in it does no extra read at all. Machine consumers should be on --tier internal --ids, where the question costs nothing.

Every page states its own coverage in an ids block:

The root lookups line appears only when the page needed one. It is one call per distinct root, not per row: measured on 40 rows of #100 field 7, 39 references resolved by root and it cost 3 lookups.

--ids does not combine with --tier raw (IDS_RAW_TIER): that tier returns data nodes, which have no field types to resolve references from. Under --with-multiples the map covers the record’s own fields and says so — a sub-record’s pointers belong to the sub-file’s dictionary, which this map is not built from.

A direct sub-file of a top-level parent depth-walks. #200.02 (the DIVISION multiple under #200 NEW PERSON) pages across every parent’s sub-records at once; each row carries its full iens, and population reads sub:<file>:

iens is child-first with its trailing comma ("500,1," = sub-record 500 under parent 1) — reading a row’s own IEN off iens rather than off ien alone is what lets you tell three sub-records with the same sub-IEN, under three different parents, apart.

--parent scopes the read to one parent instance — the parent’s own IENS, child-first with its trailing comma ('1,' for a direct sub-file one level up; 'd1,d0,' two levels). Scoped, each row’s iens is implied and only the sub-record’s own ien is printed, and population records the scope:

--with-multiples — the record WITH its sub-records. A plain * is flat and declares what it left out; --with-multiples projects every non-word-processing multiple inline under its field number, recursively, each sub-record carrying its own iens:

Under the flag projection.excluded is empty — there is nothing to exclude — and the note says so. A #63 LAB DATA record comes back with its 63.04 chemistry panels, each carrying its own sub-sub-records: one invocation, decoded, no client-side reassembly.

The crossover — cohorts inline, bulk per sub-file. The inline tree is for a cohort: records you can name, read whole. For bulk extraction of a deep file, prefer the per-sub-file streams (rows 63.04 --out, rows 63.041 --out) and join them downstream by iens — a single lab patient’s subtree can exceed any byte budget, and a bulk run that names hundreds of over-budget records is honest but the wrong tool. The two forms compose: same iens vocabulary, same manifest shape.

When a record’s tree does not fit. The page closes at a record boundary, so one oversize record never truncates another. That record rides the stream as a typed stub instead:

U-VSL-ROW-TREESIZE names the record, the offending multiple and the paged alternative. It is deliberately not U-VSL-ROW-TOOBIG, which means one oversize value — conflating them hid which limit fired.

Every data --out manifest pairs with its dictionary. Internal-tier data is the portable tier, and it is meaningless without the DD that decodes it: sets decode in the dictionary, dates by their DD type, pointers by their target. So the manifest carries the dictionary’s fingerprint as read in the same run —

— and a consumer can verify the pair rather than trust that the two files travelled together. A file whose DD could not be read leaves the pairing unmeasured and says so in incomplete; it never poses as verified.

Nesting depth is no longer a limit. An earlier build served the unscoped walk only for direct multiples of a top-level file, and refused anything deeper. Since the depth-walk engine build (2026-08-13) it rides a generalized odometer over the whole parent chain, so a sub-file at any depth walks file-wide — verified on both engines. #63.041 nests under #63.04, itself a sub-file of #63 LAB DATA — three levels down, and it needs no scope at all:

The IENS is the address that makes it navigable: 1,7059189.8872,2, reads child-first, so this is sub-record 1 of sub-record 7059189.8872 of record 2. --parent is still there when you want one parent’s children rather than the file’s — that is a scoping choice now, not a workaround. U-VSL-ROW-SUBFILE survives for the case that remains genuinely unanswerable: a parent chain that does not resolve (over 20 levels, or a cycle in the dictionary).

(v db schema 200.02 still works — the dictionary side has no such restriction, and distribution reports sub-file depth.)

The budget demonstration. This is the single most important behaviour to understand, because it is where DDR’s central defect was:

Zero rows — but not a silent empty result. The block says exactly what happened: 500 candidates visited, all 500 rejected by the filter, the --examined budget ended the page, and there is more data behind it. Under DDR the identical request returns an empty list with no error and no indication that a scan is under way.

The plan — --explain

Section titled “The plan — --explain”

What would this read actually do, and is there a cheaper way? --explain on rows or find parses the request, reports what it would do, and exits — without reading a single data page.

It is a flag, not a verb. A standalone explain rows … would re-declare every read flag as a copy that can drift; this way there is one grammar.

What it will and will not tell you

Section titled “What it will and will not tell you”
it reports it refuses to report
the population, in the engine’s own words (file, index:B, sub:44.001, ien-list(12)) a selectivity estimate — that needs statistics this tool does not keep
a cost class: seek · seek+filter · walk · walk+filter a row estimate, ever
which index can position which clause, and under what licence a seek it cannot license (see below)
the record count — only from a --census artifact, cited with its instance and moment a count from anywhere else. Without the artifact it says unmeasured and names the command that makes one
a guaranteed-empty verdict, from a --profile artifact an emptiness it has not measured
the command to run, with its basis that the command is equivalent — that is the equivalence check’s job

The licensing rule, in one paragraph

Section titled “The licensing rule, in one paragraph”

A prefix seek is proposed over a sampled-identity key, bounded by the longest key the sample measured. Equality and range seeks are never proposed from a sample — they are listed as possible, sample-supported, residual under-return risk, because a seek over a truncating index positions past the stored bucket and the kept predicate never runs on what the seek never visits. contains and negations position nothing. A compound index positions on its leading key only. A conditional index is order-only: it holds a subset of the file. And <field> bound is answered by walking the whole index — that is a claim about membership, not keys, so truncation cannot touch it, but it needs a registration that declares no SET CONDITION.

Three artifacts, verified before they are cited

Section titled “Three artifacts, verified before they are cited”

Each is passed with --indexes / --census / --profile, and each is checked before a number from it appears: the manifest must be beside it, its verb must match, the stream must match the sha256 the manifest claims, and it must come from this instance — an artifact from another site is a typed refusal (ARTIFACT_INSTANCE). An engine that never declared an identity cannot be matched against, and the plan says so rather than assuming.

Without --indexes, nothing is licensed. Whether a key is the field’s value costs a record read per sampled entry per cross-reference — a data read, which a plan does not make. So the planner reports order only and names the command that would change the answer.

The equivalence check

Section titled “The equivalence check”

The plan’s proposal replaces a filtered walk with a positioned seek, and the two are equivalent only if the index positions exactly and holds every record. The second is unprovable for a traditional definition. Check it on your own data:

Measured 2026-08-14 on both gold engines, this agreed on every non-empty pair tried (#44 B 23=23, #19 B 348=348 vehu / 337=337 foia, #200 B 125=125 vehu / 3=3 foia, #3.1 B 5=5). It is also a standing probe — P16-equivalence in the capability sweep — so a truncating or conditional index becomes a red gate rather than a review finding.

8.9 Data — get

Section titled “8.9 Data — get”

One record’s fields by IEN — byte-exact, so .5 is a real IEN and not a typo for 5:

(Abridged — the default projection is every field, so #200 returns well over a hundred. Use --fields in practice.)

get is unpaged: it is bounded by the engine’s frame ceiling and returns one record or a typed U-VSL-ROW-NOTFOUND:

--ref — read the record a reference names

Section titled “--ref — read the record a reference names”

--ref takes one token, <file>-<ien>, which is exactly the ref an --ids map emits. It is the same address the two positionals give, in the form a pointer hands you, so following a reference never means taking it apart first:

The split is on the first -; neither half can contain one, and both ride verbatim (there is no _-for-. respelling anywhere in this domain). The machine face echoes the reference back as data.ref, so a consumer that followed a pointer can pair the answer with what it followed.

Naming a record twice is a refusal, not a precedence rule — get 200 .5 --ref 3.2-9 refuses REF_AND_ARGS, because a caller who wrote both meant two different records and answering for one of them silently is the defect class this plane exists to remove. get with no target refuses NO_TARGET; a file with no IEN refuses NO_IEN; a malformed reference refuses BAD_REF.

--ids — where each pointer goes

Section titled “--ids — where each pointer goes”

A pointer’s rendered value says what it points at, never where: 9.3 reads C-VT100, and turning that back into a record is a lookup you have to invent. --ids states it instead, as a parallel map beside the fields — the values themselves are untouched, because the value contract is load-bearing everywhere in this plane:

It works the same on rows and find, including the stored-entry walk. See 8.7 for the variable-pointer rule, the cost, and what an unresolved reference looks like.

8.10 Data — find

Section titled “8.10 Data — find”

Lookup over a named index — a declared index walk in emission order. This is the verb to use when you want to seek rather than scan, because the key bounds are pushed down to the index:

Read this carefully — the differences from rows are the point:

  • population index:B — the answer set is the index’s, not the file’s. That is stated, never assumed. If the index is incomplete, this is the field that tells you the answer might be too.
  • emitted vs distinct are reported separately and an index walk is never silently de-duplicated. A record indexed twice is emitted twice, and you can see it.
  • Entries are in emission order and are never re-sorted host-side. Sorting by IEN would clobber duplicate emissions, which is exactly the signal you need.
  • Key bounds are in STORED key space — the collated subscript, not the external value. --prefix is a byte-prefix constraint and does not combine with --from/--to.
  • The cursor is (key, ien) — note the base64 key inside the token.

A key range — inclusive on both ends, in stored key space:

--where on find filters the candidate record after the index has positioned. It does not affect the seek — which is exactly what the completeness block shows: the seek narrowed 1,496 records to 16 candidates, and the filter then rejected all 16.

An unknown index is a typed refusal, not an empty list — which is the exact DDR behaviour (a typo’d index yields an empty result with no error) that this verb exists to not reproduce:

Index types that cannot be walked safely are refused rather than approximated — MUMPS-type, trigger, compound-key, record-level, computed-style and dangling (a directory row whose definition is gone) all raise U-VSL-ROW-IXTYPE, because site-authored index logic is never evaluated. The kind column in schema’s xref table is the same classification find dispatches on — one shared classifier, so what schema calls regular is exactly what find will walk, and a refused kind names itself in the refusal message.

--out — the index population as an artifact

Section titled “--out — the index population as an artifact”

rows --out walks a file to exhaustion into JSONL plus a manifest. find --out does the same over an index population, on the same contract — so an index-driven extract is one invocation rather than a paging loop you write yourself:

Two things make the artifact readable months later by someone who cannot go back and check it:

  • The manifest names the population. details.population is the engine’s own index:B, lifted to the top of the evidence — so a reader knows this is a slice of the file chosen by a key range, not the file. Every page’s completeness block rides underneath it verbatim, never summed by the host.
  • complete means what it says. The walk has exactly one clean exit — the engine hands back no continuation token. Every other stop (a failed page, the --max-pages bound) appends a named reason to incomplete, and the command exits non-zero. A truncated artifact that looks whole is the single worst thing this verb could produce.

It also carries the same dictionary pairing rows --out does: a fingerprint of the DD the values were decoded against, so --tier internal data and its dictionary travel as a pair you can verify rather than a discipline you have to remember.

List a file’s indexes with schema:

The stored-entry walk — find --raw

Section titled “The stored-entry walk — find --raw”

Look at that list again. On #200, one cross-reference is regular and the rest are mumps — and find refuses every one of the mumps ones, because the logic that maintains them is site-authored M this tool will never evaluate. Measured across the database the ratio is worse and more interesting: 354 of #2 PATIENT’s 386 cross-references are mumps, and those subtrees are how VistA is actually navigated. #100 ORDER’s AR is the patient-orders path.

--raw is the door to them. It does not seek and it does not interpret: it walks the cross-reference’s own subtree and emits one row per stored node, with the whole subscript path.

Four things in that output are the whole design, and each of them exists because the obvious alternative is wrong.

--at takes the key AS STORED, which is not the key you expect. “This patient” on #100 AR is 100000;DPT( — a record id with its global root appended, the variable-pointer spelling — not the bare 100000. Every first attempt that passes the bare id returns nothing, correctly and uselessly. --at repeats, one per subscript level, and the levels must be contiguous from the first. Its value is taken byte for byte: a stored key containing a comma (SMITH,JOHN) is one level, never two.

The record id is read from a MEASURED position, never from the last subscript. Look at the path above: (patient key, inverse date, ORDER id, sequence). The record number is at position 3 of 4. A walk that assumed the terminal subscript would have read the trailing sequence number as an order number — silently, on the most valuable path in the database. So every page samples up to 20 entries, tallies how often each position resolves to a live record of this file, and reports the verdict with its evidence:

verdict what it means
elected one position out-resolves every other; that is the one used
pinned you supplied --ien-at N; the measurement is still reported, so a pin that disagrees with it is visible
ambiguous two or more positions resolve equally often — nothing is claimed, entries come back with paths and no candidate
none no position resolved; the entries are real, but they are not subscripted by this file’s records
unsampled there was nothing to sample

ambiguous is common and it is a measurement, not a failure. #19 AD stores (item, OPTION id, sub-id), and its key is a small integer that collides with live record numbers, so positions 1 and 2 both resolve 20 out of 20 on both gold engines. Guessing between them would report a menu item as an option. Pin it once you know which it is:

Asking for a projection (--fields or --tier) when nothing was elected refuses rather than handing back every row unprojected. Without either flag there is no projection at all: the walk’s product is the path, and no record is read.

A candidate that is not a live record is NAMED, never skipped. The row comes back flagged dangling with the subscript still reported, because that is a finding about the cross-reference — three stock cross-references were measured with live entries whose definition is gone, and this is the only instrument that can reach them. An entry with fewer subscripts than the elected position is flagged short, which is a different fact and says so.

A declared cross-reference that stores nothing here refuses (U-VSL-ROW-NOSUBTREE) instead of returning an empty page — 70% of the non-walkable ones store nothing on a given instance, and “this instance files nothing here” is a different answer from “your --at matched nothing”, which is an empty page. A name the dictionary does not declare refuses U-VSL-ROW-NOINDEX: --raw reads declared cross-references, never an arbitrary subtree.

--ids works here too, and needs no --fields. The reference map is asked for by name, so the walk fetches the reference fields itself — which turns a page of subscript paths into a page of places to go:

That is this patient’s orders, each entry carrying the ordering provider, the dialog and the location as addresses rather than as renderings. See 8.7 for the rules and the cost.

Flag notes. --from/--to/--prefix and --where refuse under --raw — a seek positions a walkable index over a key range and this walk positions with --at, so accepting either and ignoring it would answer a wider question under exit 0. And --raw is not --tier raw: --raw chooses the population (stored entries), --tier raw chooses the projection grain (a record’s data nodes). They compose.

That second one is a genuine name collision, and it comes from the accepted design rather than from an oversight — so the tool signposts it instead of relying on you to have read this paragraph. Whenever find, count --index or distribution --index refuses a cross-reference as unseekable, the refusal now carries the way out:

--tier raw is the word most people reach for first when they want “the raw thing”, and it lands on exactly this refusal — which used to be a dead end. A correct refusal that leaves you with nowhere to go is how a capable tool reads as an incapable one.

--out lands the whole walk as JSONL plus a manifest, on find --out’s contract. The manifest lifts the population, the elected position and its verdict to the top of its evidence, and keeps every page’s declaration block — because a file of subscript paths whose record-id position is not recorded with them is a set of subscripts nobody downstream can resolve.

8.11 Data — distribution

Section titled “8.11 Data — distribution”

Bounded distinct-value / top-N distribution of one field — the variety axis FileMan has no API for. On a multiple field it reports sub-file depth instead.

On a multiple, the same verb reports sub-file depth instead of values — how many sub-entries each parent record carries:

#200’s DIVISION multiple: 725 users have none, 762 have exactly one, and nine have between two and four. Note examined 2279 against records 1496 — the 783 sub-entries are each charged too, because the per-candidate cost law does not stop at the top level.

Other notes:

  • --top bounds only what the human face prints; the machine face always carries the full map.
  • outside the map tallies empty and oversize values separately — they are counted but never merged into a bucket, so a field that is 57% empty cannot masquerade as a value.
  • Every run names its verdict: complete (the walk finished — this map is the distribution), partial (a budget or --one-page bounded it mid-flight, so the tallies and buckets are a prefix), or unique-valued-at-scale (below).
  • This verb is how you answer “is this field actually used?” before writing an extract against it.

When a field is too varied to summarise

Section titled “When a field is too varied to summarise”

--distinct-cap is the walk-level distinct cap (default 4,096, ceiling 65,536), forwarded to the engine’s page maps as well. Crossing it does not produce a shortened top-N — it produces a verdict, and the verdict is a finding about your data rather than a missing answer:

Three things to read carefully there:

  • It exits non-zero and publishes no buckets. Handing you the 4,096 values it happened to collect first, under a success code, would be exactly the silent truncation this refusal exists to prevent.
  • distinct is stated as a lower bound, because that is what it is: the merge stops the instant the cap is crossed, so the number is the cap’s shadow, not the field’s variety. Raise --distinct-cap if you need the real figure — #4’s true distinct on vehu is 4,560, and #100’s is 40,947, a number often quoted as 17,796 because that quote was itself a capped view.
  • The machine face carries all of it, under data.overflow, beside ok:false — so a catalog can render “effectively unique-valued (at least 4,560 over 5,053 records)” in a cell instead of leaving the cell blank.

--where — the distribution of a subset

Section titled “--where — the distribution of a subset”

The same filter table again, applied before the tally: a rejected candidate is charged to examined and filtered, and tallied nowhere. So v db distribution 200 9.3 --where '53.1 bound' is “what terminal types do the users who have a service set actually use” — one walk, not two.

--index — the index’s own keys, and what that is NOT

Section titled “--index — the index’s own keys, and what that is NOT”

The cheap distribution. It tallies the keys the index already holds, so the cost is index entries rather than record reads and no retriever runs at all. That is where real selectivity comes from when you want it — a measurement you chose to pay for, not a statistic the tool cached and hoped stayed true.

Two structural consequences of never reading a record:

  • A dangling entry still tallies. There is no record for it to be missing from.
  • --where is refused here (U-VSL-ROW-FILTER). A predicate needs a record to evaluate against, and quietly turning a key walk into a per-record retrieval would erase the reason to use this at all.

And the caveat that matters more than any of that: a key distribution is not the field’s distribution. It describes the records the index covers, and the verb prints so on every run:

Read caveat 2 against #200’s field 9.3 above: 850 of 1,496 records are empty there. A key tally over an index on that field would report the 646 non-empty ones and be entirely correct — and anyone reading it as “the distribution of 9.3” would be wrong by more than half the file. You can watch that arithmetic directly with --where, which reaches the same 646 from the other side:

1,496 examined, 646 tallied, and empty falls to 0 — because bound removed exactly the records an index would never have held. Same 646 either way; only the key tally gets there without reading a record.

The caveats ride the machine face (data.caveats) and the --out manifest too, because the artifact outlives the terminal that printed it.

The counts are of entries, so the denominator changes with them: the table’s column reads Entries, not Records, and the % column is a share of entries.

--index here needs VSL*1.0*56, one patch above the VSL*1.0*55 the other three aggregate flags need. The parameters all landed together in *55; what *56 fixed is that the key tally’s door tested “was a field supplied?” in a form no host could satisfy, so every host key tally on a *55 engine refused for naming a field it had not named.

8.12 Data — fields-profile

Section titled “8.12 Data — fields-profile”

How many records hold a stored value in each field of a file — the whole dictionary tallied in one walk.

This is the instrument this database’s sparsity demands. VistA sites extend a file by adding fields: #63.04 (the chemistry/haematology results multiple) carries 965 of them, because each site’s lab tests arrive as columns. So the first question any extract asks — which of these columns actually hold data here? — used to cost one full walk of the file per column, 965 of them. It now costs one:

--empty flips the listing to the other half of the same answer — the columns holding nothing — which on a wide file is usually the half you came for. --top 0 lists them all; the machine face always carries every field.

What “bound” means. A scalar is bound when its ^-piece of its storage node is non-empty. A multiple is bound when its sub-file 0-node is set — “this record has sub-entries”, answered without enumerating them. Both are the same notion the bound predicate reads (§7.4 and --where "<field> bound"), and deliberately so: this verb tells you which columns are worth predicating on, so it must agree with the predicate about what stored means. It does, by construction — one shared decision in the engine — and the accuracy sweep checks it in both directions.

What cannot be measured is declared, never zeroed. A computed field, a field the dictionary gives no storage node, and a field stored at an extract location rather than a readable piece each get a row carrying their reason instead of a tally:

A zero there would be indistinguishable from the answer you are looking for. They are counted apart on both faces: measured + skipped = fields, and populated + empty = measured.

It reports field NUMBERS, not names. The dictionary serves a field’s name one engine visit at a time, so decorating 965 rows would cost the 965 visits this verb exists to avoid. Join them from v db schema <file> — and when you write the profile to disk, the --out manifest carries that dictionary’s fingerprint, so the pairing is verifiable rather than remembered (§8.8 has the same pairing on data extracts).

Sub-files. Without --parent, a sub-file is profiled across every parent’s instance (the whole depth walk) — which is what makes the #63.04 answer above a statement about the instance rather than about one patient. With --parent <IENS>, it is scoped to one multiple instance.

Paging. Every page carries every field, and the pager merges by summation. That is why a zero is a real zero rather than something you infer from a dictionary you also had to fetch: a field that appears at 0 on every page is empty here. An empty population still reports the whole dictionary at zero and says so, rather than rendering a blank:

Budgets. The row set is the dictionary, whose size is known before the walk starts — so a file too wide for --bytes refuses before doing any work, rather than dropping fields to fit. That is the opposite of distribution, which defers mid-walk; deferral is only honest when the thing being bounded genuinely grows as the walk proceeds.

Engine floor: VSL*1.0*57. An older engine does not have the verb.

8.13 Authorize — policy

Section titled “8.13 Authorize — policy”

Show or declare the instance’s authorization surface. Enforcement is engine-side at every data verb’s door — this command is a window and a forwarder, never the enforcer. There is no host-side check you could patch out.

The machine face separates what is declared from what is read live:

prod is not a declaration — it is the live reading of Kernel’s own production tripwire. class is what you declared. When those two disagree, the engine believes the tripwire.

The declaration grammar is a closed set, enforced engine-side (a bad key or value is U-VSL-POL-ARG, naming the offending token — never a host guess):

key values effect
class demo | real what kind of instance this is
read-enable on | off the read gate
read:<file> allow | deny per-file read policy
write:<file> allow | deny per-file write policy

One declaration or revocation per invocation, and both are mutations — they need --yes and they are audited:

Writes are default-deny. Reads are allowed unless denied. That asymmetry is the whole posture: a read of the wrong file is a mistake, a write of the wrong file is damage.

8.14 Write — put

Section titled “8.14 Write — put”

Create a record, or a sub-record. Values are external by default, validated whole-request, and the whole thing runs inside TSTART/TCOMMIT so a fault rolls back rather than leaving a partial record.

The gates, demonstrated in order. Without --yes:

With --yes but no declared write policy for the file:

After declaring the policy:

Details that matter:

  • --value is repeatable, one field per flag: --value '.01=NAME' --value '4=R'.
  • External by default. The input transform always runs. --internal is an explicit, separately named opt-in for pre-validated internal values — never inferable from the shape of the data, because that is precisely how DDR’s filer came to bypass every transform.
  • A missing required identifier refuses the whole request, with FileMan’s own text:
    Supplying the missing field (1=MENU TEXT) succeeds:
  • --ien requests a specific record number (byte-exact). This is what makes fixture-scoped writes at unallocatable IENs possible — use it for test data you intend to delete.
  • --iens is the creation IENS; the engine default is +1,. A sub-record put carries the parent path: --iens '+1,42,'.
  • --laygo admits ?/?+ lookup nodes (find-or-create). Off by default. Note the measured semantics: a found record’s accompanying values still file — this is ensure-with-these-values, not find-or-nothing.
  • DINUM files are a pinned refusal (U-VSL-ROW-DINUM). All three DBS add shapes were measured defective on stock FileMan — one files correctly then errors against its own new record, the other two hard-fault leaving a partial record — so put refuses the file class rather than emitting an outcome it cannot distinguish from a genuine collision.

8.15 Write — edit

Section titled “8.15 Write — edit”

File values into an existing record. <iens> is the record’s concrete IENS — 42, for a top-level record, 1,42, for a sub-record.

One invalid value refuses the whole request — nothing partial is ever filed. The two refusals worth memorising:

The first is the cheapest and most consequential guard in the domain. One accepted write of a ^ splits the record’s storage node, after which the retriever reads the field truncated while the index keeps it whole — permanently disagreeing, with no error at any stage. ^ and control characters are refused in non-word-processing values, in both external and internal modes. Word processing is exempt, because those lines are stored whole and measurably do carry ^ — see text.

The second is DDR’s silently-discarded-unknown-field defect, inverted: FileMan’s own error array is read and projected rather than destroyed.

@ clears a field. Required fields and .01 are protected; clearing the .01 is entry deletion and is delete’s job, not edit’s.

8.16 Write — delete

Section titled “8.16 Write — delete”

Dry run by default. With no flags it reports exactly what would go and mutates nothing:

--commit --yes actuates. Both are required — --commit says what, --yes confirms:

The dry run is self-confirming: it needs no --yes because it mutates nothing, and that is engine-proven rather than a host promise. If the delete files without error but the record remains, the verb refuses to report success (U-VSL-ROW-DIERR) rather than claiming a deletion that did not happen.
