Note what is not here: there is no general lock verb. DDR’s accepts an arbitrary global root, so a client can lock ^DPT and block every FileMan write to PATIENT site-wide. Locking in v db is internal to the write verbs, scoped to the record, with a bounded timeout and release on every path including the error path.

8.17 Write — reindex

Section titled “8.17 Write — reindex”

Rebuild one record’s cross-references — IX1^DIK, SET logic:

One record, top-level file, byte-exact IEN. Whole-file reindex is deliberately not a verb — it is an unbounded operation with no natural page, and admitting it would put an O(file) job behind a single confirmation.

8.18 Write — text

Section titled “8.18 Write — text”

File or read one word-processing field. This is a verb DDR never had at all: VAL^DIE refuses word-processing fields, the FDA loader accepts them anyway, and DDR never calls WP^DIE — so a client submitting word-processing text got a silently malformed write attempt.

<file> is the file holding the WP field, never the WP sub-file — for #19 OPTION’s DESCRIPTION (which is sub-file 19.06), pass 19 and field 3.5.

Writing. Lines are ordered; --line is repeatable:

Blank lines must ride --from-file. The flag parser drops an empty --line '' value silently, so the verb counts the --line occurrences in the raw argument vector and refuses the mismatch loudly rather than filing text you did not write:

Use a file instead:

Reading — --show needs no --yes, because it mutates nothing:

The ^ came back byte-exact and the blank line survived. That round trip is the verb’s whole point.

Append and clear:

--clear takes no lines. An empty line array never implicitly clears a field — deletion is always the explicit mode, so a bug in your line-building code cannot silently erase a description.

The door is inverted from what you might expect: a scalar, computed or multiple field is refused, because text files WP fields only:

There is deliberately no dry run on text: a text dry run would only echo your own input back at you.

8.19 Utility — version and menu

Section titled “8.19 Utility — version and menu”

These two live on the standalone v-db binary and on the v umbrella itself — not under v db. Mounting a domain contributes its domain verbs, not a second copy of the umbrella’s utilities, so v db version is a usage error (exit 2) and v version is what you want.

menu opens an interactive palette over the command surface — the same grammar, browsable. It needs a TTY. Use v menu under the umbrella, or ./dist/v-db menu standalone.

The domain also emits its own machine-readable contract, which is what the v umbrella aggregates and what a drift gate checks:

8.20 Inspect — integrity

Section titled “8.20 Inspect — integrity”

(Numbered after the Utility section to keep every existing anchor stable; it belongs with the Inspect verbs in §8.1–8.5.)

The instance-integrity census: the whole-instance engine sweeps — the header ledger (every file’s stored count/last-IEN claim against the walked truth, plus hollow records), the pointer plane (every stored plain and variable pointer resolved against its target root, the malformed class split into dictionary type-history and noncanonical-but-resolving values, and one ptr-pair-dangling row per (source file, target root) pair carrying dangling mass — no threshold, VD-D114), declared-type conformance (set membership with case-drift its own sub-class, FM internal-date shape, numeric canon — grammar only; input transforms never execute), the declaration-driven index audit in BOTH ruled directions (VD-D113: a row is fed both when the record→entry leg’s preconditions hold — the .01 among its keys, no SET CONDITION, no storage TRANSFORM — and entries when only the entry→record leg is defined on it; the leg that did not run lands as the named non-fact index-records-not-run, never a zero), depth-1 hollow sub-records, the full-depth sub-file descent (VD-D112: the pointer and type predicates restated per (top-level file, sub-file), with hollow-sub-deep at walk level ≥ 2), the key-uniqueness check (VD-D111: every measurable KEY-register promise checked over the declared-shape tuple — FileMan’s two promises, two classes), and the DD census — plus the cross-reference register sweep the index feed derives from. Counts with denominators, never a verdict: a stock release build is measurably nonzero in nearly every one of these classes, so no absolute count sets a failing exit, and red belongs to the baseline/delta comparison, not to this verb.

Things to read off that face:

  • Every class is present with its count, zeros included — 0 denied:policy is a measurement, not an absent word. The per-file rows (that run: 21,289 of them) ride the machine face and --out; the human face is the summary.
  • The index-plane accounting is closed, per direction: every stored subtree lands in exactly one bucket, and the buckets sum to the stored denominator — with the fed set split fed:both / fed:entries (VD-D113: the entry direction is fed wherever it is defined, and the newly admitted entries-only population is where the findings actually live). The unmeasurable share is the D107 ruling’s stated quarter; inexpressible is what the engine’s terminal2 vocabulary cannot express (entries not shaped (key, ien)), counted rather than guessed at.
  • The audit-class exclusion is loud: #.6/#1.1 store per-file subtrees at their first subscript, so they are contract-verified, counted by name, and walked in no sweep (A4/D108).
  • The audit paces itself against its own priced workload: the descent sweep is a legitimate ~5-minute single engine visit on vehu, so this verb pins its own derived per-visit bound (24m) when --timeout is unset — an explicit --timeout always wins.
  • --out <dir> writes the committed-artifact form — one JSONL row per audit row plus the shared manifest; the contract a downstream consumer (including the baseline/delta comparison) reads is integrity-jsonl-contract.md.
  • --to <file#> bounds every walk for a dev/smoke run; the artifact records the bound as a NAMED incompleteness and the run takes the check exit — a baseline is never captured from a bounded run.
  • Accuracy: the rows are verified against the frozen harness-tier oracle — exact per-(class, file) row agreement, counts and content folds, on both gold engines, driven through this shipped binary, with a planted divergence per sweep required to red (see §12 for the pattern and docs/design/surface-coverage.md for the disposition).

8.21 Inspect — integrity-compare

Section titled “8.21 Inspect — integrity-compare”

The delta comparison the census exists for — and the audit’s only red (VD-D106). OFFLINE: two committed artifacts in, an outcome word out. Three named bases, four pinned words, no two sharing a meaning:

word meaning exit
clean row-identical to the named base; nothing beyond the floor 0
delta ≥1 row differs from the NAMED base — reported per (class, file, sub, value) row, never an aggregate; the only red 3 (DELTA)
attention one-sided excess vs the shipped-state ledger — standing local state until repaired; never red (red once would be red forever, 4.1’s forbidden shape) 0
stopped no verdict: an input artifact is incomplete or --to-bounded — certifying against a partial audit would launder it 3 (STOPPED)

A real run, same-day, both bases at once (the fresh vehu baseline against the morning’s committed run and the cross-build floor):

Things to read off that face:

  • The expectation’s identity prints beside every verdict — engine, station, the VSL build it was generated against, when it was written, the content sha, the row count. Red is never a bare adjective. (That run’s clean is itself a measurement: the whole 21,289-row artifact was byte-identical across two captures 2.4 hours apart — a quiet gold instance really is row-stable at that scale.)
  • Any row difference vs the base is delta — clean has exactly ONE meaning. The report splits deltas into finding-row deltas (the signal) and context-row deltas (population/denominator/census movement that explains them — a register drift is a population-row delta), but the split governs the reading, never the exit.
  • A build mismatch between subject and base is stated, not refused — comparing across a sanctioned install is exactly how #19‘s movement was found — with the re-baseline sentence printed. Cross-INSTANCE comparison refuses (WRONG_INSTANCE): two sites’ damage is not a delta; cross-build shipped state is the ledger’s job.
  • The checksums are armed: both inputs are re-hashed against their manifests before any verdict (COMPARE_CHECKSUM). A deliberately edited expectation is passed with --assert, and the verdict then labels it an explicit assertion instead of a committed run.
  • The committed baselines live in baselines/integrity/<engine>/, one current baseline per engine, with the ledger derived beside them (scripts/integrity-baseline-check.py --write) — and the make-check baseline gate reds from a VSL ship’s pin refresh until the baselines are recaptured, which is VD-D106’s re-baseline obligation made mechanical.
  • Accuracy: the outcome vocabulary is red-proved through this shipped binary against planted copies of the real committed baselines — each word fired ALONE on both engines (docs/design/instance-integrity-harness/instance-integrity-compare-redproof.py).

8.22 Inspect — integrity-report

Section titled “8.22 Inspect — integrity-report”

The VD-D109 attribution view: WHY the pointer plane’s findings are what they are, from one artifact. Pointer findings attribute by TARGET — reported per source they are noise; grouped per target and joined to the target’s own header-ledger row they split into explained mechanisms and the residue worth eyes:

Things to read off that face:

  • A mechanism target is ONE finding, however many sources dangle into it: the licensed-content scrub (#81‘s header claims 26,877 while 2,351 exist) explains 21 source files’ mass in one sentence. Three mechanism arms, each a fact about the TARGET: header claim ≠ walked truth; a target holding NO records at all (foia’s #81: claim empty, walk 0, ~948k inbound dangling — every inbound pointer dangles by construction); a target with no header-ledger row at all (never walked on this instance).
  • The worth-eyes class is the residue: dangling into a target whose header is healthy (#409.68/#393 → #40.8) — the anomaly the audit exists to surface, per target, source list attached.
  • Root→file is the engine’s own answer — fileOf^VSLDD, one dispatch per DISTINCT root, memoized; its four verdicts ride verbatim, so an unclaimed, ambiguous or badroot root is a NAMED state grouped under the root itself, never an error and never a guess.
  • The live join must be the SAME machine the artifact measured: the engine’s declared station is checked against the artifact’s manifest, and a mismatch refuses (WRONG_INSTANCE) before anything is presented.
  • The malformed split stays out of the attribution — malformed-freetext is dictionary type-history about the FILE (never the values, and there is no target to attribute); noncanonical-resolving is live data an exact-match consumer misses. Sub-file dangling is listed after the targets WITHOUT attribution — the pair matrix rides the top-level pointer sweep (VD-D114 as measured), and the report says so rather than folding planes.
  • Accuracy: red-proved live through this shipped binary on both engines — a planted pair row must appear under its target AND trip the pair-sum cross-check loudly; a planted header divergence must flip its target’s class; the wrong live engine must refuse (docs/design/instance-integrity-harness/instance-integrity-report-redproof.py).

8.23 Inspect — bundle

Section titled “8.23 Inspect — bundle”

A bundle is the whole picture of one instance’s dictionary and its behaviour, interoperability and UI-join planes: a directory holding one artifact per component, each with its own manifest. Until 2026-08-23 it was produced by a shell script carrying 32 hand-written invocations — adding a plane meant editing bash in four places, and the answer to “what is in this bundle?” was to read that bash.

bundle runs a run set instead: a committed TOML file naming each component, its group, and a sentence saying why it is in the bundle. sets/dd-bundle.toml is the committed one.

Ask it what it exports, before running anything

Section titled “Ask it what it exports, before running anything”

--explain reaches no engine and writes nothing. It is worth running first for a reason that is not politeness: every component is resolved against the tool’s own generated command contract before any engine work begins. An unknown verb, an unknown flag, or a flag that belongs to a different verb refuses here — so a typo costs a second instead of thirty-seven minutes. All the problems are reported, not the first, because a set is edited by hand.

Run it

Section titled “Run it”

Each component lands in its own directory under --out, with its own manifest.json — the same artifact each verb writes on its own. Beside them the run writes bundle.json (the record) and set.toml (the set that produced it, byte-identical and digested).

Four things about a run are worth knowing before you start one:

  • The whole set holds the engine for the sum of its components. On vehu the export alone is about a quarter of an hour. A busy run-lock is therefore probed and refused before the first sweep, not forty minutes into one.
  • A failing component STOPS the run at that component. Nothing after it is dispatched; bundle.json names where it stopped, which check fired, and every component that never ran (stopped), and each component already on disk is marked refused (below). A producer that cannot vouch for one component must not keep industrialising more of them.
  • What is not run is named with its reason — the components a --group run left out, and the components the set itself declares it does not carry. An absence you can read is a fact; an absence you have to notice is not.
  • A number that was not measured is absent, never zero. A component that wrote nothing reports records: unmeasured.

Every component is certified as it lands

Section titled “Every component is certified as it lands”

Immediately after a component is written — never as a final sweep — the run re-reads it and certifies five layers, in order, stopping at the first red. The re-read shares nothing with the writer: its own file handle, its own hash, its own line count, so the writer’s claims are checked by a second oracle rather than repeated by the first.

layer what it checks what it catches
integrity independent re-read and re-hash; line count against records; every line parses truncation, a partial flush, a hash over something other than what landed
shape every record’s keys against the schema generated from the tool’s own serialising types, shipped in the bundle as schema.json a key silently added, renamed or dropped by a producer change
completeness the manifest’s complete claim re-derived, and the per-page evidence’s own arithmetic a page that stopped early and said so in a field nobody read
density per key, how many records carry a non-empty value — counts over denominators, recorded in certification.json keys intact, values gone — the failure that actually happened on 2026-08-18
drift records, bytes and per-key density against a named previous bundle (--base) a change that impoverishes the payload without breaking anything

The results land beside each component as certification.json (the full five-layer record, density included) and in bundle.json as each pass’s certification verdict. schema.json states, per stream, whether its schema was reflected from the serialising Go types or declared (the rows envelope, whose records are rendered engine-side) — the two carry different guarantees, and the consumer is entitled to know which it holds.

Drift compares only against a base you name. --base <dir> points at a previous bundle directory; record and byte drops are reported loudly, and a density collapse — a key that carried values there and carries none here — refuses the run at that component. Without --base, drift is recorded as unmeasured; the run never goes looking for “the last bundle” on its own.

When certification refuses, everything already written is marked. Each component directory the run produced — the failing one included — receives a refused.json naming the component that stopped the run and the check that fired. The artifacts stay on disk for diagnosis, but each one says out loud that its bundle refused; a partial bundle must never read as a smaller whole one. A later green run into the same --out re-certifies and clears the marks.

The bundle checks itself against its own set — in both directions

Section titled “The bundle checks itself against its own set — in both directions”

bundle.json carries a reconciliation block, and it is published whether or not it found anything: an empty finding list is a measurement, and omitting it would make a clean run indistinguishable from one that never looked.

finding what it means
missing a component the set declared landed no complete artifact
unasked a directory in the bundle no component asked for — a leftover from an earlier, larger set, which otherwise reads as part of this one
instances the distinct instances the components measured. More than one is a bundle assembled from two places, which nothing downstream can untangle

Any of them, on a run that reached its end, exits 3 with BUNDLE_INCOMPLETE. A run that stopped — a component failed, or its certification refused — exits 3 with COMPONENT_REFUSED instead, naming the component and the check that fired.

Selecting one plane

Section titled “Selecting one plane”

--group is repeatable. A group no component carries is refused rather than run: it would otherwise select nothing and report a clean, complete, empty bundle.

What a set may not say

Section titled “What a set may not say”

A component names what to export. These flags belong to the run and are refused inside a component — --out, --engine, --lock-wait, --timeout — because a set that pinned them would work against exactly one instance with one set of bounds, and the point of a set is that it works against any. Refused too: a verb that can change the instance (a bundle is an export), a verb that lands no artifact (there would be nothing to reconcile), and bundle itself (a set that runs itself has no bound).

8.24 Inspect — catalog

Section titled “8.24 Inspect — catalog”

The catalog is one artifact describing every table of one instance on three planes — structure (the dictionary: every field, cross-reference, index inventory row and reference edge), volume (the walked count, or a named reason there is none), and condition (the integrity rows naming the table, as counts over denominators — never a verdict). Each entry also carries the package attribution derived in-org with its rule and its contested set, an explicit classification absence, and the build’s provenance (build id, engine identity, source pin, dictionary fingerprint) copied onto every entry so a copied line cannot lose it.

It is built offline, from two things that already exist and already certified themselves: a bundle (§8.23) and an integrity capture (§8.20) of the same instance under the same source pin. Nothing in catalog reaches an engine. The join is a producer too, so it is certified like one (VD-D126): an independent certifier re-reads what was written and reconciles it in both directions against the component streams — every component row accounted for in an entry or named as unjoined, every entry fact traced back to a component row or to a named derivation rule — measures per-key density against a named previous build, and refuses the artifact if anything is off. A refused build is marked refused.json and no reader will open it.

catalog build

Section titled “catalog build”

--bundle and --integrity must be complete, certified, of one instance and under one pin; anything else is CATALOG_INPUT before a byte is written. --previous names an earlier build to measure density drift against; without it the build publishes previous: none — a named non-fact, never a manufactured baseline. What lands:

file what it is
catalog.jsonl one entry per declared table (§5.3 of the proposal): identity, the three planes, attribution, classification absence, provenance
index.jsonl the search corpus: one document per table and per field, with its name and description tokens
ranking.json the ranking rule as data — weights, formula, tie-break, tokenizer — so a second reader ranks the same way from the file alone
ranking-fixture.json the conformance queries answered over this artifact by the producer, so any reader can check itself against the catalog it holds
manifest.json the build record: engine identity, generatedAgainst (the one pin every read derives staleness from), the three planes’ denominators, the attribution rule and its tally, the index denominator, the default browse order, and every input row that joined nothing — named
certification.json the certifier’s layers, findings, reconciliation counts and density

Two denominators, never one. The headline reads “100 % of the data definition, and a stated fraction of the volume”: structure covers every declared table; volume counts every non-word-processing sub-file table that the descent walked (a non-zero count or an emitted zero) or that the build derived to zero transitively under an empty parent, states the word-processing tables as declared exclusions, and states what is left as uncovered — a table with no count from any source renders no number, not a zero and never an inherited parent count.

Attribution is derived, and the rule travels. Longest-matching-prefix over #9.4 PREFIX plus #9.4014 ADDITIONAL PREFIXES, minus #9.432 EXCLUDED NAME SPACE, matched against each top-level file’s global root. Every entry carries the rule, the namespace matched, an outcome word (single-valued, tied, unmatched, or inherited for a sub-file), the claimant set, and — separately — the many-valued #9.44 claims as data. A tie publishes its claimants and never an owner. Classification is absent by construction: a data class enters only as an operator-supplied input by reference (VD-D116), and the class-absent default browse is attribution-first, never size.

catalog browse

Section titled “catalog browse”

Lists tables from the artifact. --order attribution is the default (owner, then the contested set, then unmatched — file number breaking ties); --order number sorts by file number; --order size sorts by walked count and is available only by name. An artifact whose manifest declares any other default order is refused (BAD_DEFAULT_ORDER) by every reader.

catalog search

Section titled “catalog search”

Ranks tables and fields over the embedded index under the artifact’s own ranking.json: every query term must match a name or description token; names outrank descriptions; an exact whole-name match earns a bonus; ties order tables before fields, then by file number. A negative answer is a claim about the search, so it always carries the corpus denominator (how many tables and fields, and how many of each have a description at all) and the build’s age; a result that would lack either is refused (CATALOG_DENOMINATOR) rather than emitted.

Staleness is derived, never stored. Both readers compare the manifest’s generatedAgainst with the source pin this binary carries and render staleAtPin on the read; the entries themselves never carry a staleness key — a build that wrote one would fail certification.

8.25 Inspect — selection

Section titled “8.25 Inspect — selection”

A selection says which tables to extract; a run set (§8.23) says which verbs to invoke. They are different artifacts on purpose, and selection compile is the seam between them.

The selection is the artifact you edit. It holds one entry per table — at any depth, so a sub-file or a sub-sub-file is an ordinary entry — with that table’s field projection, projection tier and row filter. The component kinds no table selection can express — the whole-instance sweeps export, census, indexes and refs — ride beside them as passthrough entries: a verb and its arguments, carried unchanged. Compiling turns both kinds into one run set, which v db bundle runs exactly as it runs a hand-written one.

It is not a query language, and the compiler is why. Every key of a table entry maps onto a flag rows already has, one for one. A file that is not a file number is refused (NOT_A_TABLE) rather than special-cased, and a passthrough naming rows is refused too (PASSTHROUGH_IS_A_SELECTION) — carried that way, the selection would stop saying which table it reads, which is the whole point of having one.

compile and explain reach no engine. size does — one bounded probe per table, after deciding offline whether the selection can be sized at all.

selection compile

Section titled “selection compile”

Every entry — table-derived and passthrough alike — is resolved against the generated command contract before anything is written: an unknown verb, an unknown flag, a flag that belongs to the run rather than to a component, a verb that could mutate, or a verb whose stream certification cannot grade all refuse here, in a second, instead of thirty-seven minutes into a run. All the problems are reported, not the first, because a selection is edited by hand. A refused compile writes nothing, so there is never a half-valid run set on disk for someone to run later.

The compiled set is deterministic — passthrough entries first, then table selections, each in declaration order, with no timestamp and no host path in it — so two compiles of one selection are byte-identical and a diff of two compiled sets shows only what actually changed.

Lineage rides in the compiled set, which the bundle then embeds byte-identically, so a bundle can say what chose its components without a second artifact to lose:

A selection that was built from a catalog says so instead, in a [lineage.catalog] block naming the build, the rule that chose the entries, and whether that build was verified. Pass --catalog <dir> and the compile reads that build’s manifest: a build id that disagrees with the artifact refuses (CATALOG_MISMATCH) rather than publishing either version. Without --catalog the declared build travels as the claim it is, saying so in its own reason — an unverified lineage that did not say so would read as a measured one.

selection explain

Section titled “selection explain”

The same report, writing nothing: every entry, the verb and argv it becomes, the lineage that would attach, and every problem if it has any.

selection size — know the interval before you run

Section titled “selection size — know the interval before you run”

Nothing is extracted before it is sized, and a selection that cannot be sized refuses rather than proceeding (VD-D119). Every component is sized as N × b̄ × shape, each factor from its cheapest source (VD-D120):

  • N comes from the committed catalog build at zero engine cost — the census walked count for a top-level file, the integrity sub-census count for a sub-file, a zero where the descent emitted or derived one. A table the build has no count for (uncovered, or not in the build at all) is unsized, never inferred from its parent.
  • b̄ — mean bytes per row as rows --out will write it — comes from one bounded probe at exactly the projection, tier and filter the component compiles to, so the shape factor is folded in by construction. A top-level file is probed by a spread over its row-id space (a golden-ratio sequence over [1, max], max read from the integrity header-ledger — planning the probe is free and offline), read as one ien-list page per visit. The spread widens — 50, 100, 200, 400, 800 fresh hits, asking n/density positions over a sparse id space — until the band (a Student-t band, so two hits cannot “converge”) is inside ±10 % or five engine visits are spent, whichever first, and the row says which (stopped: converged / visit-budget / exhausted).
  • The answer is an interval, never a point. Every row carries the sample size, strategy, hit count, dispersion and band, and every band declares its method: sample-dispersion band, no tail guarantee. A small sample of a heavy-tailed file can be confidently narrow while missing the tail; the label is the defense, and the ±10 % / 5-visit constants are pinned-provisional until the validation in baselines/sizing/ (three deliberately different non-WP shapes, each against a same-session full sweep) says otherwise — make sizing-gate re-derives that verdict from the committed files on every make check.

A sub-file is prefix-probed, and its row says so. Measured on vehu the day this shipped: the file-wide sub-file index walk is instance-major and a key bound filters within each instance, so no single-visit read spreads a sub-file over its parent axis. Its b̄ comes from the front of its own file-wide walk — one visit per widening, never one per parent — with strategy: prefix, a declaration on the row and the caveat in the band’s method, and it never claims convergence: it spends the visit budget, because the front of a walk has no sampling dispersion to be inside of. That is the biased case VD-D120 names, and it is labelled rather than hidden — measured on the validation shape, a prefix band was ±0.0 % with the truth outside it, while every spread and every exhaustive row bracketed its truth. A top-level file whose row ids are not integers (#1’s are file numbers) takes the same declared path.

Whole-instance sweeps are sized from their last certified run. export, census, indexes and refs have no row population to probe. Pass --prior <bundle dir> and each passthrough entry whose name, verb and arguments match a certified, complete pass in that run is sized from its measured bytes — strategy: prior-run, method prior-run measurement, no growth guarantee. Without --prior, a selection naming a sweep is unsized.

A word-processing sub-file refuses, naming its reason — WP_UNSIZED, carrying the catalog’s own word-processing sub-file: a line is not a row and the fact that WP sizing is demand-triggered (VD-D119 rev 5): the first selection to need one is the event that triggers measuring the host-side WP line read, and no probe is built ahead of it.

The refusal comes before the engine. Sizability is decided from the committed artifacts alone; a selection with an unsizable component exits 3 UNSIZED naming every such component and its per-component code (NO_PRIOR_RUN, NO_COUNT, NOT_IN_CATALOG, NO_CEILING, WP_UNSIZED), with the rows it could size offline still reported and no verdict — fits is absent, not false. The --integrity capture must be the one the catalog build was joined from (its manifest records the sha256); a different capture is SIZING_INPUT, because N and the row-id ceiling must describe one instance state.

Under --cap the verdict is over the interval: fits (exit 0) only when the whole interval is under the cap, OVER_CAP when the whole interval is above it, and CAP_UNDECIDED when the cap falls inside the band — a band that straddles the cap is not a coin flip. --out FILE writes the report as JSON, exactly as the machine face renders it.

The committed selection is the 32-component bundle

Section titled “The committed selection is the 32-component bundle”

sets/dd-bundle-selection.toml is the committed dd-bundle run set expressed as a selection: 28 table entries — 9 of them sub-files — plus the whole-instance sweeps as passthrough entries. Compiled, it reproduces sets/dd-bundle.toml component for component and argument for argument, which is gated offline on every make check and is the first half of Proof 1 (VD-D123): the second half runs both sets against one instance in one session and compares the payloads byte for byte.

8.26 Inspect — packet

Section titled “8.26 Inspect — packet”

The consumer of an extraction should hold the full manifest and validation before they start analyzing the data — not a manifest and nothing else, with the only record-shape checking living downstream in the consumer. v db packet assembles that hand-over.

It assembles; it does not build. Five of its six parts are already produced by the runs that made the data:

part produced by where it comes from
the per-component manifest one shared writer, every artifact each component’s manifest.json, joined to bundle.json’s pass rows
the producer certification bundle’s five inline layers (§8.23) each component’s certification.json, carried verbatim
the channel evidence every dispatch, on the way out bundle.json‘s source pin and build, the components’ instance blocks, and the delivery digests three writers recomputed
the selection’s lineage selection compile (§8.25) the [lineage] block inside the set that traveled in the bundle, with every declared exclusion
the sized run selection size (§8.25) the report named by --sizing, bound by digest, with every prefix-sampled row’s declaration intact
the condition of the data this verb the same-session integrity audit’s rows, scoped to exactly the tables that were read

packet reaches no engine. The condition is measured by v db integrity in the extraction session; this verb only binds what those runs wrote. That is also why assembling a packet can never contend for the run lock the audit just held.

The order the session runs in

Section titled “The order the session runs in”

The audit runs after the extraction, inside the same run-lock bracket. It holds the lock for the length of a whole-instance sweep, so a concurrent v db gets RUN_LOCK_TIMEOUT rather than a half-measured instance.

Same-session is mechanical, not a promise

Section titled “Same-session is mechanical, not a promise”

The packet records the extraction’s startedAt/finishedAt and the audit’s writtenAt, and brackets the one against the other. An audit measured before the extraction began refuses as PACKET_STALE_AUDIT — that is the slice the ruling forbids, and it is the one that would look right, because a gold instance is byte-stable within a day and yesterday’s rows read exactly like today’s. An audit outside the session window refuses as PACKET_SESSION.

--session-window states the bound; it defaults to one hour and the applied value rides in the packet, never as a hidden constant. What the bracket proves is adjacency, and the packet says so: it does not prove the instance was unchanged between the two, only that they were measured next to each other on one instance under one source pin. The run-lock ordering is what makes adjacency meaningful.

The condition is scoped by the class’s grain, not by the string

Section titled “The condition is scoped by the class’s grain, not by the string”

The audit’s file field carries three different two-part spellings, and which one a row uses is a property of its class:

grain spelling the row is about classes
file 2 that file header-ledger, hollow, hollow-sub, the top-level pointer/type/index families
parent/sub 101/101.01 the sub-file, on the right sub-census, hollow-sub-deep, every *-sub class
file/qualifier 100/^LRT(67, · 57.7/A the file, on the left ptr-pair-dangling, the key-* family
instance -- no table denom:*, meta:*, index-unmeasurable, index-inexpressible

A slicer that read the shape rather than the declaration would scope 100/^LRT(67, to a table called ^LRT(67,. So the grain is declared per class and a class the table does not cover refuses (PACKET_GRAIN) rather than being dropped — a slice that silently drops what it cannot read reports a cleaner instance than the audit measured.

Everything the extraction did not read is counted, not listed: the packet describes what was extracted, and the whole-instance artifact travels beside it for the rest. A selected table the audit says nothing about is named, so a measured silence cannot be mistaken for a table nobody looked at. A whole-instance sweep (export, census, indexes, refs) reads no single table, so it is named as instance-scope rather than dropped from the account.

The certification carries its layers, and every skip is named

Section titled “The certification carries its layers, and every skip is named”

A component whose drift layer was skipped — because the run named no --base — and one whose drift was measured and found clean are the same word, certified, and different facts. So the packet carries all five layer results per component, collects every skipped into one list, and states baseAbsent when the extraction named no previous run at all. Drift unmeasured is not drift clean, and the packet will not let the two share a rendering.

Counts over denominators, and attention is never red

Section titled “Counts over denominators, and attention is never red”

Two rules are inherited from the audit unchanged. Counts over denominators, never a verdict — the audit is a census, and upgrading n of N into “bad” manufactures a judgement the measurement does not support. And a one-sided excess against the shipped-state ledger is attention, never red: the instance ships with pre-existing damage, and a consumer must not read it as a defect in the extraction.

The scoped form of that second rule is the packet’s own: a fresh row is compared against the floor at the same (class, file) grain, and where the floor carries no row at that grain the excess is still attention, with the absence named. Never silently clean — which would launder standing damage into the floor — and never red.

The packet speaks the same four pinned outcome words as integrity-compare (clean · delta · attention · stopped) and mints no fifth. It compares against the floor only, so delta cannot arise here — and the packet says so rather than leaving a reader to wonder which word it is withholding. To compare two runs of one instance, use v db integrity-compare --base.

Every referent is bound, and an absent one reds

Section titled “Every referent is bound, and an absent one reds”

The packet names the run set, the audit, the ledger, each component’s manifest and each certification by sha256. The set and the manifests are verified against the digest another writer claimed; the rest are computed and stated — two different strengths, rendered differently. A referent that does not hash refuses PACKET_REFERENT, and so does one that is missing: a check that skips a missing artifact goes green over a part with nothing behind it.

The stream digests are not re-hashed here. Each was written three times by three writers that shared no buffer — the component’s own manifest, the bundle record, and the certifier’s independent re-read — and the packet reports their agreement, refusing if they disagree.

An excluded component is declared, never discovered: a component the set names that the run neither ran nor listed as not-run refuses PACKET_UNDECLARED.

What the packet is not

Section titled “What the packet is not”

It is not an analysis, not a quality score and not a recommendation. v db’s charter is browse · extract · catalog · scope · query · manage at N=1; analytics — including of its own exports — is out. The packet’s job is to hand over facts and their denominators so the analysis that happens elsewhere starts from a known position.

9. Recipes

Section titled “9. Recipes”

Is this file worth extracting? Answer variety before volume — a field that is 90% empty is not a field.

850 of 1,496 records have no value in 9.3 at all. That is the number to know before you build an extract around the field.

Page a whole file into JSONL. Loop on the token until more is false. Nothing is staged engine-side, so this is safe to run against a live instance — pace it if you are sharing.

Always check stopped before you trust a page. The one-liner that catches a scan:

13,198 candidates visited, 13,198 rejected, nothing emitted — a full scan of #19, reported as such. If stopped is examined instead of end, the page also ran out of budget before finishing that scan. Either way: push the constraint into the index with find, or accept the cost knowingly.

Find records by name rather than scanning for them. The difference is examined, and it is stark. A miss on a seek visits nothing:

The same miss expressed as a filter visits every record in the file:

Both return zero rows in under 0.3 s on a 1,496-record file — but the second number is what grows with the file, and on #757.02 it would be 855,565. This is the same asymmetry DDR had; the difference is that here you can see it.

Audit an instance’s data quality in one pass. The census’s header-divergence count is a finding, not noise:

Set up a scratch fixture and clean up after it. The pattern used throughout this guide — a requested IEN high enough that FileMan would never allocate it, and a policy declaration that is revoked afterwards:

Before you touch a file, learn who points at it.

9.1 The extraction pattern — dereference offline

Section titled “9.1 The extraction pattern — dereference offline”

The one recipe worth learning by heart. Meaning in this database lives in the links: #2 carries 228 pointer fields, 105 of them inside multiples. The obvious way to extract it — resolve each pointer as you read each record — is the wrong shape twice over. It pays a random read per pointer per record, and it bakes the site’s renderings into your data, which is not portable (§13, limitation 5: 180 divergent subjects between the two instances measured, against internal’s 1).

Extract the internal values, and dereference them afterwards, away from the engine.

1 — Extract internal-tier. The case is portability, not speed; at demo sparsity the two tiers time the same.

2 — Sweep the pointer graph once. refs --all writes every edge of every file, at every depth, in one pass. It is slow once (~17 minutes, 8,270 dumps on vehu) and free forever after.

3 — Compute the closure offline. This is the step that does not work live. refs --depth recursion costs 1,294 engine dumps and 2m50s from a six-edge file, and cannot complete #2 at all. Against the artifact it is a file read:

651 files, not 36. The design’s original figure was the top-level-only reading, and the correction is the whole argument for the sweep: the number was 18× too small and the affordable way to get the right one is a file read. Note the walk needs a visited set — the graph is cyclic (309 self-loops, 138 2-cycles on vehu), and #2 points at itself twice.

4 — Keep the dictionary with the data. Internal-tier values are meaningless without the DD that decodes them, so every data --out manifest carries the dictionary’s fingerprint as read in the same run (§8.8) — the pairing is verifiable, not a discipline you have to remember:

Pull the dictionary itself with export --out, and decode against it: sets-of-codes, dates, and pointer targets are all DD facts.

5 — Dereference by IEN, offline. The closure says which files you need; the DD says which field points where. If you would rather have the target named inline as you read, --ids does that at the cost of one companion read per page — cheap on --tier internal, where the internal value is already in hand.

One rule that decides what “complete” means. Stored fields are the complete-data notion. Computed fields are derived meaning — evaluated by site M, external-tier only — and they are never part of an extract’s completeness claim. #2 has seven of them:

An extract that silently included them would be claiming the site’s arithmetic as data; one that silently dropped them without saying so would be the omission this guide exists to prevent. They are declared either way.

10. Troubleshooting

Section titled “10. Troubleshooting”

timed out after 30s waiting for the run-lock — another process holds the engine’s run-lock. v db serializes per engine deliberately. Raise --lock-wait, wait for the holder, or diagnose with m runlock status. Long verbs (profile, list, a full census) hold it for their whole run.

A run-lock … held by pid N notice on stderr, but the command works — the lock was stale (the holder is gone). The notice is informational; the verb proceeded.

mutating verb X requires confirmation (exit 4) — add --yes. This is refused both client-side and engine-side; there is no host flag that skips it.

write policy: no declaration - writes are default-deny — declare it: v db policy --declare write:<file>=allow --yes. Revoke it when you are done.

value carries the ^ delimiter — refused at the door — by design. A ^ in a non-word-processing value splits the record’s storage node. If the value genuinely needs a caret, it belongs in a word-processing field; file it with text, which exempts ^ because those lines are stored whole.

does not contain a field N — the field number is wrong for that file. That text is FileMan’s own; v db projects it rather than discarding it. Check with v db schema <file>.

N --line flag(s) given but only M value(s) parsed — you passed an empty --line ''. The flag parser drops it silently, so the verb refuses rather than filing text you did not write. Put the lines in a file and use --from-file.

Empty result, stopped: end, more: false — that really is all of it. This is the only combination that means “complete”.

Empty result, stopped: examined — a work budget ended the page. There is more data. Raise --examined, or reconsider the filter.

emitted > distinct on a find — the index emits some records more than once. That is a real property of the index, surfaced rather than hidden. If you need distinct records, enumerate with rows instead of walking the index.

index … is compound / record-level / COMPUTED-style — that index cannot be walked safely, because site-authored index logic is never evaluated. Use a different index or enumerate.

A verb refuses with exit 4 and ENGINE_UNRESOLVED — no engine resolved. Pass --engine vehu or --engine foia explicitly. The ladder is flag, then $M_ENGINE, then committed config, then refuse — it never guesses.

U-VSL-ROW-INSTANCE — “instance classification undeclared” — the #999003 policy store has no class declaration. This is the correct fail-closed refusal on a never-declared instance, but it also appears after a VSL uninstall/reinstall cycle, which wipes the declarations (measured 2026-08-09). Re-declare the standing state: v db policy --declare class=demo --yes. A confusing wrinkle: the broker path keeps working through this state (a real principal bypasses the class rung), so “the RPC works but the CLI refuses” is the fingerprint of a wiped store, not of a broken CLI.

Broker client: does not have access to option VSL DATA PLANE — the signed-on user does not hold the context option. That is Kernel’s own XQCS access check doing its job (7.8): grant the VSL DATA PLANE option (secondary menu) to the user, or the session needs XUPROGMODE. Not a v db error.

Broker client timed out mid-RPC — raise the client’s read timeout above the verb’s worst case before retrying: the abandoned engine job can keep spinning at 100% CPU after the socket closes (measured; the reap on a gold engine is a runlock-held driver lifecycle restart). A broker client that times out is a killed client — assume its job leaked and check the engine.

Credentials. Docker-transport engine paths need none. The IRIS remote transport and the RPC/CPRS path read M_IRIS_* / VISTA_* from the environment, loaded by direnv from ~/data/vista-forge/auth.env. Broker signon additionally needs per-instance access/verify codes and the instance’s own XWB cipher table — vehu’s and foia’s XUSRB1 differ (foia’s is extracted to ~/data/vista-forge/foia-cipher; export VISTA_M_HOST there for foia broker sessions). If a repo’s session cannot see the variables, its .envrc is missing source_up.

11. Reference

Section titled “11. Reference”

11.1 Global flags

Section titled “11.1 Global flags”
flag meaning
-o, --output text (TTY-styled), json, or auto (default — text on a TTY, JSON when redirected)
--no-color disable ANSI styling even on a TTY
-v, --verbose verbose diagnostics to stderr

11.2 Engine flags shared by every verb

Section titled “11.2 Engine flags shared by every verb”
flag meaning
--engine engine profile: vehu (YottaDB) or foia (IRIS)
--lock-wait how long to wait for the engine run-lock before refusing; 0 = try once
--timeout host wall-clock bound on one engine visit; a hung page is aborted engine-side, not merely abandoned. Unset takes the derived default (180 s); negative means no bound. It bounds a visit, not a command — a paged read renews it per page, so a long sweep is not capped by it

11.3 Exit codes

Section titled “11.3 Exit codes”

The platform’s ladder, identical across every v domain:

code meaning typical cause
0 success
1 runtime error the engine refused the request (a typed U-VSL-*), IO, parse
2 usage error bad flag or argument (including v db version)
3 check found findings or drift estimate over its --cap
4 refused no engine resolved, run-lock timeout, missing --yes

Exit 3 is worth calling out: it is a gate code, not an error. estimate uses it so a CI step can red on an extract that outgrew its budget without the tool having failed. It is the platform’s ladder, so the code stays reserved for that meaning even though only estimate currently raises it.

11.4 The JSON envelope

Section titled “11.4 The JSON envelope”

Every command emits the same shape:

On failure, data is replaced by error:

command is the grammar path, not the literal argv — so db rows <file> is stable across invocations and safe to switch on.

11.5 Completeness fields

Section titled “11.5 Completeness fields”
field type meaning
population string file, index:<name>, sub:<file>, ien-list(<n>), dic, or dic:<file>
examined int candidates visited, charged per candidate including filter-only projection
filtered int candidates rejected by a predicate
emitted int rows in this page
distinct int distinct IENs in this page — below emitted when a population can repeat one (index:<name>, ien-list)
stopped enum end | rows | bytes | examined | elapsed | chunk (ien-list only: the transport ran out of chunk, not the population)

Emission order is a property of the population, derivable from that one field — there is no order field to read and none to keep in step: file ⇒ row-id order · index:<name> ⇒ that key’s collation · sub:<file> ⇒ parent-major depth order · ien-list(n) ⇒ the order you supplied.

On an ien-list page one more block rides beside these: misses, the requested IENs with no record, each with the list position that asked for it — present and empty when nothing was missing.

Beside it, page:

field meaning
more is there data behind this page
next the opaque continuation token, present only when more is true

11.6 Typed error codes

Section titled “11.6 Typed error codes”

Engine-side refusals are typed, and (since VSL*1.0*64, the typed-refusal-class patch) they render as refusals: the message is the module’s own reason alone — file 99999 has no data dictionary — at a classified exit (usage-shaped → 2 · policy/instance/audit/lock → 4 · site-M/substrate failures → 1). The classification is per-code, default usage, carried in the generated dist/errors.json (class field) with the runtime truth in $$classOf^VSLAPI. Only a genuine engine fault — a real crash — wears the trap prose verb <label>^VSL… faulted: at exit 1; that wrapper now means what it says. Branch on the typed error.code, never the prose. The ones you will actually meet:

code meaning
U-VSL-ROW-NOFILE no such file number, no DD, or no data root on this instance
U-VSL-ROW-NOTFOUND no record at that IEN
U-VSL-ROW-BADFIELD not a field number, or the file has no such field
U-VSL-ROW-FLTFIELD filter target is computed, a multiple, or has no storage location
U-VSL-ROW-FILTER malformed filter, or an operator outside the closed table
U-VSL-ROW-VALUE a control byte in a value
U-VSL-ROW-IENS malformed IENS, or the wrong shape for the verb (put creates, edit files)
U-VSL-ROW-DINUM the file forces its own record numbers — put refuses it
U-VSL-ROW-LAYGO a lookup node in the IENS without --laygo
U-VSL-ROW-NOINDEX no such index on that file
U-VSL-ROW-IXTYPE the index cannot be walked safely — the refusal names its measured kind (mumps, trigger, dangling, compound, record-level, computed-key, foreign-root), the same vocabulary schema reports. The kind vocabulary is OPEN — see below. The refusal also signposts find … --raw, which reads the stored entries of exactly these
U-VSL-ROW-NOSUBTREE the name is declared but stores nothing under this file’s data root on this instance (measured: 70% of non-walkable cross-references) — a finding, refused loudly rather than served as an empty page
U-VSL-ROW-FOREIGN a new-style FOREIGN-ROOT registration: its entries live at another file’s root, and which file its subscripts number is unmeasured
U-VSL-ROW-AT find --raw --at was given something other than a contiguous 1..k list of leading subscripts
U-VSL-ROW-IENPOS a pinned record-id position is not a positive integer, or a projection was asked for where no position measurably holds a record number
U-VSL-ROW-TOOWIDE fields-profile: the dictionary needs more envelope bytes than the budget allows — refused before the walk, because a per-field tally cannot drop fields without lying
U-VSL-ROW-IENLIST the supplied IEN set is defective: a non-IEN entry, a gap in the chunk keys, an empty list, a chunk overrunning its declared total, a chunked list with no whole-list hash, or an IEN set combined with a parent scope or a sub-file
U-VSL-ROW-CHUNK the supplied chunk does not carry the list position the cursor needs — the refusal names both; send the chunk that covers it
U-VSL-ROW-PARENT the parent scope is defective: given for a top-level file, wrong arity for the sub-file’s depth, a non-IEN piece, a missing trailing comma, or an unresolvable DD chain
U-VSL-ROW-DEPTH a ** field spec (sub-file depth) was requested
U-VSL-ROW-HDRLESS the multiple’s node;0 header is missing and filters were requested — filter evaluation runs through FileMan’s retriever, which measurably cannot address a headerless multiple (DIERR 401). Without filters the page serves, each unprojectable sub-row a typed in-stream fault
U-VSL-ROW-NRFIELD a nested-root branch projection asked for a field the location decode cannot serve (computed, storage-less, extract-location, or a multiple)
U-VSL-ROW-WFIELD the file is a word-processing sub-file — its records are lines; read them with text --show
U-VSL-ROW-TIER unknown projection tier
U-VSL-ROW-INSTANCE / U-VSL-ROW-AUDIT the instance gate refused (class undeclared or unrecognized, a real-data instance, the Kernel PROD tripwire), or the real-data read-audit write failed and the read fails closed with it
U-VSL-ROW-NESTEDROOT the file is in the measured nested-root table (#1.1, #.6): its top-level IENs are file numbers, so a top-level read would render wrong-level values
U-VSL-ROW-TREESIZE a record’s subtree exceeded the bytes budget under --with-multiples — the row is a typed stub naming the record, the multiple and the paged alternative; distinct from U-VSL-ROW-TOOBIG (one oversize value)
U-VSL-ROW-SUBFILE the sub-file’s parent chain does not resolve — over 20 levels, or a cycle in the dictionary. Nesting depth alone no longer refuses: a sub-file at any depth walks file-wide (§8.8)
U-VSL-ROW-RAWFIELDS --fields combined with --tier raw — raw returns the record’s data nodes, which a fields spec cannot select
U-VSL-ROW-PROJFAULT the retriever hard-faulted mid-projection (typically a computed field’s site M against malformed data) — typed, never a bare M fault
U-VSL-ROW-SEEK malformed key bound, or --prefix combined with --from/--to
U-VSL-ROW-TOKEN malformed token
U-VSL-ROW-STALE the token’s binding fingerprint does not match this request shape
U-VSL-ROW-BOUNDS a bound is out of range
U-VSL-ROW-TOOBIG a single value exceeds what the envelope can carry
U-VSL-ROW-DIERR FileMan itself refused — its text is projected verbatim
U-VSL-ROW-POLICY the declared policy denies this verb on this file
U-VSL-POL-ARG / U-VSL-POL-KEY a malformed policy declaration
U-VSL-API-CONFIRM / U-VSL-API-ATTRIB the @mutates gate: missing confirmation or attribution
U-VSL-ROW-ARG a malformed argument to a text write: a bad mode, an empty line set outside --clear, lines supplied with --clear, or a non-numeric line key
U-VSL-ROW-LOCKTIMEOUT the record’s bounded LOCK timed out — another process holds it (multi-process contention; retry)
U-VSL-DD-NOTFOUND the dictionary read (schema, export, the --ids companion) found no data dictionary for that file number
U-VSL-DD-INSTANCE / U-VSL-DD-AUDIT the raw dictionary read’s instance gate refused — the same M6 door and rungs as U-VSL-ROW-INSTANCE/-AUDIT, in the dictionary module’s namespace (the raw ^DD register serves stored bytes, so it is gated where the interpreted schema reads are not; no v db verb reaches it today — it serves the read-fidelity harness)
U-VSL-DD-POLICY the declared policy denies the raw dictionary read on that file’s top-level ancestor — the DD-plane twin of U-VSL-ROW-POLICY
U-VSL-POL-WRITE a policy --declare/--revoke could not be filed — the underlying VSLFS write failed
U-VSL-INTEG-INSTANCE / U-VSL-INTEG-AUDIT the instance-integrity sweeps’ instance gate refused, or their real-data read-audit write failed and the sweep fails closed with it — the same M6 door and rungs as U-VSL-ROW-INSTANCE/-AUDIT, in the integrity module’s (VSLINTEG) namespace
U-VSL-INTEG-ADMIT an audit-class file’s first-level subtree headers no longer claim its own number — the pinned A4/D108 file-subscripted-storage contract failed on-engine, and every sweep refuses rather than walking a population it can no longer exclude
U-VSL-INTEG-KEY two KEY register entries share one (file, name) identity on this instance — the keys sweep’s per-key emission identity would collide, so it fails closed rather than silently overwriting a row (a register defect, shipped at VSL*1.0*75; the host face consuming the sweep is part 3 of the 3x-b expansion)
U-VSL-INTEG-ARG a defective indexb population feed: no population, both the explicit and naive populations at once, an explicit feed combined with a walk bound, or a malformed / out-of-vocabulary / duplicate / inadmissible population row
U-VSL-ROW-PROFFIELD distribution’s field is computed, has no storage location, or was supplied together with --index — a field and an index are two different distributions

Host-side codes — the complete catalog, grouped by exit class so a script can branch on error.exit first and error.code second. Completeness here is mechanical, not a promise: make error-gate reds when a code is raised in source and missing from this section, documented under the wrong exit, or left behind after a rename — and dist/error-catalog.json is the generated registry for a consumer that would rather read JSON than this prose. It carries three layers: host (raised in v-db), lowerLayer (raised by the org packages v-db links — v-base and clikit — derived from its own imports, with the raising file and line), and engineClasses (the U-VSL-* half, classed by v-stdlib). Every entry carries documented, which says whether this section names it: the host and engine halves are total by gate, and the lower layer is inventoried rather than documented — the codes below are the ones a v db user is most likely to meet, and the registry is where you look up one that isn’t here. Every one carries code, exit, message and (where a one-flag fix exists) hint in the JSON envelope. In JSON mode every envelope rides stdout — ok and error alike, one stream to read (since clikit v0.11.3, ruled 2026-08-15); a refusal after an engine visit additionally carries data.instance. Text mode keeps the human Error: line on stderr. Exactly one ok:false envelope per failing invocation.

Usage — exit 2 (a flaw in the request; raised before any engine visit, naming the flag rather than the engine):

code meaning
UNKNOWN_ENGINE --engine names no registered profile (the standing ones are vehu and foia)
BAD_MAX non-positive --max — the engine would silently remap it to the default page size
BAD_IENS / BAD_TOKEN the supplied-IEN-set doors: both input faces at once, an empty cohort, --iens with --parent, a token from the other population, a parser-dropped empty element — §8.8
BAD_OUT_DIAL --max-pages or --pace without --out on rows/find — the walk dials have nothing to dial on a single-page read
BAD_EXPLAIN --explain with --out (a plan writes nothing) or --token (a walk under way is past planning) — or an artifact citation (--census/--indexes/--profile) without --explain, which would otherwise run the read with the artifact silently ignored. On bundle the same rule for the same reason: describing a run set writes nothing
RAW_ONLY / RAW_SEEK / RAW_WHERE / BAD_AT / BAD_IEN_AT find’s two-population doors: --at/--ien-at need --raw; seeks and --where refuse under --raw; a parser-dropped empty --at; a non-positive --ien-at
BAD_AXIS distribution was given both a field and --index, or neither
BAD_SEEK --from/--to/--prefix with no --index to position — a record walk has no keys to bound, so the constraint would be accepted and ignored
BAD_SCOPE the two-scope doors on refs and indexes: --all beside a file number, neither scope, a flag that belongs to the other scope — and refs --scope without --verify, or a --scope entry that is not a file number
BAD_FILES a malformed --files expression on estimate/export (the offending token is named)
BAD_KEY_SAMPLE / BAD_SAMPLE a negative sample size on indexes (0 skips the key pass)
NO_TARGET / NO_IEN / REF_AND_ARGS / BAD_REF get’s addressing doors: nothing named, a file with no IEN, both spellings of one address, a malformed <file>-<ien> reference — §8.9
BAD_VALUE a --value that is not FIELD=VALUE (put/edit; the value half may itself contain =)
BAD_LINES / BAD_MODE text’s doors: --line and --from-file are exclusive; a parser-dropped empty --line; --append with --clear; an empty line set (never an implicit clear); --show with write flags
BAD_DECL policy: --declare with --revoke, a declaration that is not KEY=VALUE, or --yes with nothing to confirm
IDS_RAW_TIER --ids with --tier raw — the raw tier returns data nodes, which carry no field types to resolve references from
ARTIFACT_READ / ARTIFACT_MANIFEST / ARTIFACT_VERB / ARTIFACT_DIGEST / ARTIFACT_INSTANCE / ARTIFACT_SCOPE an artifact named to --census/--indexes/--profile that cannot be cited: unreadable, no manifest beside it, written by a different verb, a stream that no longer matches its sha256, measured on another instance, or a profile of another file
COMPARE_INPUT integrity-compare was given no expectation (--base and/or --ledger is required — red is only ever a delta against a NAMED expectation), --assert with no --base, an artifact directory that is missing/unparseable/written by another verb, a damaged row, or a ledger that is malformed or names fewer than two source builds
WRONG_INSTANCE the subject and the --base artifact measure different instances (engine or station) — comparisons are same-instance, stated-build; two sites’ damage is not a delta. Cross-build shipped state is the ledger’s job
UNKNOWN_VERB the (hidden) explain shim was asked about an engine verb the pinned manifest does not carry
SET_READ bundle: the run set could not be read — no such file, or TOML this format does not know. A key it cannot place is named rather than ignored, because a key read past is an operator’s written intent dropped
SET_UNRESOLVED bundle: one or more components do not resolve against the generated command contract — an unknown verb, an unknown flag, a flag belonging to a different verb, a run-owned flag (--out/--engine/--lock-wait/--timeout), a verb that can mutate, a verb that lands no artifact, a verb with no registered record schema (its stream could not be certified), a set naming the verb that runs it, a duplicate component name, or an exclusion with no reason. Every problem is reported, not the first, and nothing was run — resolution happens before any engine visit, so a typo costs a second rather than thirty-seven minutes
BAD_GROUP bundle --group names a group no component carries. Refused rather than run, because a misspelled group would select nothing and report a clean, complete, EMPTY bundle; the refusal lists the groups the set does declare
NO_OUT bundle with neither --out nor --explain — a bundle must land somewhere
BAD_BASE bundle --base names a directory that is not a bundle (no bundle.json). A named base is an assertion of comparability, and “drift clean against nothing” must never certify — refused before anything touches an engine
SELECTION_READ selection compile/explain/size: the selection could not be read — no such file, or TOML this format does not know. The unknown key is named, for the same reason SET_READ names one
SELECTION_UNRESOLVED selection compile/explain/size: one or more entries do not compile or do not resolve. The compiler’s own refusals are a file number that is not one (a verb invocation is not a selection — it is a passthrough entry), a passthrough naming the rows verb (which would stop the selection saying which table it reads), a table entry with no file, a passthrough with no verb, an entry with no name, a name used twice across the two kinds, a selection that selects nothing, a catalog reference with no rule, a catalog supplied for a selection that declares none, and a declared build that disagrees with the artifact. The rest are the run set’s own, since the compiled set is resolved against the generated contract exactly as bundle resolves a hand-written one. Every problem is reported, not the first, and nothing is written — a refused compile leaves no half-valid run set on disk. Each problem’s own code and message are in data.problems, and §5.25 of the technical reference names them
NOT_A_CATALOG selection compile/explain --catalog names a directory that is not a catalog build (no readable manifest.json, or one naming no build). Refused rather than skipped, because a lineage verified against nothing is worse than one that says it was not verified
SIZING_INPUT selection size: an input artifact could not be read as what the flag names — --catalog is not a certified catalog build (or is marked refused), --integrity is not an integrity capture or is not the capture the catalog build was joined from (its manifest records the sha256; N and the row-id ceiling must describe one instance state), --prior is not a bundle directory. The message names which
PACKET_INPUT packet: an input could not be read as what the flag names — --bundle is not a directory v db bundle --out wrote, or its bundle.json does not parse. Named before anything is bound, because the packet’s every other refusal presupposes a readable extraction
CATALOG_INPUT catalog build refused an input before writing anything: the bundle is missing, incomplete or marked refused; a component is absent, uncertified, or its stream no longer hashes to what its manifest claims; the integrity capture is of another instance; or the two inputs were captured under different source pins. Nothing is joined that cannot be re-verified
CATALOG_DIR catalog browse/search was pointed at a directory that is not a catalog (no readable manifest.json written by catalog build, or no catalog.jsonl)
USAGE the platform’s parse-level refusal (unknown flag, missing argument) — kong’s message, before any verb runs

Check — exit 3 (a verdict or a floor, for scripts to branch on):

code meaning
AGG_SINCE this engine’s VSL build predates --where/--index on count/distribution (needs VSL*1.0*55; distribution --index needs VSL*1.0*56 — see below). Refused here rather than sent because an older engine does not refuse the flag — it never binds it and answers the wider question with ok:true
IENS_SINCE the same floor for --iens (needs VSL*1.0*54) — below it the engine reads the WHOLE file instead
OVER_CAP estimate — the selection exceeds --cap; selection size — the whole sizing interval is above --cap
CAP_UNDECIDED selection size — the --cap falls inside the sizing interval, so the measurement does not decide it: raise or lower the cap past the interval, or narrow the selection
UNSIZED selection size — the selection holds a component that cannot be sized from the committed artifacts, so there is no size and no verdict (VD-D119); every such component is named in data.sizing.unsized[] with a per-component code — NO_PRIOR_RUN (a sweep with no --prior run, or a prior pass with different arguments), NO_COUNT (no committed count: uncovered), NOT_IN_CATALOG, NO_CEILING (no header-ledger row-id ceiling for a top-level file), WP_UNSIZED (a word-processing sub-file; demand-triggered, VD-D119 rev 5) — which is a field of the report, not an error.code. Decided offline, before any engine visit
PACKET_STALE_AUDIT packet: the audit was written BEFORE the extraction began, so it describes the instance as of an earlier moment — the stale slice VD-D122 forbids, and the one that would look right, because a gold instance is byte-stable within a day. Run v db integrity --out after the extraction and assemble against that
PACKET_SESSION packet: the audit was written outside the extraction’s session window (--session-window, default 1h, always stated in the packet). The condition rows must be measured in the same session as the data they describe — re-run the audit, or state a wider window if the ordering was legitimate
PACKET_REFERENT packet: a referent does not hash, or is ABSENT — the set that traveled inside the bundle against bundle.json’s digest, a component manifest against the pass row’s, a missing manifest.json or certification.json, or a stream digest its three independent writers (the manifest, the bundle record, the certifier’s own re-read) spell differently. Absent reds like wrong does: a check that skips a missing artifact goes green over a part with nothing behind it
PACKET_UNDECLARED packet: a component the run set declares is neither run nor named as not-run, or the bundle’s own reconciliation carries a missing/unasked entry. An excluded component is DECLARED, never discovered later as an absence (VD-D122) — give the set an [[excluded]] entry with its reason, or re-run so the component lands
PACKET_STOPPED packet formed no condition: the extraction did not complete (a stopped or failed bundle), or the audit is incomplete/scope-bounded. The packet still reports, with its condition outcome the fourth pinned word stopped rather than a silence — recapture without the bound
PACKET_WRONG_INSTANCE packet: the audit measured a different engine or station than the extraction read. Two instances’ condition is not one packet’s
PACKET_PIN_MOVED packet: the extraction ran under one source pin and the audit measured under another, so the rows do not describe the bytes in hand. Re-run the audit under the pin the extraction ran on
PACKET_GRAIN packet: an audit row carries a class whose file grain is not declared, so the packet cannot say which table it is about. It refuses rather than dropping the row — a slice that silently drops what it cannot read reports a cleaner instance than the audit measured. Declare the grain in internal/packet, beside the contract-guide row it comes from
INCOMPLETE a verb finished without covering everything it was asked to cover, with no more specific cause: an artifact-writing verb whose manifest is not complete (every reason named in manifest.incomplete; the records written are still valid), or estimate withholding its verdict because the selection holds a skipped or unsized file (VD-D85 — the measured files are still reported)
SOURCE_PIN the engine’s installed VSL sources could not be verified: its build is below the source-pin floor (VSL*1.0*68), it did not answer for a routine, its answer was malformed, or its engine family has no measured fold semantics. Raised before the first dispatch, so nothing was read
SOURCE_DRIFT they were verified and they differ: a routine is absent from the engine, or its installed source folds to a value other than the build this host was generated against — a stale routine, a partial install, or an unregistered load (a container restart reverts those). The refusal names the routine and both folds
DELTA integrity-compare’s red — the ONLY red the integrity audit has (VD-D106a): one or more rows differ from the named base, reported per (class, file, sub, value) row with the expectation’s identity beside the verdict, never as an aggregate count. A sanctioned install legitimately moves rows: re-baseline, then re-compare
STOPPED integrity-compare formed no verdict (VD-D106c): the subject or base artifact is incomplete or scope-bounded (--to), and certifying against a partial audit would launder it — recapture without the bound
BUNDLE_INCOMPLETE bundle: the run finished and the bundle is not whole. Findings that survive to the end of a run, each named in bundle.json — a declared component with no complete artifact; an artifact no component asked for (the direction nothing used to check: a directory left by an earlier, larger set reads as part of this bundle); or components measuring more than one instance, which nothing downstream can untangle
COMPONENT_REFUSED bundle: the run stopped at a component (VD-D121) — the component itself failed, or its certification refused at a named layer (integrity, shape, completeness, density, drift). The refusal names the component and the check that fired; that component’s certification.json carries the five-layer result, every component already written is marked refused (refused.json), and the components after it were never dispatched (bundle.json’s stopped.notDispatched). Fix the cause and re-run — a green run re-certifies and clears the marks
CATALOG_REFUSED the join failed its own certification (VD-D126) — a dropped plane, an entry fact that traces to no component row, a density collapse against the named previous build, a dangling or missing index document, a ranking fixture that does not replay — and the artifact is marked refused.json; a reader (catalog browse/search) raises the same code on a directory so marked or lacking a certified certification.json
BAD_DEFAULT_ORDER the artifact’s manifest declares a class-absent default browse order other than attribution-first — size especially — and no reader opens it (VD-D116 rev 4)
CATALOG_DENOMINATOR catalog search was about to emit an answer with no corpus denominator or no build age — a negative answer without its denominator is a claim about the instance, not about the search (VD-D117) — and refused instead
CATALOG_RANKING catalog search found the artifact’s ranking.json or index.jsonl missing or unreadable; a reader never ranks by a rule the artifact does not carry
COMPARE_CHECKSUM an input’s data file does not match its manifest’s sha256 — a base or subject that is not the artifact its manifest describes, or a ledger that drifted from its derivation. A deliberately edited expectation is passed with --assert, which labels it an assertion instead

Refused — exit 4 (the substrate, not the request): ENGINE_UNRESOLVED (profile resolves, driver or container does not), plus v-base’s own codes — NEEDS_CONFIRM (a mutation without --yes) and the run-lock/transport refusals.

Runtime — exit 1 (a broken contract between host and engine — each one names what the engine actually sent; meeting one usually means the engine’s VSL build is not the one this host was built against): NO_COMPLETENESS / BAD_COMPLETENESS · BAD_ROW / BAD_ORDINAL / BAD_FOLD · NO_MISSES / BAD_MISSES · WRONG_POPULATION (the engine answered a different population than asked — refused rather than relabelled) · NO_PROFILE / BAD_PROFILE · NO_RAWINDEX / BAD_RAWINDEX · SHORT_PAGE · BAD_LINE (a text line outside the value contract) · IDS_NO_DICTIONARY / BAD_IDS · INTEGRITY_FAIL (the envelope failed its delivery digest — the engine’s stamp and this host’s recomputation disagree, so bytes were lost or changed in between; the refusal prints both folds and both entry counts) / INTEGRITY_MISSING (the engine answered with no delivery digest at all, at a build that owes one) · OUT (the artifact could not be written — a local disk problem, not the engine) · SIZING_INVALID (selection size produced a row its own validator refuses — a defect in v-db, not in the selection or the engine). Two exit-1 codes are findings about the data, not defects: OVERFLOW (distribution past its distinct cap — the verdict rides the envelope with the measured lower bound) and any engine-typed U-VSL-* refusal relayed from the tables above.

Four of those codes are raised by a lower layer, and they are about the ENGINE’S IDENTITY rather than your request. SOURCE_PIN / SOURCE_DRIFT (exit 3) and INTEGRITY_FAIL / INTEGRITY_MISSING (exit 1) come from v-base, the shared client — not from this repo and not from the engine’s own refusal table. Every v db invocation verifies the installed source bytes of the whole VSL build before its first dispatch, and every success envelope carries a digest stamped by the engine that the host recomputes from the decoded values before any consumer sees it. Both fail closed. The reason they exist: on 2026-08-18 an engine ran one routine older than the build this host was generated against, and every gate the producer had passed while 7,166 tables silently lost their field descriptions. A build-version floor did not catch it — an exact source check does, and a digest catches the bytes that go missing after the engine is done being right. If you meet one, the engine and the host are not the pair they think they are: converge the build (v pkg install) and re-run rather than reading the answer.

The cross-reference kind vocabulary is OPEN

Section titled “The cross-reference kind vocabulary is OPEN”

U-VSL-ROW-IXTYPE above names seven kinds, and indexes reports them as a column — but the set is not closed, and treating it as closed is how a consumer ends up silently mis-handling a kind nobody anticipated. The classifier emits whatever the dictionary declares. Measured instance-wide on vehu (9,739 cross-references), three kinds fall outside the documented set:

kind vehu what it is
kwic 45 keyword-in-context — one entry per word of the indexed value
soundex 3 a phonetic key, so the stored key is deliberately not the value
unlisted 1 declared with no classifiable type, usually on a sub-file

The rule everywhere they appear: an unknown kind rides through by name and is counted — indexes publishes it, the sweep’s kinds histogram tallies it, and kindDocumented:false marks it. Every derivation from kind (walkable / enumerable / seek licensing) default-refuses a kind it does not know rather than guessing a safe-looking answer. A sub-file-heavy instance probably holds more than these three; that is the point of the design, not a gap in it.

11.7 Filter operators

Section titled “11.7 Filter operators”

The closed table — no client M is ever XECUTEd:

op meaning
= equal
'= not equal
> < >= <= ordered comparison, in the engine’s own collation
contains M [ containment
starts byte-prefix test
bound the field has a stored value node at all — takes no value
'bound it does not — the negation of the above

Two constraints:

  • Stored fields only. A computed field is refused, because filtering on it would execute site DD M once per candidate.
  • Predicates run against the INTERNAL value, not the external one. A filter on a pointer field takes an IEN, not a name; a filter on a date takes FileMan internal date form. This is deliberate — the external value is the retriever’s product, and requiring it per candidate would price every filter at the projection rate.
