bound is the one predicate that reads storage rather than a value. An absent node, a stored empty string and FileMan’s @ are three different states that every other operator sees identically, and bound names exactly one of them: is there a node here at all. Two consequences worth knowing:

  • It is the only operator admissible on a multiple — a multiple is bound iff its 0 node is set, which answers “does this record have any sub-entries?” without enumerating them. Every other operator on a multiple refuses U-VSL-ROW-FLTFIELD.
  • It is a two-token clause — --where '9.3 bound'. Supplying a value (--where '9.3 bound X') is a typed refusal, never an ignored argument.

Every verb that takes --where takes the same table: rows, find, count and distribution. There is one grammar, so a predicate you can express in one you can express in all of them.

A clause is ONE shell argument, taken byte-for-byte. VistA values carry commas (SMITH,JOHN is one name), and every --where treats a comma as data, never as a list separator — repeat the flag for AND: --where '.01 = SMITH,JOHN' --where '9.3 bound' is two predicates; --where '.01 = SMITH,JOHN' is one.

11.8 Default bounds

Section titled “11.8 Default bounds”

Engine defaults, overridable per invocation:

verb rows bytes examined elapsed
rows / find 4000 786432 75000 10000 ms
count — — 300000 / page 10000 ms / page
census — engine default engine default 10000 ms / page
distribution — engine default engine default 10000 ms / page
text --show — 786432 — —

bytes is derived from the smaller of the two engines’ maximum string lengths (YottaDB 1,048,576 against IRIS 3,641,144), which is why there is no engine branch anywhere in the byte accounting.

11.9 Files used in this guide

Section titled “11.9 Files used in this guide”

Every example uses a stock VistA file, so they reproduce on any instance:

file name why it appears
#3.1 TITLE small, one field — the simplest possible read and write target
#19 OPTION has a word-processing field (3.5 DESCRIPTION, sub-file 19.06) and thousands of records
#200 NEW PERSON the B index demo; .5 is a real IEN (POSTMASTER)
#757.02 CODES the blackout file — 855,565 records that DDR returns as zero rows

Write examples were run against a class=demo instance, at requested IENs FileMan would never allocate, and every fixture was deleted and every policy declaration revoked afterwards. Do the same.

12. Hardening — how far each claim has been tested

Section titled “12. Hardening — how far each claim has been tested”

v db went through a dedicated hardening effort (A: accuracy · P: portability · C: catalog), closed 2026-08-13. This section says what was actually proven, so a reader can tell a gated claim from an untested one.

12.1 The three properties that were gated

Section titled “12.1 The three properties that were gated”
property how it is held evidence
No false positives the capability sweep emits zero FALSE-POSITIVE rows; a DD-independent oracle, red-proven by planting 0 on both engines; the plant produced exactly 558 designed failures
No silent omissions '*' declares its exclusions in the envelope; every read carries a completeness block star ≡ dictionary minus declared exclusions on every non-vacuous file
Counts are honest three independent instruments must agree 15/15 oracle files, both engines; #757.02 = 855,565 by three paths

12.2 What “red-proven” means here, and why it is the load-bearing word

Section titled “12.2 What “red-proven” means here, and why it is the load-bearing word”

A gate that has only ever passed has not been shown able to fail. Every gate in this tool was made to fail on purpose, by planting the defect it exists to catch, before being trusted:

  • the index-truth gate: a planted wrong bucket
  • the write-path oracle: a real record through the shipped write path
  • the surface gate: a planted new verb
  • the catalog gate: a renamed JSON key, and a changed total
  • the portability floor: a planted below-floor FileMan version, on both engines

This matters because several defects in this tool’s history were instruments reporting confidently wrong things — a harness that read the opposite of the truth on one engine; a suite that aborted after its first case and reported 0/0 while the lane stayed green.

12.3 Portability — measured, not assumed

Section titled “12.3 Portability — measured, not assumed”
  • A version floor at the request door. Below the declared FileMan version (22.2, the measured floor) every guarded verb refuses typed rather than degrading. 45 dispatch verbs = 15 exempt + 30 guarded, and the split is gated so a verb added later is protected without anyone remembering.
  • Which projection tier travels was measured corpus-wide — external carried 180 rendering divergences across two instances where internal carried 1. Every read now declares it (§7.9).
  • Every result says which instance produced it, refusals included.

12.4 The catalog is gated against its own generator

Section titled “12.4 The catalog is gated against its own generator”

A recorded fixture (51 real census pages) is replayed on every make check and the regenerated artifact must be byte-identical — writtenAt is the single excluded field and that exclusion is itself checked, so a second varying field reds. The fixture’s faithfulness is measured, not assumed: its replay hashes identically to a live whole-instance run.

12.5 The parity instrument red-proves itself on every run

Section titled “12.5 The parity instrument red-proves itself on every run”

Proof 1 (§8.25) claims two runs of one set against one instance produce the same data. The comparison that grades it — scripts/parity-compare.py — cannot run inside make check, because its inputs are two live bundle runs and those are not committed. What make check keeps alive instead is the comparison’s ability to fail: three planted differences (a dropped field, a component silently omitted, a payload byte flipped), plus the controls that prove each exclusion is by name rather than a normaliser — a manifest field beside an excluded one still reds, a real argv difference beside the normalised --out still reds, a changed page aggregate still reds — and the fail-closed arms (a missing record, a missing payload, an incomplete run, two different instances). A comparison that has never failed is indistinguishable from one that cannot.

What is excluded, and why it is not a normaliser. Three things differ between two runs by construction, and each is a digest over something that carries a timestamp rather than a fact about the data: the manifest’s writtenAt, the pass-level digest taken over that manifest, and the record’s schema digest. The digest is dropped by enumerated name — and the document it stands for is then compared in its place, with only its own timestamp excluded, so two runs shipping different record shapes still red. The run-owned --out inside each component’s argv is dropped the same way, by name.

One more block is folded rather than dropped: details.pages. Pages stop on the engine’s elapsed and byte budgets, so two runs split one file differently while emitting the same rows — measured on vehu, one component byte-identical across four runs with page 1 emitting 599 rows in one and 611 in another. The boundaries are not a comparable fact; distinct/emitted/ filtered summed are, and that is what is compared. examined is not: a page that stops on the byte budget examines the record that did not fit, so its total is emitted plus one per bytes-stopped page — measured 1,741 · 1,739 · 1,740 · 1,740 across those same four byte-identical runs, against 3 · 1 · 2 · 2 bytes-stopped pages. It counts page seams.

12.6 What hardening did NOT establish

Section titled “12.6 What hardening did NOT establish”
  • Correctness of estimate — no oracle exists (§8.6).
  • Anything beyond two instances at FileMan 22.2, both demo data. Every percentage in this guide is of that corpus.
  • The sampled-size pass is not under the catalog gate (the fixture is captured --no-sizes), and estimatedBytes is a published number.

13. Limitations, risks, and what to do about them

Section titled “13. Limitations, risks, and what to do about them”

Ordered by how much damage the risk does if you do not know about it.

# limitation risk mitigation
1 --where is a SCAN, not an index seek. No optimizer chooses an index for you A filter on a 2.5M-row table walks every row. Measured: a reject-all screen scanned 2.14M records to return nothing Ask first: --explain reports which index can position which clause, the cost class, and the command to run — reading zero data pages (§8.8). Then find <file> <index> for the seek it names. Bound every read (--max, --examined, --elapsed). --where stays a convenience on already-bounded sets — the planner proposes, it does not rewrite your query
2 A record is a TREE, not a row. Non-word-processing multiples are excluded from --fields '*' An extract that reads only the top level silently loses nested tables The exclusion is declared in the envelope on every star read — check projection.excluded. Read sub-files with --parent; distribution <file> <multiple> gives depth
3 estimatedBytes is sampled (≤20 records/file) A skewed file is sized badly; a migration plan built on it can be far off The sample basis is printed in words. For anything load-bearing, count the file and measure real records
4 claimed (FileMan’s stored count) is often wrong — 121 of 2,919 files on vehu; #81 CPT claims 26,877 against a real 2,351 Sizing or reconciling against the header is wrong by up to 183× Always use walked. claimed ships beside it only as an integrity signal
5 External rendering is instance-specific — 180 divergent subjects vs internal’s 1; every external date in FileMan’s MMM DD, YYYY grammar differs between the two instances measured A parser written against one site does not span another Use --tier internal for machine consumption. Every read declares its tier’s contract
6 Most cross-references are not walkable — 3,434 of vehu’s 9,739 are mumps-kind, and a seek refuses them “There is an index on that” is frequently false in the way that matters indexes <file> inventories both registers with walkable, subtree and the key class; indexes --all does the whole instance in seconds. When a seek refuses, find … --raw still reads the cross-reference’s stored entries — the access paths the database was designed around, which a seek locks out
6a What points AT one record has no affordable answer “Who references this patient?” cannot be counted per record without a full scan Measured and declined 2026-08-14, not overlooked: the seek that would make it cheap exists for 8.7 % of inbound pointer fields on vehu (§14.1). refs --all answers the question at file level completely; per record, use find --raw on a specific index you have checked
6b A variable pointer’s stored root may name a file the dictionary does not declare such a reference could be named but not addressed CLOSED 2026-08-15 (VSL*1.0*63). 9.3 % of #100’s references store an undeclared root; --ids now resolves them against ^DIC(f,0,"GL") — FileMan’s own ownership statement — and marks them resolvedBy: "root" so the provenance stays legible. A root no file claims is still named, never guessed
7 find’s key bounds are in STORED, COLLATED key space The same command returns different boundaries on two sites Treat bounds as site-specific; the instance block says which site a boundary came from
8 Word-processing text must not be ^-pieced — 196 of 45,295 OPTION description lines contain a literal ^ Re-splitting corrupts the text Read WP fields with text --show; they project as line arrays, never ^-pieced
9 Six files cannot be read normally (nested-root, subfile-anomaly, nodata) A query against them returns nonsense or nothing They are named in the census with a typed state — never silently absent
10 Two instances, FileMan 22.2, both demo data Nothing here evidences a production site or another FileMan flavor The onboarding procedure (guides/v-db-onboarding-a-new-vista.md) is what a third instance runs on first contact
11 Writes are single-record and audited; there is no bulk write path A bulk correction is many calls Deliberate. delete is dry-run by default; every mutation is confirmed, attributed and audited engine-side
12 An engine visit is bounded and can be stopped mid-answer A page can be partial Every read carries a completeness block naming why it stopped. Branch on it, never on row count

14. Planned work — what is not here yet

Section titled “14. Planned work — what is not here yet”

Recorded so the absences are known rather than discovered. Items struck through below have since been built — the strike-through is deliberate: a planned-work list that quietly deletes what shipped stops being a record of what was missing and why.

14.1 Querying — the next effort

Section titled “14.1 Querying — the next effort”

This list is now closed. It was written when v db could seek an index (find), filter (--where) and aggregate (count, distribution) but had none of the connective tissue that makes those usable correctly and affordably. All four gaps were built in the query-plane effort, 2026-08-13 to 2026-08-14, and the entries are struck through rather than deleted so the record of what was missing survives:

  1. An instance-wide index inventory — built 2026-08-14: indexes --all inventories every cross-reference of every file, walkability included, in one engine-side pass.
  2. A path from predicate to index — built 2026-08-14: --explain reports which index can position which predicate, under a licensing rule that will not propose a seek it cannot defend.
  3. An instance-wide pointer (foreign-key) graph — built 2026-08-14: refs --all sweeps the whole dictionary into an edge artifact, and a closure over it takes under a second.
  4. Honest cost signalling on the scan path — built 2026-08-14: --explain reports the cost CLASS (seek · seek+filter · walk · walk+filter) and, from a named census artifact, the population size. It still does not estimate selectivity, and says so.

The same effort also built the populations those four gaps assumed: --iens for a named record set, --with-multiples for the decoded tree, find --raw for the access paths a seek refuses, --ids for navigable identity, and fields-profile for which columns of a wide sparse file carry data at all.

Two things did not get built, and both are decisions rather than backlog. The string surface — a query language over the flags — waits on a consumer that cannot pass structured flags — the RPC face, say; until then the flags are the surface.

Per-record referrer counts (refs --ien) were measured and declined, 2026-08-14 — not deferred for lack of time. Counting what points at this one record affordably needs the pointing field to carry a walkable, identity-keyed cross-reference, and it usually does not: measured over the inbound pointers of the oracle files, the seek is available for 8.7 % of them on vehu and 1.6 % on foia, with a ceiling of 15.3 % on both. The reason is structural — 44.9 % of pointing fields carry no cross-reference at all, almost always on files that are indexed, just not on the pointer. VistA indexes what records are looked up by, not what they point at. The file-level question is fully answered by refs --all; the per-record one stays open.

14.2 Also absent

Section titled “14.2 Also absent”
  • Sort order on reads — the walk is IEN order; there is no ORDER BY.
  • Whole-file reindex — single-record reindex only, deliberately.
  • Data-dictionary writes — v db reads the DD; it does not change it.
  • Bulk write (limitation 11).

15. Out of scope — decided, not deferred

Section titled “15. Out of scope — decided, not deferred”

These are rulings, not gaps. v db provides the tooling to browse, extract, catalog, scope, query, and manage the data in one VistA system. Everything below is somebody else’s job, on purpose.

not in v db why where it lives
Analytics of any kind — including of v db’s own exports keeping the tool robust, reliable and cleanly scoped; an analysis path inside a measurement tool blurs what is measured and what is inferred downstream, from the exported JSONL
Cross-VistA comparison a different product at a higher bar — it needs full-fidelity DD extraction from two or more systems. Conflating them would let a catalog-grade comparison masquerade as a fidelity-grade one downstream, from two exports
Data classification of any kind (this repo carried PIKS until 2026-08) a label is a purely analytical derivative of the export — an inference on top of what this tool measures, never a measurement. A ~3,860-line classifier was REMOVED in 2026-08 for exactly this reason, and the PIKS line RETIRED 2026-08-17 the bundle analysis, derived from the export
National-dictionary labels the national dictionary is incomplete and untrusted today, and an untrusted source must not be joined into an artifact whose charter is that every cell is a fact or a named non-fact a consumer joins them itself, at whatever trust level it can defend
Ranking, scoring, proposing normalizations the machine narrows and explains; it does not decide the human, downstream
A UI or a browser the output is an input the bundle explorer, where the human interaction happens
Storage, journaling, backup, engine tuning engine-level, below the VistA line the m toolchain

The seam between them is the JSONL. v db exports the data, the metadata and the data dictionary as JSONL plus a manifest that says which instance it came from, when, what was asked, and whether the artifact is complete (the input contract). Everything downstream reads that file. The dependency runs one way — consumers read v db’s output; v db does not read theirs.
